(ESPM), São Paulo.

RESUMO

O objetivo deste trabalho foi investigar as relações peculiares e idiossincráticas que os
consumidores cultivam com as marcas, sejam elas negativas, positivas, neutras ou ambíguas.
Nossa pesquisa revelou que as marcas funcionam como sinalizadoras de identidade pessoal,
carregam significados simbólicos, atuam como parceiras em relacionamentos, enfatizam
sentimentos polarizados e desencadeiam comportamentos e emoções negativos. Com base em
uma abordagem fenomenológica, aplicamos uma gama de métodos qualitativos para investigar
as relações entre consumidor e marca, incluindo entrevistas em profundidade, netnografia e
dados secundários. Contribuímos para a teoria ao identificar e definir 34 relacionamentos
idiossincráticos nov os ou pouco teorizad os, como terapeutas/pacientes, vigaristas/ trouxas,
prazeres com remorso e agnosticismo. Uma segunda contribuição diz respeito a como essas
relações auxiliam os consumidores em seus projetos de identidade, influenciando seus eus
individuais e sociais. A terceira contribuição consiste em uma proposta de modelo para explicar
as relações negativas entre consumidor e marca, abrangendo personalidades sombrias da marca,
avaliação de situações, emoções suscitadas, relacionamentos falhos, bem como mecanismos e
comportamentos de enfrentamento. Este trabalho também tem implicações sociais relacionadas
à saúde mental (por exemplo, bullying e dependência), à proteção dos direitos do consumidor
e aos Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável da ONU.

Palavras-chave: relacionamento com marcas, branding, relações idiossincráticas da marca ,
comportamento do consumidor, gestão de marcas.

ALVES, Antonio Pedro Cruz Costa. Brand relationship idiosyncrasy: the peculiar bonds
consumers have with brands they love and hate . 2026. Doctoral Thesis (PhD in Business
Administration) – Postgraduate Research Program in Administration, Higher School of
Advertising and Marketing / Escola Superior de Propaganda e Marketing (ESPM), São Paulo.

ABSTRACT

The objective of this work was to investigate the peculiar and idiosyncratic relationships that
consumers foster with brands, either negative, positive, neutral, or ambiguous . Our research
revealed how brands work as beacons of self -identity, carry symbolic meanings, function as
relationship partners, emphasise polarised feelings, and trigger negative behaviours and
emotions. Drawing on a phenomenological approach, we applied a range of qualitative methods
to investigate consumer -brand relationships, including in -depth interviews, netnography, and
secondary data. We contribute to theory by identifying and defining 34 new or less theorised
idiosyncratic relationships, such as therapists/patients, crooks/suckers, guilty pleasures, and
agnostics. A second contribution regards how these relationships help consumers with their
identity projects, influencing their individual and social selves. The third contribution concerns
a proposal for a framework to explain negative consumer -brand relationships, encompassing
dark brand personalities, appraisal of events, elicited emotions, flawed relationships, and coping
mechanisms and behaviours. This work also has social implications regarding mental health
(e.g., bullying and addiction) , consumer rights protection, and the UN’s Sustainable
Development Goals.

Keywords: brand relationship, branding, brand relationship idiosyncrasy, consumer behaviour,
brand management.

CHAPTER 1 - INTRODUCTION

1.1 Motivation for the research
Several authors have studied brand relationships since the seminal work of Fournier
(1998), who introduced the brand relationship quality (BRQ) framework and examined the
various m eaningful relationships between brands and consumers (Alvarez et al., 2023) .
Consumers develop deep emotional bonds with brands, which vary in polarity and strength
(Fetscherin et al., 2019; Fetscherin & Veloutsou, 2024) . In this sense, t he brand relationship
research stream expanded the brand loyalty construct, considering the interconnections with
brands as a dynamic phenomenon more in line with the post -modern fragmented consumer
(Fournier & Yao, 1997). Researchers have delved into the myriad of relationships and followed
several streams related to brand trust, brand communities, brand love, brand cult, self -
connection, culture, and storytelling (Fetscherin & Heinrich, 2015).
First, scholars explored the positive emotions and behaviours associated with the
connection between brands and consumer s. The brand love construct was proposed , which
comprises positive emotional associations, self -brand integration, and passion -driven
behaviours (Batra et al., 2012). In this sense, consumption products are used to create meanings,
extending the self (Belk, 1988) , as the effort dispensed in loved objects helps consumers
establish a coherent self and solves potential existential conflicts (Ahuvia, 2005). Brand love is
also associated with brand loyalty and positive word of mouth, with the effect being more
significant in h edonic categories (Carroll & Ahuvia, 2006) . Depending on the consumer’s
susceptibility to influence and the brand’s self -expression, consumers can experience
harmonious or obsessive passion (Swimberghe et al., 2014).
Academics later studied negative emotions related to brand -consumer relationships. In
contrast with brand love and other positive-related constructs, brand hate, avoidance,
retaliation, anti-consumption, and other subversive behaviours were identified (Wilson et al.,
2022) but are less theorised (Mushtaq et al., 2024; Yadav & Chakrabarti, 2022) . The intensity
of consumers’ negative emotions towards brands can range from severe to mild, influenced by
personality traits (Kucuk, 2019) . Brand hate has active and passive components, with
behavioural outcomes including c omplaints and negative word of mouth (Zarantonello et al.,
2016; Zhang & Laroche, 2020).

16
Not only have studies investigated negative and positive emotions and behaviours
related to brands, but they have also explored polarised relationships. Oppositional brand
loyalty refers to the meanings consumers derive from brands they consume, rather than those
they do not (Muñiz & Hamer, 2001) . Identifying with a brand makes consumers oppose rival
brands, as these rivals m ight threaten t heir self -concept (Liao et al., 2021) . Scholars have
discussed brand rivalries and found that they are related to schadenfreude (feeling happy at
others’ misfortunes) (Phillips-Melancon & Dalakas, 2014), humour and ridicule (Ewing et al.,
2013), an increase in the likelihood of adopting new products (S. A. Thompson & Sinha, 2008),
and enhance brand and consumer group distinctiveness (Berendt et al., 2018) . The effect of
polarisation might also be harmful, with a negative impact on returns but a lower perception of
risk (X. Luo, Raithel, et al., 2013; X. Luo, Wiles, et al., 2013). More recently, brand polarisation
has been studied as a more general phenomenon, with scholars arguing that rivalry is a
particular type (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019, 2024).
Apart from studies on individual relationships and emotions, another academic stream
examined brand communities and how they foster deep connections among consumer groups
and brands. Brand communities partake in rituals, foster a sense of members’ distinctiveness
from outsiders, and share a sense of moral responsibility (Muñiz & O’Guinn, 2001) . They
develop collective and collaborative values via practices, behaviours, and performances (Schau
et al., 2009). Brand communities enhance community engagement, though they also stimulate
reactance to normative rules (Algesheimer et al., 2005) and heighten tensions against the brand
to preserve the community’s independence (Kornum et al., 2017).
The intense emotions associated with brand -consumer relationships and a sense of
community are intrinsic to how people understand themselves. Consumers’ self -concept is
based on contrasting ingroups versus outgroups (Tajfel & Turner, 2004). Therefore, individuals
have a stronger self-brand connection with brands that are consistent with their ingroup (Escalas
& Bettman, 2005), a s they seek self -congruity (Sirgy, 1982, 2018) . The brand -consumer
connection can go further when individuals feel an identity fusion with brands (Swann et al.,
2012), being immune to transgressions and negative feedback (Lin & Sung, 2014).
Although brand relationship scholars focused on positive and negative emotions and
behaviours towards brands, explored the functioning of brand communities, and investigated
brand-self interactions, few studies explored intense and idiosyncratic relationships between
consumers and brands, focusing more on particular types of relationships such as brand love,
hate, and friendships (Alvarez et al., 2023). Moreover, brand hate and avoidance remain nascent

17
topics in the literature, as scholars have paid more attention to positive relationships such as
brand loyalty , love, and attachment (Mushtaq et al., 2024; Roy et al., 2022; Yadav &
Chakrabarti, 2022) . Regarding brand polarisation, which comprises positive and negative
emotions towards brands, the topic is still scarcely studied (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019) and
underdeveloped (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2024).
1.2 Research objectives
First, we explore consumers’ idiosyncratic connections with their most loved and
admired brands in light of the consumer-brand relationship theory and consumer culture theory
(CCT). The CCT examines how consumers perceive meanings embedded in brands and
consumer products to make sense of themse lves and incorporate them into their lifestyles
(Arnould & Thompson, 2005). Second, our work investigates some brands that elicit polarised
consumer feelings, as they have lovers and haters. Brand polarisation comprises four
dimensions: brand passion, self -brand benchmarking, intra -group identification, and inter -
group dissociation (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2024). Third, this thesis explores the negative or dark
side of the relationship with brands, focusing on negative feelings and behaviours . Brand hate
is a multidimensional construct (Yadav & Chakrabarti, 2022) that includes negative emotions
(anger, contempt, fear, disappointment , etc.), which lead to reactions such as attack (negative
word of mouth) , avoidance (reduction or cessation) or approach (complaining and protest)
(Zarantonello et al., 2016).
In summary, our doctoral thesis explores consumers’ peculiar relationships with brands,
which can be positive or negative, and brands that provoke both polarising feelings, answering
a call to investigate new brand-consumer relationship types (Alvarez et al., 2023) . To clarify
what we understand by idiosyncratic relationships, we provide the following definition: brand
relationship idiosyncrasy concerns the peculiar and characteristic bonds, mannerisms, habits,
and mental conditions that consumers have towards brands, which are susceptible to particular
stimuli. We intend to answer the following research question: How do consumers have intense,
idiosyncratic relationships with brands they love and hate?
We adopted qualitative methods to better understand the idiosyncratic relationships
consumers have with brands, a research stream that remains underdeveloped and less theorised.
While positivist ontology and quantitative studies focus on measuring reality and proposing
general laws, interpretative approaches hold that reality is socially constructed and emphasise
understanding behaviour rather than predicting it (Hudson & Ozanne, 1988) . Choosing a

18
qualitative approach for the current thesis is adequate since few qualitative studies researched
the different types of brand relationships (love, passion, hate, friendships, addiction, and others)
in the past years, and the most prominent methodological approaches were Structural Equation
Modeling (SEM) and experiments (Alvarez et al., 2023; Gilal et al., 2023; Mushtaq et al., 2024;
Yadav & Chakrabarti, 2022).
1.3 Contributions
This research examines why consumers have peculiar bonds with the brands they love
and hate, unearthing new types of idiosyncratic relationships and how they are enacted. More
specifically, we contribute to theories of the self in consumer behaviour and branding, exploring
their interconnections with brand identity, personality, and core values. The intensity of the
relationship can be beneficial, nurturing passion and love (Gilal et al., 2023), helping structure
the self and provide meaning (Fetscherin & Heinrich, 2015), or might be associated with hate
(Mushtaq et al., 2024; Roy et al., 2022; Zarantonello et al., 2016; Zhang & Laroche, 2020) ,
addiction (Cui et al., 2018; Mrad et al., 2020; Mrad & Cui, 2017) , and aversion (Park et al.,
2013b).
More specifically, t his thesis contributes to consumer -brand relationship theory as
follows: (1) by theorising and defining the idiosyncratic relationships; (2) by understanding
how the relationships affect the consumer self and are a reflection of culture; (3) by proposing
a flawed consumer-brand relationship framework to explain the connections among dark brand
personalities, relationships, emotions, and coping mechanisms . The practical implications of
our study are to show marketers how consumers interact passionately with their brands and how
businesses can respond, nurture, foster, or manage these unique relationships.
1.4 Thesis structure
To accomplish our goals, we divided our doctoral thesis into three articles. The first
article focused on the positive pole of the idiosyncratic brand-consumer relationship, explaining
why consumers have tattooed brands. The second article discussed brands that elicit polarised
consumer reactions, examining the different motivations that lead consumers to either love or
hate them. The third and last paper explored flawed consumer-brand relationships, proposing a
framework to explain the interactions with negative brand personalities, elicited emotions, and
coping mechanisms.

19
Figure 1.1 shows the overall structure of the doctoral thesis. The first article on brand
tattoos represents the positive pole of brand relationship idiosyncrasy: consumers’ most alluring
feelings toward a brand. The second article concerns the negative and positive emotions and
behaviours that polarising brands elicit in consumers . The third and final article is at the
negative pole, discussing brands consumers dislike. The three articles examine consumers’
idiosyncratic behaviours when engaging with brands.

CHAPTER 2 – POSITIVE POLE: BRAND LOVE VIA BRAND TATTOOS1

2.1 Introduction
Consumers have relationships with brands as they would with people (Fournier, 1998;
Fournier & Alvarez, 2012). They develop deep emotional bonds with brands, sharing affinities
and enthusiasm with other like -minded individuals in communities (Fetscherin et al., 2021;
Fetscherin & Veloutsou, 2024). Scholars have studied the deep consumer-brand bonds, such as
brand love (Batra et al., 2012; Carroll & Ahuvia, 2006; Rahman et al., 2021) , brand passion
(Gilal et al., 2023; Swimberghe et al., 2014), brand attachment (Park et al., 2010; Shimul, 2022;
Thomson et al., 2005), brand engagement (Fernandes & Moreira, 2019), and brand pride (Kaur
& Verma, 2024) . Strong connections with brands have also been theorised under negative
relationships of brand hate (Mushtaq et al., 2024; Zarantonello et al., 2016; Zhang & Laroche,
2020) and, more recently, polarised brands, which attract passionate feelings of love and hate
(Monahan et al., 2023; Osuna Ramírez et al., 2024).
Although studies have advanced in understanding consumer-brand connections, there is
a gap regarding new brand relationship types to capture the diversity of connections, their
valence and strength (Alvarez et al., 2023; Fournier & Alvarez, 2013) , and how they interact
with the consumers’ identity projects. The literature is also silent about multiple and dynamic
relationships consumers have with the same brand, as scholars have theorised only about single
steady relationship types (e.g., brand lo ve, pride, addiction, friendship, and hate) (Alvarez et
al., 2023) or changes from one to another (e.g., love turning to hate or vice versa) (Grégoire &
Fisher, 2008; Langner et al., 2016; Zarantonello et al., 2018).
Consumer Culture Theory (CCT) scholars complement the brand relationship literature
describing consumers’ profound feelings for their beloved brands and discuss consumers’
identity projects under a fragmented sense of self (Arnould & Thompson, 2005) . The
understanding that people use objects and brands as part of their extended self (Belk, 1988) is
an evolving set of ideas which is transitioning to digitalised (Belk, 2013) and transhuman (Lima
& Belk, 2024) versions of personhood. Consumer researchers are shifting their view from
considering people to have stable core selves to understanding them as a network of assembled
experiences, practices, and narratives (C. J. Thompson, 2024) . This view has also been

21
discussed under the dialectical division of the consumer’s self and body as agentic and stable
versus unbounded and dynamic (Appau et al., 2020; Preece et al., 2024).
This paper discusses particular and multiple interrelations between brands and
consumers, epitomised by brand tattoos. There are few studies focused on extremely sturdy
connections between consumers and brands, including brand sacredness (Fuschillo et al., 2024;
Wang et al., 2019) and brand addiction (Cui et al., 2018; Ghorbanzadeh, 2024; Mrad & Cui,
2017). From this perspective, brand tattoos represent a deep bond between consumers and
brands but are only tangentially mentioned in the literature. For instance, studies show Harley-
Davidson aficionados tattooing brand symbols to represent their devotion (Rahman et al., 2021;
Schouten & McAlexander, 1995).
The interrelatedness between loyal consumers and tattooed brands seems
straightforward due to the identification of the self with the brand lifestyle (Orend & Gagné,
2009). However, a small number of studies have discussed the meaning of tattooed brands and
have not explored it from the consumer perspective, focusing on sponsorship tattooing
(Weidner et al., 2016) , tattooist perceptions related to brand tattoos (Bengtsson et al., 2005) ,
the body commodification by tattooed corporate logos (Orend & Gagné, 2009) or the extension
of brands to the body via advertising (Bjerrisgaard et al., 2013).
Scholars have explored the relationship between tattoos and post-modern consumption,
which considers the individual fragmented, seeking freedom of movement and not subjecting
to a single reality or way of being (Firat & Venkatesh, 1995). Tattoos are in the middle of the
fragmented tension between the post -modern self and the search for a coherent identity
(Patterson & Schroeder, 2010) . Tattooing brings out contemporary cultural contradictions,
showing a dynamic tension between durable versus transient consumption (Steadman, Banister,
et al., 2023; Steadman et al., 2019). It exposes the body’s and identity’s malleability, although
permanently marking them (Patterson, 2018), and fits the self -narrative as points of reference
that allow individuals to control their lives and express their idiosyncrasies (Oksanen &
Turtiainen, 2005).
This study aims to analyse the intense bond between consumers and their tattooed
brands by understanding why they tattoo them and theorising implications for the brand
relationship literature. Since there is scarce theorisation about branding and tattoos, this work
aims to fill this lacuna by contributing to the literature regarding consumer-brand relationships,
self, body, and tattoos and presenting the results from consumer interviews. Interpretative

22
Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) was adopted to explore the following research question:
what types of relationships do consumers have with the brands they tattoo?
This research has two main contributions to the literature. First, it extends the brand
relationship literature by discussing new types of consumer -brand connections uncovered
through brand tattoos that are new or scarcely theorised (Alvarez et al., 2023; Fournier &
Alvarez, 2013) : best friends forever (BFF), family ties, childhood buddies, teammates,
dealers/addicts, therapists/patients, gurus/disciples, soulmates, partisans, and vintage mates.
Second, this study reveals that consumers can have multiple and dynamic relationships with the
same brand, impacting their identity projects. Brand tattoos are polysemic and incomplete
symbols representing a desire for a stable sense of self.
2.2 Literature Review
2.2.1 Consumer-Brand Relationships
The relationship between consumers and brands has been extensively researched over
the past decades since the first seminal papers in the 1990s (Fetscherin & Heinrich, 2015;
Fetscherin & Veloutsou, 2024) . This research stream assumes that individuals see brands as
relationship partners (Fournier, 1998), while the level of passion determines the strength of the
connection (Fetscherin et al., 2019). Consumers develop feelings and want to be close to brands
(Veloutsou, 2007) , cultivating several interconnections (Bagozzi et al., 2021) and
psychologically benefiting from engaging with them (Razmus, 2025).
A variety of relationships have been proposed and analysed, such as arranged marriages,
best friendships, and enmities (Bagozzi et al., 2021; Fournier, 1998) . Even after years of
development from the original brand relationship typology (Fournier, 1998), only brand love
came up as a core construct in the last decades (Alvarez et al., 2023). There is a need for more
studies concerning new brand relationship types to capture a broader aspect of the phenomenon
(Alvarez et al., 2023).
Moreover, scholars have not focused on consumers’ multiple and dynamic relationships
with the same brand, studying single positive and negative consumer -brand bonds (Fetscherin
et al., 2019, 2021; Fetscherin & Heinrich, 2015; Fetscherin & Veloutsou, 2024) . Existing
research has focused on changes in the relationship (Alvarez et al., 2021), such as love turning
to hate (Grégoire et al., 2009) , ruptures that lead to divorce (Ferraz & Dallabrida, 2024) ,
functional, symbolic, and moral transgressions triggering consumer animosity (Tolunay &

23
Veloutsou, 2025), in paths that evolve from neutral or disliking to brand love (Langner et al.,
2016) or trajectories culminating in brand hate (Zarantonello et al., 2018) . Another recent
research stream has discussed polarised brands, which simultaneously have haters and lovers
(X. Luo, Raithel, et al., 2013; X. Luo, Wiles, et al., 2013; Osuna Ramírez et al., 2024) but not
examined multiple or mixed relationship types with the same brand (e.g., love-hate).
The literature has also focused more on positive relationships than negative ones
(Bagozzi et al., 2021; Brandão & Popoli, 2022) , which led some researchers to propose that
brand relationship should be defined as a bond based on positive experiences (Schreuder et al.,
2024). Scholars have explored the strength and intensity of relationships, proposing constructs
such as brand attachment (Park et al., 2010; Shimul, 2022; Thomson et al., 2005) , brand love
(Batra et al., 2012; Carroll & Ahuvia, 2006; Rahman et al., 2021; Robertson et al., 2022), brand
passion (Gilal et al., 2023; Swimberghe et al., 2014), brand engagement (Fernandes & Moreira,
2019), brand spirituality/sacredness (Fuschillo et al., 2024; S. Luo & Hamlin, 2022; Wang et
al., 2019), and brand pride (Helm et al., 2016; Kaur & Verma, 2024).
Although consumers seem to benefit from positive interactions with brands, they might
as well develop addictions to fulfil self -expression needs and status (Mrad et al., 2020) , have
compulsive and obsessive uncontrollable urges (Cui et al., 2018; Le, 2021) , be influenced by
their dark personality traits intensifying competitive behaviours (Shimul et al., 2025) or develop
brand addiction as a consequence from love and jealousy (Ghorbanzadeh, 2024). Addiction is
just one negative side of consumer-brand relationships since consumers can be subversive and
incorporate harmful behaviours, leading them to engage proactively or reactively against firms
(Wilson et al., 2022). They might take extreme measures like brand sabotage (Kähr et al., 2016)
and anti-brand activism (Dessart et al., 2020; Rodrigues et al., 2021; Romani et al., 2015) , or
less strong reactions such as brand avoidance (Lee et al., 2009; Odoom et al., 2019) .
Nevertheless, most studies explored hate towards brands as a more general phenomenon,
characterised as an attitude, motivation, or emotion (Mushtaq et al., 2024) . There is
multidimensionality in brand hate, which comprises a constellation of emotions such as dislike,
fear, and hatred (Yadav & Chakrabarti, 2022; Zhang & Laroche, 2020) , with consumers
showing passive or active brand hate (Zarantonello et al., 2016).
In sum, the literature review shows a need for further studies concerning new types of
brand relationships and a lack of investigation of multiple and dynamic relationships with the
same brand. There was a concentration on positive relationships and less on negative ones, with
few discussions related to mixed feelings.

24
2.2.2 Self & Body
The way that consumer research scholars discuss the mind -self-body interrelations is
first related to a contraposition between the inner self (personal) and the outer self (social)
(Featherstone, 1982, 2010; Kuuru, 2022), which is a dynamic socio-cultural process that varies
in a continuum (Turner et al., 1994) . The social structures are embodied by constituting
practices external to the person (Murphy et al., 2018), reflecting preferred social meanings and
ideologies of self-control (Thompson & Hirschman, 1995). For instance, there are tensions and
anxieties related to the mothering body against the exercising body (Spotswood & Gurrieri,
2024), advertising depicting women’s bodies (Balog, 2024; Joy & Venkatesh, 1994) , normal
versus deviant personal appearances (Holbrook et al., 1998), or changes during pregnancy and
immigrants’ acculturation (Min & Peñaloza, 2019).
The second focus is related to the fragmentation of the post-modern self (Belk, 2017) as
the extended self (Belk, 1988) transitions from a coherent and stable state to an assemblage of
life narratives structured under consumer distributed networks (Thompson, 2024). Consumers
are agentic and self-determined individuals with a core stable self and clear internal and external
boundaries. At the same time, they are also unfinished and dynamic dividuals with many porous
composites in which social structures are embedded (Appau et al., 2020) . Multiple
embodiments separate the person from the self-identity via disembodiment and re-embodiment
(Min & Peñaloza, 2019; Preece et al., 2024) , which can be a permanent or transient process
(Appau et al., 2020) . The fragmentation can eventually lead to merging with technology or
creating new versions of transhumans or even post -humans that transcend bodies and selves
(Lima & Belk, 2024).
The third dialectical discussion in consumption related to mind -body-self regards
perceptions and practices. Several forms of embodiment happen when consumers are involved
in bodily sensorial engagements that affect their behaviours and thoughts (Merleau-Ponty,
1962; Zanette et al., 2024) . For example, body techniques like swimming and motorcycling
help people embed shared knowledge and social practices (Murphy et al., 2018) . Consumer
subcultures mingle mind, body, and senses via embodiment (Kuuru, 2022), which can help
people feel inside and outside themselves, culminating in a cathartic moment (Preece et al.,
2024).
Consumer research also deliberates on imaginative and subjective relationships between
consumers, brands, and bodies. Even though it is impossible to escape one’s body when using

25
masks, tattooing the skin, and putting on makeup, people are projected into an imaginary
utopian body when doing so (Foucault, 2006; Roux & Belk, 2019) . In this sense, brands and
consumption objects are imbued with aesthetic meanings, passing through a process of
aestheticisation that transforms them into sublime, beautiful, and moving things (Dagalp &
Hartmann, 2022). The brands’ aestheticisation is incorporated and embedded by consumers via
their bodies and tattoos.
To summarise, scholars have contraposed inner (personal) versus outer (social) selves,
exploring the fragmentation of the consumer identity. There is a change from a coherent state
to an assemblage of narratives and distributed networks, as consumers are d ivided between
individuals with single, finished, and stable selves to dividuals with multiple, unfinished, and
porous characteristics. The meanings, subcultures, and knowledge are incorporated and
embedded by consumers via aesthetics, perceptions and social practices.
2.2.3 Tattoos, Culture, and Consumers
It would be possible to consider tattoos as symbols without meaning, fashion accessories
or temporary body modifications (Sweetman, 1999) since they are increasingly consumed and
widespread (Roux & Belk, 2019; Sierra et al., 2013) . However, tattoos are different from
consumption objects because they are permanent, cannot be divorced from their production,
and are a combination of body modification and cultural artefacts (Sweetman, 1999). Tattoos
are time markers as they inscribe memories on the body, bring continuity and stability
(Steadman et al., 2019) , delineate the body’s limitations (Fisher, 2002) , and are used as a
medium to cope with life transitions (Krtalić et al., 2025) . However, neither identity nor
meanings attributed to tattoos are necessarily fixed in time (Owens et al., 2023; Steadman,
Banister, et al., 2023).
As the self acquires meaning when expressed through an assemblage of narratives
(Thompson, 2024), the same process occurs with tattoos. People tattoo themselves to control
their lives and to serve as reference marks for their stories and personal myths (Oksanen &
Turtiainen, 2005; Velliquette et al., 2006). Since the body is intimate and controllable, it offers
a safe, close, and unique place for tattoos that remind deceased loved ones (Steadman, Medway,
et al., 2023) . Tattoo consumption reproduces a coherent and personalised narrative that
connects the past, present, and future (Patterson, 2018).
Some authors examined how people tattoo themselves and their motivations, from
aesthetics to personal narratives, affiliations, resistance, and spirituality (Wohlrab et al., 2007).

26
Body art is part of the extended self and brings satisfaction, but it might also lead to addiction
and regret (Velliquette et al., 1998) . Once considered a form of transgression, stigmatisation
and marginalisation, tattoos are increasingly accepted by society, although there are still
negative attitudes associated with tattooed individuals (Zestcott et al., 2018) . The decision to
tattoo oneself is influenced by trust in the tattooer and a desire for self-expression (Sierra et al.,
2013).
Tattoos are employed in advertising, digital media, and brands as a marketing strategy.
When tattoos are used in advertising, they reproduce subcultures and express the fashion
industry mindset (Bjerrisgaard et al., 2013). For instance, for younger people, digital tattooed
influencers are seen as unique and authentic, as their non -conventional appearance can help
build trust and effectiveness (Fernandes et al., 2022) . On the other hand, when athletes are
sponsored to tattoo corporate logos, the connection between the consumer and the brand will
be higher when there is congruence between the sport and the tattooed athlete (Weidner et al.,
2016).
The literature also explored consumer identity by scrutinising tattoos through CCT.
Consumers’ tattoos are polysemic emblems of identity construction, agency, and deviancy, part
of a body with permeable borders between self and the world (Patterson & Schroeder, 2010).
Tattoos personify consumers’ tensions, contraposing the body’s plasticity and self -expression
against the act of permanently marking it (Patterson, 2018). Tattooed individuals seek personal
projects to fit themselves in better places, considering body modifications enlightening and
transforming the body into an enacted mythical utopia (Roux & Belk, 2019).
Apart from discussing motivations, cultural meanings or personal narratives, some
academic studies have adopted a more critical approach. The body is commodified when
individuals tattoo corporate logos since it expresses loyalty to the cultural industry, particularly
brands and their lifestyles (Orend & Gagné, 2009). Corporate logo tattoos reproduce symbols
of capitalism, transforming people into human billboards (Orend & Gagné, 2009) and helping
construct post-modern consumer identities. They can also imprison consumers as companies
control the brand meanings, which might be changed according to the marketing strategy
(Bengtsson et al., 2005) . Nevertheless, tattooing is a way to reappropriate the physical body
against the social and diseased one, resisting the cultural forces that commodified it (Fisher,
2002).

27
In sum, studies contrapose the permanent and transient tattoo characteristics, as
memories and meanings are not unavoidably fixed. Tattoos are a collection of personal stories
and myths that connect past, present, and future. They are polysemic emblems of consumers’
identity projects and fragmented selves, wishing to propagate their self -expression and
reappropriate their bodies. The brand tattoos are in the middle of a contrast between being
creative and personalised with the dangers of becoming commodifie d symbols controlled by
marketing strategy.
2.3 Method
This exploratory research intends to understand why individuals tattoo brands and how
they make sense of them. The Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) was adopted to
answer these questions. The IPA examines the personal experience, combining
phenomenological and hermeneutical approaches, and recognises the need to interpret a
person’s involvement with the phenomenon (Smith et al., 2009) . The interpretative
phenomenology method opens the expectation that previous findings will be challenged and
new assumptions will be uncovered, respecting the participants’ voices, actions, and texts
(Benner, 2008) . IPA is adequate when the researcher wants to understand the person’s
interaction with the phenomenon, interpreting and attempting to make meaning from it (Smith
et al., 2009).
The phenomenological interview format was used to explore the participants’
experience in a first -person view, allowing them to describe the phenomenon in detail
(Thompson et al., 1989) . The interviews followed an interview guide, opening with a non -
directive question to be as unobtrusive as possible, called “grand tour” questions (McCracken,
1988): “Can you tell me about the relationship between your brand tattoos and yourself?”.
Additional questions covered how the person experienced brands and the decision to tattoo
them, the possible regret of tattooing a brand, and how the participant would fee l if the brand
owner were to change the brand meanings.
Participants were recruited by snowball sampling and mainly via Instagram using
hashtags such as “Coca-Cola tattoo”. After that, the posted images and videos were analysed to
ensure they had brand logo tattoos. The users were directly messaged and invited to participate
in the research. Table 2.1 shows the list of participants and the interview duration, which lasted
an average of 49 minutes. The interviews were conducted online, recorded, and transcribed
verbatim. Before beginning, the interviewer explaine d the study’s objective, that the

28
participation was voluntary and confidential, and that pseudonyms would be used, asking if the
interviewee agreed to participate. The participants were also asked if they would consent to
share a photo of their brand tattoos. The ones that agreed (12 out o f 18) decided to grant the
rights to use their tattoo images for academic purposes.
The inductive reasoning and axial coding were used to analyse the results, following the
premises of grounded theory (Corbin & Strauss, 2015) and IPA’s hermeneutical approach
(Smith et al., 2009) . The analysis was conducted with the support of Atlas.ti to code and
categorise data. The transcripts were understood and interpreted as a whole. After that, each
interview was related to each other to see commonalities, using axial coding to reduce and
reassemble initial coding (Saldaña, 2013) with a mix of emic and etic perspectives.
Four global themes emerged from a higher level of abstraction (Corbin & Strauss, 2015;
Smith et al., 2009; Thompson et al., 1989): close friendship and intimacy, acute bonds, catharsis
and sublimation, and ideology and subculture belonging. Each theme was analysed using a
hermeneutical circle approach, where the meaning of the whole text is determined by the
individual parts and vice versa (Arnold & Fischer, 1994).

2.4 Findings
The four identified themes represent the dimensions that organise consumers’
relationships with the brands they tattooed. The first two are realistic relationships, and the latter
are idealistic. Close friendships are realistic and outward -directed, compri sing relationships
related to family ties, childhood memories, best friendship bonds, and teammates. Acute bonds
are also realistic but inward-directed, surfacing sturdy connections related to therapists/patients
and dealers/addicts. On the other hand, cat harsis and sublimation are idealised and inward -
directed relationships between gurus/disciples and soulmates. Ideological and subculture
belonging are idealised and outward -directed, consisting of partisanships and nostalgic
memories.
2.4.1 Close Friendship and Intimacy
The interviewees considered their tattooed brands similar to close friends. They built
relationships and anthropomorphised their loved brands (Fournier, 1998), applying human-like
characteristics to them (Sharma & Rahman, 2022) and reciprocating the brand’s social and
economic investment in customer-brand relationships (Krishna & Kim, 2021).
Best friendships concern high trust, intimacy, and attachment (Fritz et al., 2014). They
also involve constant interactions, self -disclosure, self -congruity (Su et al., 2015) , loyalty,
dependence, mutual obligations, and social support (Price & Arnould, 1999). The participants
considered their relationship with the tattooed brand as best friends forever (BFF), trustful and
a partner when needed. Peter tattooed Skol and Instagram brands ( Figure 2.1) because they
helped him cope with loneliness: “Usually, on weekdays, I’m always there with a can, and it’s
a can of Skol, right? ... But that’s because my company is Skol, you know?” Similarly, the
reciprocity and mutual obligations (Price & Arnould, 1999) needed to be perpetually
materialised for Mark, who tattooed Skol to represent his connection with his best friends
(Figure 2.1).
The close bond between consumers and their tattoo brands can be associated with family
ties and be seen as childhood buddies. The participants showed loyalty to brands that reminded
them of their familial roots and positive associations with the past (Shields & Johnson, 2016).
One example is Melody’s M&M’s tattoo (Figure 2.1), which makes her feel close to her family
since the three M&M’s letters represent each family member’s favourite colour and their
interpersonal relationship: “But the meaning of the tattoo, in fact, it isn’t the brand, it’s not that
I like M&M’s (although I like them a lot) … I don’t know, it’s my family”.

The participants explained how they viewed the bonds with their favourite brands, not
having a stable and unique relationship but dynamic and multiple ones. For example, brands
were simultaneously considered teammates to help achieve professional goals and childhood
buddies. That is the case for Thomas, who tattooed Nike because he has been a fan since he
was very young, and the brand is the biggest seller in his sneakers store today. Another example
is the intersection of familial ties with teammates. Aman da uses her Sony camera to work,
achieve her professional goals, and express her creativity and independence. At the same time,
the camera is a connection with her mother, a professional photographer, and her childhood.
2.4.2 Acute Bonds
Acute bonds are concerned with the extreme personal relationships consumers have with
brands. These bonds can be positive, as in a therapist and patient relationship where the brand
helps the consumers cope with their problems, and, in turn, they reciprocate with higher loyalty
and commitment. However, the acute relationship can also be harmful, as in an addictive bond,
where the consumer feels threatened and anxious if prevented from consuming the brand.
The first acute bond regards the dealers/addicts relationship. Brand addiction refers to
a constant urge to buy brand products and services comprising dependence, obsession, lack of
self-control, hoarding, and other compulsive feelings and behaviours (Mrad & Cui, 2017) . It

33
also involves positive affectivity, gratification, irritability, bonding, and mental and behavioural
preoccupation (Cui et al., 2018).
Some participants described their relationship with the tattooed brand as beyond loyalty,
with a feeling of dependency and an irresistible desire to be together with it. One example is
Jessica’s addictive relationship with Coca -Cola Zero Sugar. She experie nces an abstinence
crisis when not drinking it (bad mood), and even family members and store clerks hide some
bottles in case the brand is out of stock (they know she cannot live without it). The brand tattoo
(Figure 2 .2) expresses Jessica’s strong relatio nship with her favourite brand, which is
anthropomorphised and compared to an animal companion who is always there with her. The
brand addiction is so strong that Jessica thinks it would be a tragedy if the flavour ever changes
or the brand stops being sold.
Apart from the beneficial feelings of loyalty and dedication, the negative emotions felt
by the participants in their dealers -addicts relationship with the brand contrast with previous
research that focused more on positive emotions and behaviours (Cui et al., 2018; Mrad & Cui,
2017). Besides the abstinence crisis that Jessica felt, Linda expressed her synchrony with the
Opala brand (Figure 2.3) and her obsession with it. When her husband crashed her car, and it
was a total loss, she was devasted: “It felt like a piece of me was being taken away”. Tattooing
the brand and the car was her creative way of compensating for her loss (Belk, 1988).

The dealers-addicts relationship can represent a symbiosis between tattoos and hedonic
pleasures that are impossible to resist. Barbara has two sets of brand tattoos ( Figure 2.4): one

34
has food brands like Lindt and Oreo, and another has luxury brands like Chanel and Hermès.
She faces dichotomies related to living more relaxed and joyfully (represented by the food
brands) and paying tribute to glamour and sophistication (represented by luxury). Both are part
of her compulsion for tattoos and brands, contrasting her new life as a veterinarian student
looking to indulge herself with candies with her former life in the status -driven law business.
Even though luxury brands signal admired life styles and bring differentiation and belonging
(Mrad et al., 2020) , she is conscious of their high prices. Tattooing was how she managed to
own them: “Well, actually, I love Chanel, and the quickest way for me to have a Chanel bag
was this tattoo [laughs]. I’m not going to spend R$ 30,000 on a bag!”.
The other relationship that fosters acute connections is the therapists-patients dyad.
Some participants expressed deep feelings about their tattooed brands and how they are related
to dealing with depression or marking decisive life moments. Brand tattoos were therapeutic,
helping them cope with troubles. Carol explained that she was not happy with her profession
and job, which led to depression and a feeling that she was not listening to herself. Her life
changed when she quit her job, bought a Harley -Davidson, and tattooed the logo in a visible
place. Carol tattooed the brand on her arm (Figure 2.3) in a place she could see while riding her
bike:
I’m always seeing it [Harley tattoo]. If I’m driving, I’m seeing it. If I’m going to say
hello, I’m seeing it. So, it’s a symbol to me that [says] “You’re awesome!” … “You
rock! You’re different. Go ahead!” Because I had depression … I had a very difficult
time with depression. So, having this symbol for me does me a lot of good (Carol).
Linda also talked about her depression and anxiety crises. She mentioned a passion for
drag racing and how it helped her forget her problems. When driving an Opala, Linda wants to
give her best, which brings more pleasure than anything else. Her connection with tattoos, the
brand, and drag racing contraposes criticisms for being a tattooed woman and not following the
stereotype of a sweet nurse. The same feeling is shared with Barbara, who started tattooing
when she had postpartum blues, lost a family membe r, and decided to change her career from
lawyer to veterinarian.

2.4.3 Catharsis and Sublimation
Catharsis is the process of releasing intense emotions to cleanse and purge them
(Aristotle, 1992). The result is a desired renewal brought to people, detaching them from the
work of art and author and resulting in exhilaration (Frye, 1957). Brand tattoos serve as a form
of revelation to the interviewees, as a cathartic moment (Oksanen & Turtiainen, 2005) to mark
a turning point in their lives and a symbol of healing and salvation from a personal crisis
(Velliquette et al., 2006). The brand is seen as a magical entity capable of saving the participants
and restoring their lives, for which they can be grateful and devote themselves (Fuschillo et al.,
2024).
Catharsis and sublimation are experienced in the gurus/disciples relationship. This
relationship has a veneration and enchantment component (Wang et al., 2019), as participants
are mesmerised by what the brand represents. It is also a totemic relationship between
consumers and brands expressed by their brand tattoos. The tattoo totems signal the individual
feelings of attachment ritualised in collective conduct, fixed or materialised into emblems or
arbitrary signs (brand tattoos) representing the group (Lévi-Strauss, 1963).
The brand is the guru that guides disciples and enlightens their path to the greater good.
The tattooed participants considered their loved brands as moral models to inspire their conduct,
devoting themselves to learning from their masters and being gratef ul for achieving higher
development. Daniel tattooed his university logo (Figure 2.5) after receiving his master’s degree
and starting his PhD studies. The university embraced the participant and was a tutor that

36
allowed him to achieve his dreams. The brand tattoo is a trophy he can display and a way to
thank his guru, incorporating it into the self.
Figure 2.5 - Brand tattoos: Daniel (Univali), Clara (Mercedes), and Andrew (Linux).

The relationships between gurus/disciples are consecrated with the brand tattoo,
condensing the spiritual connection and the symbolic meanings. For instance, Clara tattooed
the Mercedes logo on her right arm ( Figure 2.5 ), which she considers her spiritual side, to
symbolise what she wants to accomplish as a symbol of prosperity, success, and status.
Similarly, Steven believes that the most essential things in his life must be marked. His tattoos
are visible on his right arm, stressing that they are indeed his “right arm”, supporting him: “For
example, whenever we are going to take some kind of oath … we always raise our right arm,
you know? It’s always something that is used to symbolise”.
The consumer-brand relationship of soulmates triggers another cathartic and sublime
experience. The soulmate theory states that there is only one right and idealised person to be
loved passionately and discovered, contrasting to work-it-out theorists who believe that partners
can change and be moulded (Franiuk et al., 2002). For soulmates, assuming that the partner is
ideal is crucial for the satisfaction of the relationship. It can make them positively distort the
perception of the idealised partner, downplaying the faults, or negatively distort them if they
think they are not with the right person (Franiuk et al., 2004).
Andrew’s connection with Linux is strong and is related to collaborating with other
enthusiasts: “Linux, for me, represents a philosophy, a philosophy of life: the philosophy of
collaboration, that we all collaborate for the greater good”. The Linux brand is an idealised
soulmate that can teach about rebellion and creativity, free from the perils of commodification
and commercialisation. The Linux penguin mascot (Tux) symbolises a totem filled with the

37
brand’s values, which Andrew tattooed to reinforce his attachment to the brand (Figure 2.5) and
his communal relationship. The participant’s personal myth (Oksanen & Turtiainen, 2005;
Velliquette et al., 2006) is to think about the brand as a linchpin that allows his career change
from music teacher to IT programmer, which interlaces with the guru and disciple relationship.
2.4.4 Ideology and Subculture Belonging
This study understands ideology and subculture belonging as a wish to be part of a
cultural group of like-minded people. The participants expressed their values and related them
to what they understood to be the brand’s cultural codes, myths, and ideology (Holt & Cameron,
2010). They are affected by marketplace mythologies, which construct an ideal consumer
lifestyle towards an ideological direction, although not free from competing interests (C. J.
Thompson, 2004).
The socio-cultural and ideological relationships with the brand tattoos are expressed via
partisanship and nostalgic proneness. Both are idealised views of society concerning the present
and the future (partisanship) or the past (nostalgia). The brand purp ose impacts them, which
involves contributions to the betterment of society and transcends the company’s profits (France
et al., 2024). Brand activism also influences these brand-consumer relationships, as it involves
the discussion and challenge of existing moral judgements via persuasion or controversies
(Sibai et al., 2021) and is a result of a process that formulates, articulates, and implements the
activism as a marketing strategy (Pimentel et al., 2024).
The first type of ideology and subcultural belonging is related to partisans. Participants
expressed their ideological preferences and connected them with their brand tattoos. For
example, Keith tattooed the Nike Jordan tennis to show his affinity with the brand’s cultural
codes and activism, which are linked to the black movement, rap and ghetto, and the biding of
fashion (streetwear) and aesthetics:
So, today, Nike is a brand that sponsors many black people, taking many activities
and things to suburban areas to somehow help and collaborate with this culture,
which itself created around it … mainly in sports. So, I think there’s a lot of that too,
you know? … This victory issue, the suburban issue. It’s a combination of many
things that led me to be part of this club, to be a fanboy, up to the point of marking
my skin somehow (Keith).
Another strong subculture affiliation is outlined by Steven, who tattooed the Vans brand
and its slogan (“Off the wall”). He praises the brand for sticking with skating since the

38
beginning, rebuffing Louis Vuitton’s sponsorship of a Brazilian professional skater as
illegitimate and opportunistic (Sibai et al., 2021) since it is not part of the underground spirit of
skating. Steven summarises the “off the wall” subculture ideology as this:
When you skate, I think your view of the city changes. Because if you don’t skate,
you’ll see a sidewalk. You’ll say: “A sidewalk”. And, if you skate, you’ll look at that
sidewalk and say: “Wow, that trick would be perfect here!”… So, I think this
different vision would be “off the wall” (Steven).
Partisanship can also be expressed via participation in brand communities (Muñiz &
O’Guinn, 2001; Schouten & McAlexander, 1995) , which was the case of interviewees who
tattooed the Harley-Davidson logo. However, the brand meanings and cultural influences were
not the same for them. Paul engaged with aficionados of the Harley Owners Group (HOG),
considering himself a brand fan stereotype and associating the brand with conservative values:
“So, the Harley-Davidson owner, the Harley-Davidson guy, is a right-wing guy. That is because
Harley is an American brand, right?”. He cannot conceive that any Harley fan would not be
close to the idealised brand consumer (e.g., Caucasian, man, tall, and strong).
Carol shares another point of view about the brand. She praises the brand’s heritage, the
status it brings her, and family and friendship values. On the other hand, she is empowered as
a woman to strive despite struggles and win in a men’s world, deciding not to be part of the
HOG and ride with a women -only Harley group or with bikers who own other brands. She
understands the brand from a feminist perspective, rejecting male superiority and subverting
males-dominated culture (Joy & Venkatesh, 1994) . The contraposition between Paul’s and
Carol’s visions shows the competing views of Harley’s marketplace mythology.
The same feeling of feminine empowerment is shared with Linda. She is part of the first
women’s Opala brand community (Chevrolet’s car brand launched in the 1970s in Brazil).
Linda explains how the members gather at events and share their experiences and p assions,
stating that the Opala community is 90% masculine. However, she stresses her feminist point
of view that she can strive in a male-dominated environment, tattooing the Opala and Chevrolet
brands (Figure 2.3) and expressing her affiliation with drag racing.
The second idealised relationship is associated with nostalgic proneness: a favourable
longing for the past and days of yore (Holbrook, 1993). Nostalgia proneness is a broad concept
that can be narrowed to bonded nostalgia when focussed on a particular object or childhood
brand nostalgia, a positive attachment to a brand due to fond memories of one’s youth (Shields

39
& Johnson, 2016) . Brands might explore nostalgia via symbolic stories, utopian past worlds,
the contrast between old and new, and authenticity (Brown et al., 2003).
Some participants thought about their tattooed brands as vintage mates. James has a
special connection with the Kombi brand, which reminds him of the good old times and how
everything was better assembled. The brand epitomises a utopian past when life was simpler
and easier, as everyone could travel freely without worrying a bout troubles. Similarly, Linda
thinks that the Opala brand is an iconic brand that reminded her of the car's history, how it was
presented to the public in the 1960s and 1970s, the chan ges it has gone through and even that
former presidents used it. The brand is her connection with this idealised past, which is
consecrated via an old car brand community.
2.5 Discussion and Conclusion
2.5.1 Theoretical Contributions
This paper’s objective was to understand why consumers tattoo brands and how this
phenomenon contributes to their identity projects. This research’s first major contribution
concerns identifying new or under -theorised brand-consumer relationships, which an swers a
call to expand and diversify the coverage of relationships (Alvarez et al., 2023) . The second
significant contribution adds to the literature that consumers can have multiple and dynamic
relationships with the same brand since they transit between a core stable self and a multiple
porous one (Appau et al., 2020).
First, this research extends the brand relationship literature by presenting new types of
brand-consumer relationships (Table 2.2). Previous studies have pinpointed and commented on
some of these relationships, such as best friendships (Alvarez et al., 2023; Fournier, 1998; Fritz
et al., 2014), childhood friendships (Fournier, 1998; Shields & Johnson, 2016), dealers/addicts,
therapists/patients, teammates, and soulmates (Fournier & Alvarez, 2013). However, they have
neither defined nor explained how consumers could express them. The brand -consumer
relationships are organised under four quadrants, depicted in Figure 2.6. The first axis concerns
consumers’ inner and outer connections, and the second refers to the realistic and idealised
bonds with brands.
Recent research has conceptualised the relationships between consumers and brands
(Schreuder et al., 2024) , stating that consumers experience them as more functional and less
emotionally intense. Nevertheless, the inner consumer -brand relationships show that the

40
interviewees undergo deep feelings in a relationship exchange, benefiting from the interaction
(Veloutsou, 2007) and creating a bond and a sense of oneness with the brand (Yoshida et al.,
2021). These relationships can be mixed -valenced as some participants expressed their
addiction to brands (Cui et al., 2018; Ghorbanzadeh, 2024; Mrad & Cui, 2017) while others
sought therapeutical and soulful characteristics in them (Franiuk et al., 2002, 2004; Fuschillo
et al., 2024). Brand tattoos end up acting as mnemonic signs of crucial events (Steadman et al.,
2019), giving meaning to life (S. Luo & Hamlin, 2022).

On the other hand, the outer consumer-brand relationships show that consumers are not
simply human billboards (Baudrillard, 1998; Orend & Gagné, 2009) , contained in predefined
stereotypes (Bjerrisgaard et al., 2013) , commodified bodies (Bengtsson et al., 2005; Orend &
Gagné, 2009) or reflecting the cultural industry message (Horkheimer & Adorno, 2002) . The
practices, knowledge, and brands’ cultural discourses are incorporated (Kuuru, 2022; Murphy
et al., 2018; Spotswood & Gurrieri, 2024) as a person’s sense of self is constructed by
interconnections of the body with society (Merleau-Ponty, 1962).
On the realistic and idealistic axis, consumers seek down -to-earth relationships based
on close familial and friendship ties or as comfort for their troubles and problems. At the same
time, they develop idealised bonds with brands, using their brand tattoo s as totems (Lévi-
Strauss, 1963), reinscribing and reinforcing group affiliation (Razmus, 2025) and subculture
belonging (Fisher, 2002), and being affected by media culture imagery (Velliquette et al., 1998).

41
Interviewees are proud to be part of marketplace cultures (Patterson, 2018; Patterson &
Schroeder, 2010) while simultaneously expressing themselves as cultural producers.
Contrapositions and contradictions exist in the brand -consumer relationships, which
place one foot in reality and another in idealisation. For example, brand tattoos can empower
participants, particularly women, to resignify brand values, incorporate them to fit their life
stories, and not be subject to dominance, submissiveness, and weakness (Balog, 2024; Foucault,
1995). However, they might as well reinforce prejudice and be incorporated by consumers as a
type of polarised partisanship (Schoenmueller et al., 2022) , which could lead to buycotts,
boycotts (Flecha-Ortiz et al., 2024) and culture wars (Hashmi et al., 2025) . The idealised
relationships are also ambiguous since they positively and negatively distort brand
characteristics, potentially triggering passionate consumer behaviours and emotions that can
impact brand equity.
Finally, this research shows how consumers build their sense of self through brands
(Holt, 2002; Razmus, 2025), cultivating multiple relationships with them and broadcasting their
brand commitment through dynamic bonds. Brand tattoos symbolise polysemic and incomplete
meanings, representing a search for a desired and stable self (Appau et al., 2020) that stands out
and reclaims the body. They also reinforce individuality by representing personal life stories,
homages, and myths (McAdams, 1993; Oksanen & Turtiainen, 2005; Steadman, Medway, et
al., 2023; Velliquette et al., 2006).

2.5.2 Managerial Implications
Marketers aim to build strong customer relationships and create and sustain iconic
brands. The first practical implication of this study is that adopting a cultural strategy for a
brand pays off. Highly attached consumers have deep emotional connections wi th brands,
expressing their authenticity and values by tattooing them. Brand -tattooed consumers can be
considered cultural brand codes, reinforcing the brand’s identity and personality.
Understanding their behaviour and bonds with loved brands can guide marketers in developing
their cultural strategies and avoiding culture wars (Hashmi et al., 2025).
Companies should be aware of consumers’ multiple relationships with their brands.
They need to understand the different types of bonds and how they are formed. Through brand
tattoos, consumers signal a solid relationship and manifest their sturdy bonds. Ho wever, they
can also broadcast their relationship strength via different expressions, such as cosplay or cult-
like interactions. Marketers need to identify the cues that tie consumers and brands and
understand what types of relationships they fit in. For e xample, a guru/disciple relationship
could require more counselling, while subcultural belonging should be enhanced for
partisanship connections.
The findings also show that consumers might present mixed feelings, either negative or
positive, and ambiguous relationships with brands. They can resist brand identity changes or
twist it to fit their cultural values, reinforcing prejudices or stereotypes . The implication for
practitioners is strategically managing the relationship types and fostering initiatives to
influence positive behaviours and affection while minimising negative ones.
2.5.3 Limitations and Future Research
This paper presents some limitations that need to be pointed out. Only participants in
Brazil were interviewed, although with a balanced sample regarding age, gender, and number
of tattoos. Since the brand tattoo phenomenon is global, the perspectives of other cultures might
differ from what has been concluded in this paper. Interviews were conducted with consumers
who have tattooed mainly consumer goods brands but not B2B, sports teams, or music bands.
Future studies could compare the types of brand tattoo s and understand if their meanings are
different.
Future research could study other dynamic and multiple relationships between brands
and consumers. Understanding how these diverse relationships affect brand identity,

45
personality, equity, and other brand constructs is necessary. Scholars should also investigate
harmful relationship types, how they are formed and stimulated, and the consequences for brand
management. It would be interesting to compare single with dynamic relationships and negative
with positive ones, adding to the attachment -aversion theoretical proposal (Park et al., 2013a,
2013b) and the recent polarisation research stream (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019, 2024).
Further research should also look into how archetypes and storytelling interact with
brand tattoos and the psychological implications for brands. Are tattoos enacting personal
archetypes or reflecting brand ones? How can both co -exist? Researchers could st udy the
relationship between brand tattoos and other tattoos on consumer bodies. Since they also tattoo
unbranded products and symbols, what are their connections?

CHAPTER 3 – POSITIVE-NEGATIVE POLES: POLARISED BRANDS2

3.1 Introduction
Polarising brands attract both lovers and haters, aiming to boost positive outcomes while
avoiding harmful consequences (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019) . The more polarised a brand is,
the greater the heterogeneity in evaluations, which has a direct impact on stock returns but with
lower risk due to less price sensitivity or brand switching (Luo et al., 2013) . Relying on
polarised brands can be advantageous because they offer stronger self -expression,
distinctiveness, and a sense of belonging (Berendt et al., 2018; Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019). On
the other hand, intense rivalry can lead to avoidance, trash-talking, schadenfreude, and harmful
actions (Liao et al., 2023; Marticotte et al., 2016) , impacting brand equity (Luo et al., 2013;
Phillips-Melancon and Dalakas, 2014).
Brand polarisation differs from brand rivalry since it involves the simultaneous presence
of love and hate, not necessarily requiring a feud or a strong opponent (Osuna Ramírez et al.,
2024). Brand rivalry is a particular type of polarisation in which, instead of considering strong
feelings towards one brand, two rivals are considered (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019) . While
polarised brands have been scarcely theorised and studied (Monahan et al., 2023; Osuna
Ramírez et al., 2019, 2024) , brand rivalry has received more attention in the literature. It has
been conceptualised as oppositional brand loyalty since consumers define themselves by what
they consume and do not (Muñiz and Hamer, 2001). The rivalry is considered an ongoing battle
between competing brands (Alvarado-Karste and Kidwell, 2022; Berendt et al., 2018, 2024), is
driven by consumer-brand identification (Liao et al., 2021) , and enhanced by participation in
brand communities (Cheng et al., 2024; Thompson and Sinha, 2008).
Although brand polarisation studies addressed its conceptualisation (Osuna Ramírez et
al., 2019), proposed a scale to measure it (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2024) , analysed the effect of
hate-acknowledging ads (Monahan et al., 2023), and the impact on stock returns and risk (Luo
et al., 2013) , there is a gap in the literature on understanding the conditions that foster brand
polarisation (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019), how consumers behave toward it, and the similarities

and differences between negative and positive feelings concerning polarised brands (Osuna

This paper aims to address this lacuna by posing the following research questions. RQ1:
Why do polarised brands elicit antagonistic consumers’ feelings and behaviours? RQ2: How
does this polarisation process unfold? Previous research investigated polarised feelings of love
and hate toward brands (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019, 2024) but did not seek to understand why
particular brands evoke those feelings. Drawing from studies that identified polarised brands
and brand rivalries (Berendt et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2013; Monahan et al.,
2023; Muñiz and Hamer, 2001; Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019; Phillips -Melancon and Dalakas,
2014), five brands were chosen since they trigger intense polarisation: Apple, Coca -Cola,
McDonald’s, Nestlé, and Starbucks.
This exploratory study interviewed consumers to understand their relationships with
polarised brands, adopting the Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis method (Smith et al.,
2009) to investigate the significance of the phenomenon and how consumers experience it, as
most research in brand polarisation and oppositional brand loyalty relied on quantitative
methods. The main contribution of this paper concerns understanding the brand p olarisation
phenomenon more broadly as a lightning rod effect. This effect occurs because polarised brands
elicit strong responses from consumers, who consider them as either iconic (loved) or anti -
iconic (hated), precipitating four distinct emotional stat es: brand salvation, brand damnation,
brand ambiguity, and brand agnosticism. They are driven by underlying, basic individual values
(Schwartz et al., 2012) and the expectations associated with the brand promise (Bhargava &
Bedi, 2022).
3.2 Literature Review
3.2.1 Brand Relationship Extremes: Love and Hate
The brand relationship literature has been growing over the last decades, investigating
consumer-brand deep bonds, polarity, and strength (Fetscherin and Veloutsou, 2024) . It has
developed under diverse streams of brand loyalty, love, community, self -connection, and
storytelling (Fetscherin and Heinrich, 2015) . Drawing from the seminal initial works that
identified different types of relationships (Fournier, 1998) , scholars have discussed intense
affectionate connections such as brand love (Batra et al., 2012; Carroll and Ahuvia, 2006;
Robertson et al., 2022) , hate (Kucuk, 2019; Mushtaq et al., 2024; Zarantonello et al., 2016;
Zhang and Laroche, 2020), and passion (Gilal et al., 2023).

48
Depending on the degree of intensity, the brand -consumer relationship can vary from
brand satisfaction or indifference to love and hate (Fetscherin et al., 2021). The brand love and
hate constructs are related to brand attachment, which is associated with self -brand
interrelations and prominence (Park et al., 2010). To measure the strength of emotional
attachment, scholars identified three first-order dimensions: affection, passion, and connection
(Thomson et al., 2005).
Another perspective analysed both brand attachment and aversion, including
consumers’ negative relationships with brands (Park et al., 2013) . However, this model was
criticised for not adequately capturing these negative relationships, as they are not necessarily
the opposite of positive ones (Fournier and Alvarez, 2013) . For example, some relationships
(e.g., secret affairs and masters-slaves) are mixed-valenced and imbalanced. In contrast, others
are neutral, lying midway on the attachment-aversion continuum (Fournier and Alvarez, 2013).
Although studies have explored the extremes of brand love and hate, less attention has
been given to other brand -consumer relationships, and most research has focused on broader
marketplace phenomena instead of scrutinising one type of relationship (Alvarez et al., 2023).
Additionally, recent research has explored the phenomenon of love turning to hate (Tolunay
and Veloutsou, 2025), but few studies have investigated ambivalent, contradictory, and mixed-
emotion relationships.
3.2.2 Oppositional Brand Loyalty
Scholars have studied rivalries between brands, such as Coke versus Pepsi, coining the
term oppositional brand loyalty to describe antagonistic choices that help consumers define
themselves (Muñiz & Hamer, 2001). Previous research has identified the ambivalent effect of
rivalries (Berendt et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2013), focusing on their negative consequences. The
intense competition leads to schadenfreude, which is the pleasure felt from others’ misfortune
(Cheng et al., 2024; Marticotte et al., 2016; Phillips-Melancon and Dalakas, 2014), and to trash-
talking against contestants (Ewing et al., 2013; Liao et al., 2023; Marticotte et al., 2016;
Phillips-Melancon and Dalakas, 2014). Stronger feelings may also be elicited by brand rivalry,
such as anti -brand actions (Cheng et al., 2024), rumination, resentment, and feelings of
unfairness (Alvarado-Karste and Kidwell, 2022), as well as a desire to harm the opposing brand
(Marticotte et al., 2016).
The rivalry between brands influences not only the consumers’ behaviour, but also
represents a risk to brand equity (Phillips-Melancon and Dalakas, 2014) , lower stock

49
performance (Luo et al., 2013), a threat to consumer identity (Liao et al., 2021), and, if used in
communication pieces, it might backfire (Berendt et al., 2024). On the other hand, studies have
identified positive aspects of oppositional brand loyalty, such as defending the brand that is
under attack (Muñiz and Hamer, 2001) , reinforcing the brand’s distinction and uniqueness
(Berendt et al., 2018) , ingroup identification (Ewing et al., 2013; Phillips -Melancon and
Dalakas, 2014), engagement, and willingness to pay a premium price (Cheng et al., 2024).
Studies have also debated the antecedents of brand rivalry regarding three main aspects:
brand, self -identification, and engagement with rivals. The brand aspects that influence
oppositional brand loyalty include brand prestige, uniqueness (Liao et al., 2021) , and loyalty
(Marticotte et al., 2016). Consumer self-brand connection (Liao et al., 2021; Marticotte et al.,
2016), moral identification (Cheng et al., 2024), identification with the preferred brand (Liao et
al., 2023; Phillips-Melancon and Dalakas, 2014), and disidentification with the opponent brand
(Liao et al., 2023) concern the psychological motivations that enhance rivalries. Regarding the
engagement with rivals, the literature identified as crucial aspects of oppositional brand loyalty
the brand community participation (Ewing et al., 2013; Marticotte et al., 2016; Muñiz and
Hamer, 2001; Thompson and Sinha, 2008) and long-running rivalry history (Alvarado-Karste
and Kidwell, 2022; Berendt et al., 2024; Ewing et al., 2013; Muñiz and Hamer, 2001).
3.2.3 Brand Polarisation
Brand polarisation is defined as “an affective phenomenon where beliefs and emotions
of a significant number of people induce a simultaneous move to the extremes involving
passionate positive and negative feelings and convictions towards the brand, like -minded
consumers and opposite-minded consumers” (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019, p. 620) . However,
few studies have investigated brand polarisation (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019) , as it remains
underdeveloped in the literature (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2024) and has received limited attention
(Monahan et al., 2023).
The brand polarisation construct was conceptualised based on characteristics from
political science, social psychology, polarised products, and oppositional brand loyalty (Osuna
Ramírez et al., 2019) . Polarisation in political science refers to partisanship, the tendency to
identify with one party, viewing co-partisans positively and adversaries negatively (Iyengar &
Westwood, 2015). Polarisation can be affective and lead to animosity, but it is not necessarily
ideological (Iyengar et al., 2019). Polarised feelings shape consumption patterns, as consumers
acquire products as a defence mechanism against events that threaten their identity or group

50
affiliation, such as the election of an opposing party or when a brand takes a political or
ideological stand (Schoenmueller et al., 2022).
Brands face a double-edged approach to polarisation. Their communication might lead
to boycotts and buycotts (Flecha-Ortiz et al., 2024), and their marketing communication might
be seen as a moral failure (Biedenbach, 2025). Brand activism could be considered inconsistent
(Malik et al., 2025), trigger advocacy or backfire (Kim & He, 2025). Nevertheless, remaining
politically silent can be seen as a betrayal and a lack of care (Zaman Malik et al., 2025).
In social psychology, scholars have studied group polarisation. When exposed to group
discussions, individuals adjust their position to maintain social desirability (Myers & Lamm,
1976), not deviating significantly from their ideal position and remaining close to the group’s
central one (Isenberg, 1986). Polarisation happens when there is a shift toward the preferred
pole, while extremisation is the movement away from neutrality (Myers & Lamm, 1976). This
change depends on the number and strength of pro and con arguments, but they will be
considered invalid and unpersuasive if there is intense animosity toward an outgroup (Isenberg,
1986).
Past research has applied social psychology and political science definitions and
concepts to brand polarisation, revisiting the oppositional brand loyalty construct (Osuna
Ramírez et al., 2019, 2024) . In this sense, brand rivalries were considered a special type of
polarisation involving intense hatred and love among supporters and detractors toward two
opposing brands rather than one (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019).
Although the literature has discussed consumers’ perceptions about the advertising of
polarised brands (Monahan et al., 2023) , the performance of polarised brands in the stock
market (X. Luo, Raithel, et al., 2013) , and identified the dimensions of brand polarisation
(Osuna Ramírez et al., 2024) , there is a gap on understanding why and how particular brands
evoke polarisation, which the present research aims to fill. More exploratory research is also
needed since most papers employed a quantitative research strategy (Table 3.1), primarily using
structural equation modelling and conducting experiments.

3.3 Method
The Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis was employed in this research, as it is
suitable for understanding consumers’ relationships with the world, focusing on the attempt to
interpret and make sense of their behaviours and activities (Smith et al., 2009). The emphasis
is on analysing the informants’ experiences and points of view, grasping the phenomenon’s
essence and broad cultural perspective (Spiggle, 1994).
The interpretative phenomenology method enables researchers to uncover new
assumptions and challenge existing ones (Benner, 2008). It also stresses that reality is socially
constructed, multiple, holistic, and contextual, and that it involves an interactive and
interpretive research relationship (Hudson & Ozanne, 1988) . As the brand polarisation
phenomenon is scarcely researched and underdeveloped (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2024) ,
interpretative phenomenology can yield new understandings and propositions by combining
phenomenological and hermeneutical insights.
Since this work aims to investigate why particular polarised brands elicit negative and
positive feelings and behaviours, five brands were selected: Apple, Coca -Cola, McDonald’s,
Nestlé, and Starbucks. These brands were chosen based on past research on oppositional brand
loyalty and brand polarisation (Table 3.1). To recruit consumers to participate in the study, the
authors searched online communities on Reddit and Instagram posts using the brand’s name
and negative keywords such as “fuck”, “boycott”, or “sucks”. The same process was undertaken
using the brand’s name and positive keywords such as “love”, “enthusiast”, and “fan”. The
authors scrutinised the posts to ensure that the users were active members, directly messaging
and inviting them to participate in the research.
In-depth online interviews were conducted in English, Portuguese, and Spanish, with 26
consumers from the selected brands (13 lovers and 13 haters), as seen in Table 3.2. The
interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim, lasting an average of 61 minutes. Verbal
consent was obtained during the interview, with participants informed that it was confidential,

54
voluntary, and recorded, in accordance with procedures approved by the local ethics committee.
Data collection ceased when theoretical saturation was reached, as the sample was deemed
adequate for theory development, and further efforts would lead to redundancy or the discovery
of minor new elements (Saunders et al., 2018).
The software Atlas.ti was used to codify and analyse the data. The codification
considered the grounded theory premises (Corbin & Strauss, 2015), using structural coding as
the first cycle method and axial coding as the second (Saldaña, 2013). The data structure was
organised into first-order concepts, second-order themes, and aggregate dimensions, following
the Gioia methodology to explain the phenomenon of interest with increasing abstractness
(Gioia et al., 2012) . The hermeneutical circle was employed to complement the interpretative
phenomenology, allowing for the understanding of the meanings of the entire set of interviews
as determined by the individual elements, and vice versa (Arnold & Fischer, 1994).
