asymmetrical power and the brand controls the relationship, the consumer benefits. It might be
contradictory, but there is a positive outcome for the person. Bruce complain s about Verizon
and how the company has got worse over the years: “ I remember back in the day, when you
had Verizon, there was a difference in quality (...) Right now, hell no! Verizon is like cricket.
Damn near like the same shit! [laughs].” However, when he was provoked by the interviewer,
saying he kept using it, Bruce confessed that he has been with Verizon for 20 years and was
sincere: “But every time that I try to leave, they’d be giving me some nice deals, and I just keep,
you know? [laughs] (...) But the thing is what I’m paying, what I’m getting... It’s gonna be hard
to match it.”
Psychopathic consumer-brand relationships. Psychopathic brands lack empathy for the
consumer, being insensitive and causing harm. The first relationship concerns domestic abuse,
which is different from a forced marriage since it involves mistreatment and stronger negative
emotions. However, the consumer benefits from the interaction with the brand, or does not have
better options, even though they suffer abuse.
Sophia told two consumption stories that illustrate this relationship. She flies Ryanair
from Portugal to other countries because it is a low -cost airline that suits her needs. Sophia
described a bad experience at the airport when travelling with her girlf riends. A Ryanair
employee checked her bags to see if they fit with the stipulated measures: “ And the lady was
really mean to us, like, I ended up having to put my backpack there [into the bag sizer] four

100
times, even though mine fit right away .” The employee told another that the girls were a
problem, and started complaining that Sophia had brought a second item:
So, I went to swipe my ticket, and the lady who called the supervisor saw that I had
my wallet. And she turned to me, looked me in the eyes, and shouted, “I already told
you that you can’t bring the second item!” And I just looked at them, “Look, your
colleague said I could,” “But I’m the one in charge here!” (Sophia)
Sophia also had a hard time with Ticketmaster. As a Harry Styles fan, she was anxious
to buy a good seat for the show and slept two nights in a mall to be one of the first in line. When
her way finally came, the Ticketmaster website crashed because of high demand, forcing her to
try several times without any luck: “And I think they do it on purpose, because years and years
go by and nobody likes buying concert tickets, because it’s always awful!” She felt devastated
by not being able to buy the tickets she wanted: “I cried a lot, and it was very dramatic because
I spent two nights at the mall, which was horrible!”
Different from domestic abuse, a criminals/victims relationship regards stronger brand
wrongdoings, causing severe damages to the consumers, either psychologically, emotionally,
or financially. Oliver had a serious problem with a Brazilian phone carrier, C laro, which sold
two cell phone lines without his consent. He was not a client, but Claro used his name, ID, and
a fake address to sell the lines. Eventually, the unpaid bills were sent to a debt collection agency,
as he was trying to fix the problem cause d by the brand: “ Trying to solve it with them was
awful, terrible! In fact, it’s not fixed. I'm taking them to court because of this.”
Another psychopathic relationship concerns moral enmity. Consumers have strong
negative feelings towards brands that deviate from moral standards or act against the person’s
values. Maya dislikes Hobby Lobby for denying employees access to birth control in their
insurance, finding it unethical: “ And I don’t think that you , as my employer, except in very
specific roles, get to determine what religion I follow, what my ethics or morals are, as long as
I’m not doing something illegal.” Zachary also hates Hobby Lobby for being immoral: “I would
never, ever shop with them! I consider them just immoral and decrepit in six ways to Sunday.”
He explains that the company is anti -LGBT and was convicted of stealing historical artefacts
from Iraq: “I teach history, and it’s just the fact that they would be ripping off (...) relics from
people’s home countries (...) and lying about it, is just as terrible corporate behaviour as you
could possibly imagine!”

101
The last psychopathic relationship is related to bullies/bullied. In this type of
relationship, the brand bullies consumers, is neglective, or creates an environment that lets
inappropriate behaviour happen, as in the case of sexism, racism, ageism, or any derogatory
conduct. Jane used to play League of Legends, but she no longer does. She dislikes how the
game is toxic for women, as a lot of men play it, harassing them: “People will make fun of you,
saying things like, ‘Oh, it had to be a woman, go wash the dishes!’, you know? So, sometimes
there are these really annoying extremes.” Similarly, Barbara suffered prejudice and sexism for
being a woman playing games, sometimes using a male username or muting gamers to deal
with the stress: “[Fortnite] i s not very accessible for girls to play with . There are a lot of
perverted men there.” She also stressed that if a player did not perform well in a match, some
users would bully them, without any reaction from the game developer: “ That doesn't provide
a good experience; it becomes really toxic, you know? It makes playing Fortnite, or any other
online game, a really bad experience.”
Machiavellian consumer-brand relationships. Machiavellian brands deceive consumers
by manipulation and exploitation, promising something and not delivering. Brands are seen as
crooks who build trust, but ultimately trick them and make them feel like suckers. Hugo bought
a cleaning robot from a brand called Neato, which worked fine. At some point, Vorwerk bought
the brand and promised to maintain the infrastructure to keep the robot working, since it
depended on cloud servers. However, Hugo was one day warned by the company that it would
no longer support the product. He felt frustrated and deceived by the lack of care:
I was livid! I mean, I had a working robot vacuum that I used at least five times a
week, and now I can’t use it anymore. It’s basically useless! (...) So, from one
moment to another, they turned a functioning robot vacuum into a pile of garbage.
And I can’t do anything about it, and they’re not compensating me. So, yeah, I’m
furious! [laughs] (Hugo)
Sometimes brands are not directly or necessarily deceiving consumers, but exploiting
them in host/parasite relationships. Alexander was a loyal user of Adobe products for years,
since he depended on them for graphic design. He is particularly annoyed by th e subscription
model, which he sees as a money grab, and has led him to stop buying Adobe’s products.
Alexander goes on to say that the company’s mindset is not beneficial for the consumers since
the prices are too high, and users depend on their products: “It’s geared towards professional
users who need it. And it’s almost like the mafia. These professional users have to use Adobe.
(...) So, it’s kind of, you know, like highway robbery in a sense.”

102
On the other hand, another parasitic relationship concerns Airbnb, as Claire explains
how the brand exploits the city where she lives, driving up rents and house prices, and gradually
replacing local shops and culture with an infrastructure to serve tourists. Airbnb behaves like a
parasite, taking advantage of its host and changing the city for the worse, which might even kill
it:
I do think it is parasitic. (...) So, whenever those people, the culture bearers of the
area, the reason why people come here, can’t afford to live here, then the city’s going
to die. Then, I think at a certain point, people won’t want to come here if it’s just a
bunch of half -empty houses being rented as Airbnbs. It won’t be interesting
anymore. So, I could see it even killing the culture of a place. (Claire)
Machiavellian brands also resort to asymmetrical power, such as in relationships
between dealers and addicts. Three distinct negative aspects of Instagram illustrate this type of
relationship. Barbara reports the first one, calling attention to how people are not themselves
on the platform, only praising their qualities, especially influencers: “ It's very bad when
someone uses the platform to do evil, to show off a life they don't have. ” She used to spend
eight hours per day on Instagram and felt an abstinence crisis after deciding to stop using it.
A second harmful aspect concerns social comparisons and a sense of group. Ann felt
bad using Instagram because she compared herself with slimmer girls who went to the gym and
had beautiful bodies. After leaving the platform, she was surprised that her friends did not look
for her, as if they had a fake bond: “ So, the impression I get is ... after I left social media, I'm
dead. I'm dead! I don't feel like I have any real friends, like, that I can count on, you know?”
The third negative aspect concerns consumerism. Jane was addicted to Instagram,
spending a lot of money on things she did not need. She tried to avoid ads, but the app continued
to bombard her with them, as a dealer filling her with drugs: “I kept saying I didn’t want to see
it anymore, but then another one would come along. (...) No matter how many ads you don ’t
wanna see, they’ll put one back in its place.” Reflecting on how social media works, Zoe sums
up the relationship with them: “Not feel like I’m forced, like I have to keep looking. And I can
turn it off when I want to. It’s like somebody stopped giving me cocaine. It’s really nice
[laughs].”
The last Machiavellian relationship regards how consumers feel spied on by brands, as
if they were targets. Wilson works with IT and, because of that, he knows how technology
companies have been making their products worse over the years, calling it enshittification, a

103
recurring theme among most informants and Reddit users. He is worried about brands spying
on what he does, as he comments about Microsoft: “This is my computer, I want to use it, and
I don’t want you and your over 3000 partners to know what I’m doing on my computer.” Wilson
complains that Google is forcing users to provide their real names and IDs to develop
applications. He also affirms that Apple listens to conversations even when told not to: “ They
also sell your data. They also collect a lot of your data. I could pull up my pie hole statistics
right now and see that every 15 minutes , my wife’s MacBook is sending a ping to Apple’s
servers.”
Tim also dislikes how brands gather data that they were not supposed to store,
explaining that Google had information that he lived in a rented apartment based on his search
history: “That’s when things start to get scary when you don’t explicitly provide them, because
it gives them a lot of power over how they present the information or (...) how they want you
to act online and as a consumer. ” Cecil shares the same level of worry about technology
companies spying on consumers and getting annoyed by ads tha t stalk him across the internet.
However, he sees it more as spying rather than stalking: “ It’s espionage, definitely, because
they are taking data about you without your consent and without your knowledge.”

Confronting brands. Some informants dealt with the stress of flawed consumer -brand
relationships by planning actions to address the problem or by expressing their emotions. Layla
is disappointed with Tim Hortons for lowering their service quality over the years and losing
their Canadian tradition, eventually being sold to an international group. She coped with the
situation by boycotting the brand, which is also true for other brands sold to American
corporations: “I’ve always, in my whole life of being , boycotting America [ laughs]. (...) So,
yeah, of course it bothers me to see that slowly but surely other companies , basically, be
swallowed up by American ones.”
Another confrontational strategy is when consumers vent their rage against brands to
make it even with them. Even after 10 years of a bad experience with Eir, a telecommunications
provider in Ireland, Aaron does not get tired of complaining and spreading n egative word-of-
mouth, which was his main motivation to participate in the interview: “Any opportunity I have
to talk about Eir, I’ll convince people to stay away from them. They’re just brutal! They’re
really, really bad. ” When participants expressed hatr ed, it reverberated in their behaviour, as
Xavier avoids being near Fiat cars and warns everyone about them: “ I don’t like seeing them,
and I avoid stopping near them. (...) I even have a friend who (...) wants to buy a Fiat Doblò.
So I tell him not to, because it will ruin his life.”
In some situations, participants had to file formal complaints to solve their problems or
even go to court. That happened to Damian, who had his flight cancelled by American Airlines

105
and was left without accommodation or meals, leading him to file a complaint against the
company. Another type of reaction regards how consumers creatively resort to subversive
actions to cope with a bad experience. Martin does not approve of how Disney is using AI in
their productions and decided to boycott its newer movies, but still consumed the old content.
However, Martin decided to be subversive: “I would gladly pirate their content to avoid giving
them money because I don’t like what they’re doing now.” Similarly, Oliver cancelled Netflix
after realising that the third Twin Peaks season was not available and decided not to trust the
streaming services anymore, resorting to piracy as well.
Distancing from brands . Another way that consumers cope with flawed relationships
with brands is by avoiding, quitting, or fleeing them. Cecil avoids Trago Mills, a British retailer,
since the company does not care about the environment. Also, the CEO was involved in
controversies and discriminatory behaviours: “(...) he’s an extremely homophobic man who
advocated for gay men to be chemically castrated immediately, which isn’t really a good look
for a large company [laughs]. ” With the same rationale, Alexan der explains that he avoids
companies for their lack of moral values, such as Nestlé and, particularly, Japan Tobacco:
They know they’re harming society, and they do it anyway. I was going to work with
Japan Tobacco at one point. They wanted me to be an account manager for their
consumer research projects. And they wanted me to figure out a way to get smokers
not to quit. (...) “They’re already smoking. Why quit? And let’s find out what we can
say to them, so they don’t quit”. And I quit that job. I quit that company, the company
I was working for. “No, I’m not going to do that”, and I just left. (Alexander)
The way companies operate and their philosophy also prompt participants to avoid them,
as Raymond and Louise noted that Hewlett -Packard forces consumers to subscribe to its
services while delivering a poor experience. Louise once trusted the brand but chan ged her
mind: “(...) your printer doesn’t function right if you don’t sign up for their subscription has
completely changed the way I feel about them . (...) I will avoid that brand because of that. ”
Raymond has a similar understanding, which stopped him fr om using his HP printer: “ They
were trying to get me to buy a subscription for printer ink. The moment it was plugged in! (...)
That feels rather predatory in ways.”
Reframing the brand relationship. Not only do consumers confront brands and distance
themselves from them, but they also re -evaluate their appraisal of the relationship. Some
participants rationalised their choices, understanding that they were the best available option.

106
Although disliking American brands, Layla still shops at Walmart: “They’re cheaper. I hate the
fact that they’re Walmart and they’re American. But what can you do? ” In the same sense,
Sophia explains she grew up with fast-fashion retailers like Zara and is familiarised with them,
but avoids Shein: “They’re both bad, but Shein is like ten times worse.”
Another strategy to reframe how the brand is perceived is to cultivate a positive mindset.
Zachary commented on the way Chick -fil-A, an American restaurant chain, supported causes
he disagreed with. However, he reformulates his thinking to justify going there: “(...) they offer
amazing customer service. And they’re locally managed , and locally they’re franchises. (...)
And, you know, they get back to the community and all that. ” Maya also minimises the fact
that Chick-fil-A corporation was accused of being anti-LGBT: “(...) we finally, you know, have
a Chick-fil-A where I live here, and I go , I would say about half the employees are clearly
LGBT. So, it’s like what their corporate says and what they do seems quite different.”
Accommodating to the brand experience . The last coping strategy concerns how
consumers resign themselves and accept the flawed relationship with the brand. Even though
having negative feelings towards Google, Louise keeps using it because the research results are
good, conforming to the situa tion: “And I think that that’s part of the conversation , that how
difficult will it be to make a switch or find an equal alternative over just accepting something
that’s an annoyance .” Sometimes, the product can be irre sistible, despite the bad brand
reputation. Zoe thinks Nestlé is an evil company, but makes an exception: “ But do I still buy?
Did I buy a chocolate chip cookie, Nestlé cookies , literally this morning? Yes, they’re in my
fridge. (...) But I really want a cookie, though [laughs].”
There are also situations in which the consumer feels helpless, unable to confront the
situation. Several informants reported that they could not do anything other than accept having
a relationship with a particular brand. This situation is common for public concessions, such as
water, energy, and gas. Xavier commented that the water company in his area is not trustworthy,
as it fails to keep a steady water supply, but conforms to the situation: “ It’s like you’ve been
forced only to have this option your whole life, you know? You never expected another
alternative. So, I think it’s a conditioning to accept it.” It is an unescapable harsh reality to be
forced to buy from some companies, as Aaron points out: “ It’s just the price of electricity and
gas has gone very expensive. But everyone has to pay. So, what can you really do?”
Although consumers tolerate a bad brand relationship, that does not mean they are happy
with it. In some cases, they yearn for what the brands used to be. Louise dislikes how Chips

107
Ahoy tastes today to the point of giving up on it: “I used to love Chips Ahoy, and now we buy
them, and we don’t even finish the package because they’re just like, ‘Nah!’”. However, she
still got excited about a new co-branded packaging with Stranger Things, reminding her of her
childhood in the 80s. Ellie also feels nostalgic about Fiat, which reminds her of her young years
living in Italy. Nevertheless, she is mad about the corporate fusion with Chrysler, but it did not
prevent her from buying a Fiat car: “I felt sad. (...) But I will tell you, I did buy a used Fiat
Cinquecento. Used. It was five years old, stick shift. I missed Italy! [laughs].”
4.5 Discussion
This research reveals how flawed consumer-brand relationships are triggered, appraised,
developed, and coped with. We extend knowledge of a growing body of studies on negative
aspects towards brands, including brand hate, betrayal, avoidance, sabotage, and divorce
(Ferraz & Dallabrida, 2024; Kähr et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2009; Weitzl & Hutzinger, 2025;
Zarantonello et al., 2016) . Our research answers a call to investigate new brand relationship
types, define triggers, and explore the interactions and outcomes of these relationships (Alvarez
et al., 2023).
Since the initial work by Fournier (1998), whose primary focus was on positive
consumer-brand relationships, few studies have proposed frameworks to organise and explain
negative consumer-brand relationships. We expand on prior literature that proposed typologies
and theoretical models directed to brand contestation (Dietrich & Russell, 2021) , consumer
subversion (Wilson et al., 2022), and brand sabotage (Kähr et al., 2016). Our research also has
implications for negative brand personality (Malär & Giuffredi -Kähr, 2024), showing how it
interacts with emotions, behaviours, and coping mechanisms.
We make three interconnected contributions to literature. First, a framework is
introduced to explain the flawed consumer -brand relationships and their connection to stimuli
and coping mechanisms. Second, we discuss that dark brand personalities, appraisals of events,
relationships, emotions, coping strategies, and behaviours are interrelated and
multidimensional. Third, we build on the fragmented literature on brand hate to examine how
negative brand-related constructs relate to emotions and coping mechani sms. We detail these
contributions next.

108
4.5.1 Development of flawed consumer-brand relationships
Flawed consumer-brand relationships are developed through a series of processes and
interactions, as shown in Figure 4.1. Consumers face negative experiences triggered by the dark
brand personality traits (Malär & Giuffredi-Kähr, 2024). Their emotions will be influenced by
appraising the events along five dimensions (Roseman et al., 1990) . Motivation refers to
seeking awards or avoiding punishments, while the situation determines whether they are
present. Probability concerns whether the event is certain or uncertain, and legitimacy regards
whether a positive or negative outcome is deserved. Finally, the agency determines if the event
was caused by the self, the other, or the circumstances.
Figure 4.1 - Flawed consumer-brand relationships.

Source: author’s own work.
After appraising the negative events, consumers interact with the brands, eliciting
emotions and developing flawed relationships (Table 4.3). The emotions are combined with
coping mechanisms and behaviours (Table 4.5), leading to confrontation, accommodati on,
distancing, or reframing. The proposed framework organises and explains how diverse, flawed
consumer-brand relationships are structured, developed, nurtured, and handled. Different from
other models that focused on contestation, which refers to a chang e in brand meaning by
consumers (Dietrich & Russell, 2021), or on sabotage and how consumers aggressively attack
brands (Kähr et al., 2016), our framework is more comprehensive to encompass a diverse range
of negative reactions, relationships, and coping strategies. The identified negative consumer -

109
brand relationships surface more complex and nuanced experiences, not limited to anger or
meaning hijacking.
We also contribute to the scarce research on negative brand personality (Saeed et al.,
2022) by expanding the dark personality traits identified by previous research (Malär &
Giuffredi-Kähr, 2024). Our research illustrates how the dark traits, relationships, emotions, and
coping mechanisms interrelate, as consumers struggle to handle psychopathic, Machiavellian,
and narcissistic brands. Dark personality traits influence how consumers interact with brands,
with implications for consumer -brand relationship theory and customer relationship
management.
4.5.2 Multidimensional flawed relationships
Although we present a framework that could be seen as a linear movement from stimuli
to reactions, our research revealed that consumers are affected by dysfunctional relationships
not necessarily in a linear order. They might be coping with negative experi ences for years,
unable to get rid of the brand, or they could gradually divorce from a brand relationship. Rather
than defining a monolithic phenomenon, we draw on rock music, specifically Pink Floyd’s The
Dark Side of the Moon, for a metaphor. Figure 4.2 shows that when negative events pass
through a prism (The Dark Side of Brand Use), like white light, their composition can be seen.
Figure 4.3 draws on another metaphor to illustrate how the brand’s negative event can
be broken down. In a Rubik’s Cube, there are multiple combinations of colours, as the player
can rotate it upwards, downwards, and sideways. In the same vein, negative ex periences with
brands are multidimensional, comprising dark brand personality traits, appraisal of events,
emotions, relationships, coping mechanisms, and behaviours. These dimensions can take on an
infinite number of combinations depending on the consumer ’s experience, forming a flawed
relationship cube.

Figure 4.3 - Flawed relationship cube.

Figure 4.4 illustrates how one possible combination could be formed. Ticketmaster’s
dark brand personality is psychopathic, as Sophia sees it . She struggled to buy a show ticket
that only Ticketmaster sold, as in a domestic abuse relationship. The company’s website and
system crashed, preventing her from buying what she wanted, leading her to view the event as
certain and caused by the brand. S ophia cried a lot, feeling sad, and was very angry at
Ticketmaster, considering herself a victim of a criminal ( in her words, an enemy ). However,
she went to the show because she could only accommodate the situation and conform to it. As
this example shows, multiple combinations are possible, extending the theory of dysfunctional
brand relationships.

4.5.3 Going Beyond Brand Hate
Our research shows that life exists beyond brand hate. The fragmentation of the
literature (Yadav & Chakrabarti, 2022), multiple conceptualisations, a focus on psychological
rather than behavioural aspects (Aziz & Rahman, 2022), and the lack of a cohesive framework
(Ladeira et al., 2026) have turned brand hate into a fuzzy umbrella construct. Also, there are a
multitude of negative related constructs, such as brand shame (Weitzl & Hutzinger, 2025) ,
brand repulsion (Dessart & Cova, 2021), brand sabotage (Kähr et al., 2016) , brand avoidance
(Lee et al., 2009; Odoom et al., 2019), brand divorce (Ferraz & Dallabrida, 2024; Sussan et al.,
2012), and brand negativity (Dessart et al., 2020).
The proposed flawed consumer -brand relationship framework ( Figure 4. 1) helps
organise and integrate the different negative brand -related constructs. They can also be
combined with emotions and coping mechanisms ( Table 4.5). These combinations show that
negative experiences go beyond anger and fear, encompassing sadness and happiness as well
(Figure 4. 5). When sabotaging or expressing schadenfreude, for example, the consumer is
simultaneously angry and happy. On the other hand, it is possible to feel happy a nd sad if one
is addicted to a brand or yearns for an idealised past. In this sense, brand hate cannot account
for all negative consumer-brand emotions, relationships, and coping strategies and behaviours.
The multidimensionality of dysfunctional consumer-brand relationships shows that consumers
navigate a complex phenomenon far beyond mere hate.

112
Figure 4.5 - Brand relationship constructs and respective emotions.

4.5.4 Limitations and Future Research Directions
This research does not fully capture the complexity of negative consumer -brand
relationships. The limited interview sample and data from netnography and secondary sources
provide a partial understanding of how flawed relationships are triggered and developed. Future
research should further investigate how dysfunctional relationships can be theorised and
integrated with brand constructs, such as brand hate, shame, and sabotage. Our framework is
an initial step towards a theory of negative consumer-brand relationships, which should also be
compared and contrasted with the brand relationship quality framework from past research
(Fournier, 1998) . Future studies could empirically test our model to determine whether the
proposed appraisals, emotions, coping strategies, and behaviours align with theoretical
expectations.
We encourage future investigations to increase our understanding of negative consumer-
brand relationships. The identified types in this research are not exhaustive, as more nuanced
and distinct ones might emerge from other research. There is a need to deve lop the brand
relationship spectrum further and clarify its boundaries (Alvarez et al., 2023) , as well as to
compare negative and positive relationships. The development and the trajectories of flawed
consumer-brand relationships also deserve more attention. Future studies could investigate how
they start, grow, develop, and end over time, compari ng the trajectories of different
dysfunctional brand-consumer relationships.

113
CHAPTER 5 – CONCLUSION

The objective of this doctoral thesis was to investigate idiosyncratic consumer -brand
relationships, understanding and identifying the peculiar positive and negative bonds derived
from them. Although prior research examined a diverse range of relationships, they were
concentrated in a few, such as brand love and friendship (Alvarez et al., 2023) or brand hate
and avoidance (Mushtaq et al., 2024; Yadav & Chakrabarti, 2022) . Chapter 2 explored the
positive consumer -brand relationships, epitomised by brand tattoos, while Chapter 3
investigated polarised brands, explaining the different motivations regarding love and hate
feelings. Finally, Chapter 4 discussed the flawed relationships consumers have with brands ,
focusing on negative brand experiences.
5.1 Theoretical contributions
Our research has three key contributions to the consumer-brand relationship theory.
First, we have identified 34 new or less theorised idiosyncratic relationships, evaluated as
positive (13), negative (14), ambiguous (4), or neutral (3). The identification of these
relationships responds to a call to investigate other types that have not been previously studied
(Alvarez et al., 2023). Table 5.1 summarises all relationships identified in this work.

Vintage Mates.
Negative Absent/Orphans, Activists, Anti -Narcissists/Snobs, Bullies/Bullied, Criminals/Victims,
Crooks/Suckers, Deceivers/Deceived, Dictator/Subjects, Divorced, Forced Marriage,
Host/Parasite, Moral Enemies, Spies/Targets, and Traitors/Betrayed.
Ambiguous Dealers/Addicts, Domestic Abuse, Guilty Pleasures, and Sadists/Masochists.

The identified relationships show that consumers have complex interactions with the
brands they love and hate , which can bring intense positive emotions and benefits, as in a
therapist-patient bond, but can also be dysfunctional and stressful, as in a criminal -victim
relationship. Other relationship types lie in the middle , such as in a guilty pleasure one,
revealing ambiguous bonds that can be simultaneously beneficial and detrimental.

114
Second, our work revealed that consumers have dynamic , polysemic, and multiple
relationships with the same brands. They use brands to develop identity projects (Arnould &
Thompson, 2005), seeking a desired, s table self in a fragmented world (Appau et al., 2020) .
The connection with brands is evaluated based on consumer values and the implicit brand
promise (Bhargava & Bedi, 2022), thereby unearthing strong feelings towards them .
Consumers build their individual and social selves through intricate, complex, and idiosyncratic
relationships with brands, tattooing them (Chapter 2), developing polarised feelings (Chapter
3), or coping with negative experiences (Chapter 4).
Third, this doctoral thesis extends consumer-brand relationship theory by investigating
the dark side of brand use. Our research shows that negative brand personalities (Malär &
Giuffredi-Kähr, 2024; Saeed et al., 2022) foster broken relationshi ps, which consumers cope
with through accommodation, distancing, confrontation, or reframing. While previous research
focused primarily on brand hate as an umbrella construct, this work pursu ed a broader
investigation of negative emotions and behaviours. The proposed framework helps explain how
dysfunctional relationships are nurtured, developed, understood, and confronted.
5.2 Managerial implications
The first key implication of our research for marketing and branding managers concerns
the identification of several consumer -brand relationships. Understanding them enables
addressing consumers as idiosyncratic individuals rather than a monolith. They develop strong,
deep relationships based on emotions and experiences. Managers need to identify these
relationships, quantify them, manage their implications, and propose marketing strategies to
enhance their positive aspects while minimising their negative ones. Promotional activities can
be tailored to each relationship, enhancing the bond with the company’s brands. For example,
a vintage-mates relationship can be nurtured through the launch of nostalgic products, while
teammate-based relationship s can reinforce the idea that the brand is a vehicle for the
consumer’s success.
Given that consumer-brand relationships are dynamic and multifaceted, this should be
considered a point of attention for brand managers. Practitioners cannot consider that their
brands foster only one type of relationship. If multiple relationships occur simultaneously, it is
crucial to investigate how they interact and impact the brand’s development. It is also important
to understand whether a particular product or service fosters one type of positive relationship,
while another might trigger a negative one. For instance, a soulmate relationship is beneficial

115
to the brand, but it can also lead to addiction, which would need to be addressed by a responsible
policy from the company. Thus, there is no “one size fits all” strategy regarding consumer -
brand relationships.
The dark side of brand use demands a reflection from managers and companies.
Practitioners need to revisit how their brands interact with consumers and investigate whether
they exhibit negative brand personality traits. A change in approach is needed to address the
negative aspects , minimising or su ppressing them. Bad experiences deeply affect how
consumers buy and express their feelings, shaping how the brand performs not only in the
present but also in the long run. Even minor mistakes can haunt the brand for many years ,
condemning it to damnation. Apart from that, brand managers need to understand that even
iconic brands are not unanimous, sparking strong reactions from detractors, who consider them
anti-iconic. The management of these brands thus has to consider palliative measures to address
anti-brand activists.
5.3 Research limitations and future research opportunities
This work has some limitations that need to be disclosed. The relationships identified,
either positive, negative, ambiguous, or neutral, are pieces of a greater puzzle. Our research
does not fully capture the interrelations between them and brands. There is a need for further
development of a general theory of consumer-brand relationships that accounts for the myriad
of beneficial and dysfunctional bonds. We encourage scholars to d elve into current research
and propose innovative approaches to understanding how consumers build relationships with
brands and to discover other relationship types . As we have argued that the relationships are
multiple, complex, and polysemic, future studies need to take that into account for proposing
new theoretical perspectives. Our proposal for a flawed consumer -brand relationship
framework is a preliminary , modest step towards this end, but it focuses sole ly on negative
experiences.
Although our research unearthed new consumer-brand relationships, it was focused on
idiosyncratic ones, which can be restricted to specific groups. Future studies need to investigate
further their frequency and deepen their understanding across other brands, sectors, and
companies. In this sense, this work relied only on qualitative methodology, prioritising a
phenomenological approach. Our narrow methodological choice needs to be complemented
with other qualitative and quantitative methods. Other epistemological views would diversify
how consumer-brand relationships are understood and theorised.

116
5.4 Social Implications
The research conducted in this PhD thesis has several social implications that could be
subject to future public policies. Findings from the three studies show that consumers nurture
intense relationships with brands, which are not always beneficial. They reported addictive
behaviours towards brands that have implications for mental and physical health. For example,
some ingested high doses of sugar while others spent hours consuming digital technology. Also,
there were alarming accounts about bullying and sexist behaviours while consuming brands .
Public policies and regulations should be proposed to control and lower the exposure of
individuals to addicti ve behaviours and to punish brands for allowing bullying and
discriminatory episodes while using their services.
Another social implication regards consumer rights protection. Our informants brought
innumerable examples of flawed consumer-brand relationships that were triggered by negative
brand personalities. There were reports of mistreatment, manipulation, misleading advertising,
monopolistic enforcement, deceptive promotions, and many others. Governments could
propose regulatory measures to strengthen consumer rights protection, thereby disincentivising
predatory company behaviour and the development of negative brand personalities.
Finally, our work also has implications for environmental and social policies.
Participants reported a strong aversion to brands that polluted, mistreated workers, disregarded
unions, took advantage of universal public goods (such as water), tested products on animals,
failed to protect minorities, or backed countries that started wars. Government bodies could
rethink public policies to increase companies’ responsibility towards the United Nations’
Sustainable Development Goals (e.g., responsible production and consumption and good health
and well-being), thereby diminishing the corporate impact reported by our informants.

ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS

My academic journey began late in my career, after I had worked for several companies,
most of them in marketing. The reasoning and the types of questions that academics ask and
answer are much deeper and more challenging. I am grateful to have chosen this new life cycle
and to be able to contribute to society, academia, my colleagues, and students. Completing a
doctorate is a burdensome task that often feels overwhelming and tiring . It is an intellectually
strong effort to p ut your thoughts on paper, organ ise them, concatenate your ideas, integrate
them with theory, and make your research interesting, original, and meaningful. Learning and
effort are continuous and never-ending, not stopping after earning a degree. A doctorate gives
you critical thinking and methodological tools to move ahead and continue the goal of any
researcher: to understand and theorise about what is not known.
I want to give my deepest thanks to everyone who walked alongside me in this journey,
helping me, guiding the way, and supporting me with their friendship. First, without my family,
I would never have come this far. My family’s academic background strongly influenced who
I am and how I think, starting with my grandfather, who is an indirect influence on my academic
interests. Although he passed away the same year I was born , his influence, stories, and being
one of the most prominent philosophers in Brazil have always made me proud. My mother was
a good companion during my PhD, enhancing my critical thinking and always questioning the
status quo. My father , my stepmother, and my aunt incentivised my studies, giving me the
strength and confidence to change my career to academia. M any thanks to my brother, my
sister-in-law, and my nephews for their support throughout my academic life.

RESUMO

O objetivo deste trabalho foi investigar as relações peculiares e idiossincráticas que os
consumidores cultivam com as marcas, sejam elas negativas, positivas, neutras ou ambíguas.
Nossa pesquisa revelou que as marcas funcionam como sinalizadoras de identidade pessoal,
carregam significados simbólicos, atuam como parceiras em relacionamentos, enfatizam
sentimentos polarizados e desencadeiam comportamentos e emoções negativos. Com base em
uma abordagem fenomenológica, aplicamos uma gama de métodos qualitativos para investigar
as relações entre consumidor e marca, incluindo entrevistas em profundidade, netnografia e
dados secundários. Contribuímos para a teoria ao identificar e definir 34 relacionamentos
idiossincráticos nov os ou pouco teorizad os, como terapeutas/pacientes, vigaristas/ trouxas,
prazeres com remorso e agnosticismo. Uma segunda contribuição diz respeito a como essas
relações auxiliam os consumidores em seus projetos de identidade, influenciando seus eus
individuais e sociais. A terceira contribuição consiste em uma proposta de modelo para explicar
as relações negativas entre consumidor e marca, abrangendo personalidades sombrias da marca,
avaliação de situações, emoções suscitadas, relacionamentos falhos, bem como mecanismos e
comportamentos de enfrentamento. Este trabalho também tem implicações sociais relacionadas
à saúde mental (por exemplo, bullying e dependência), à proteção dos direitos do consumidor
e aos Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável da ONU.

Palavras-chave: relacionamento com marcas, branding, relações idiossincráticas da marca ,
comportamento do consumidor, gestão de marcas.

consumers have with brands they love and hate . 2026. Doctoral Thesis (PhD in Business
Administration) – Postgraduate Research Program in Administration, Higher School of
Advertising and Marketing / Escola Superior de Propaganda e Marketing (ESPM), São Paulo.

ABSTRACT

The objective of this work was to investigate the peculiar and idiosyncratic relationships that
consumers foster with brands, either negative, positive, neutral, or ambiguous . Our research
revealed how brands work as beacons of self -identity, carry symbolic meanings, function as
relationship partners, emphasise polarised feelings, and trigger negative behaviours and
emotions. Drawing on a phenomenological approach, we applied a range of qualitative methods
to investigate consumer -brand relationships, including in -depth interviews, netnography, and
secondary data. We contribute to theory by identifying and defining 34 new or less theorised
idiosyncratic relationships, such as therapists/patients, crooks/suckers, guilty pleasures, and
agnostics. A second contribution regards how these relationships help consumers with their
identity projects, influencing their individual and social selves. The third contribution concerns
a proposal for a framework to explain negative consumer -brand relationships, encompassing
dark brand personalities, appraisal of events, elicited emotions, flawed relationships, and coping
mechanisms and behaviours. This work also has social implications regarding mental health
(e.g., bullying and addiction) , consumer rights protection, and the UN’s Sustainable
Development Goals.

Keywords: brand relationship, branding, brand relationship idiosyncrasy, consumer behaviour,
brand management.

CHAPTER 1 - INTRODUCTION

1.1 Motivation for the research
Several authors have studied brand relationships since the seminal work of Fournier
(1998), who introduced the brand relationship quality (BRQ) framework and examined the
various m eaningful relationships between brands and consumers (Alvarez et al., 2023) .
Consumers develop deep emotional bonds with brands, which vary in polarity and strength
(Fetscherin et al., 2019; Fetscherin & Veloutsou, 2024) . In this sense, t he brand relationship
research stream expanded the brand loyalty construct, considering the interconnections with
brands as a dynamic phenomenon more in line with the post -modern fragmented consumer
(Fournier & Yao, 1997). Researchers have delved into the myriad of relationships and followed
several streams related to brand trust, brand communities, brand love, brand cult, self -
connection, culture, and storytelling (Fetscherin & Heinrich, 2015).
First, scholars explored the positive emotions and behaviours associated with the
connection between brands and consumer s. The brand love construct was proposed , which
comprises positive emotional associations, self -brand integration, and passion -driven
behaviours (Batra et al., 2012). In this sense, consumption products are used to create meanings,
extending the self (Belk, 1988) , as the effort dispensed in loved objects helps consumers
establish a coherent self and solves potential existential conflicts (Ahuvia, 2005). Brand love is
also associated with brand loyalty and positive word of mouth, with the effect being more
significant in h edonic categories (Carroll & Ahuvia, 2006) . Depending on the consumer’s
susceptibility to influence and the brand’s self -expression, consumers can experience
harmonious or obsessive passion (Swimberghe et al., 2014).
Academics later studied negative emotions related to brand -consumer relationships. In
contrast with brand love and other positive-related constructs, brand hate, avoidance,
retaliation, anti-consumption, and other subversive behaviours were identified (Wilson et al.,
2022) but are less theorised (Mushtaq et al., 2024; Yadav & Chakrabarti, 2022) . The intensity
of consumers’ negative emotions towards brands can range from severe to mild, influenced by
personality traits (Kucuk, 2019) . Brand hate has active and passive components, with
behavioural outcomes including c omplaints and negative word of mouth (Zarantonello et al.,
2016; Zhang & Laroche, 2020).

16
Not only have studies investigated negative and positive emotions and behaviours
related to brands, but they have also explored polarised relationships. Oppositional brand
loyalty refers to the meanings consumers derive from brands they consume, rather than those
they do not (Muñiz & Hamer, 2001) . Identifying with a brand makes consumers oppose rival
brands, as these rivals m ight threaten t heir self -concept (Liao et al., 2021) . Scholars have
discussed brand rivalries and found that they are related to schadenfreude (feeling happy at
others’ misfortunes) (Phillips-Melancon & Dalakas, 2014), humour and ridicule (Ewing et al.,
2013), an increase in the likelihood of adopting new products (S. A. Thompson & Sinha, 2008),
and enhance brand and consumer group distinctiveness (Berendt et al., 2018) . The effect of
polarisation might also be harmful, with a negative impact on returns but a lower perception of
risk (X. Luo, Raithel, et al., 2013; X. Luo, Wiles, et al., 2013). More recently, brand polarisation
has been studied as a more general phenomenon, with scholars arguing that rivalry is a
particular type (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019, 2024).
Apart from studies on individual relationships and emotions, another academic stream
examined brand communities and how they foster deep connections among consumer groups
and brands. Brand communities partake in rituals, foster a sense of members’ distinctiveness
from outsiders, and share a sense of moral responsibility (Muñiz & O’Guinn, 2001) . They
develop collective and collaborative values via practices, behaviours, and performances (Schau
et al., 2009). Brand communities enhance community engagement, though they also stimulate
reactance to normative rules (Algesheimer et al., 2005) and heighten tensions against the brand
to preserve the community’s independence (Kornum et al., 2017).
The intense emotions associated with brand -consumer relationships and a sense of
community are intrinsic to how people understand themselves. Consumers’ self -concept is
based on contrasting ingroups versus outgroups (Tajfel & Turner, 2004). Therefore, individuals
have a stronger self-brand connection with brands that are consistent with their ingroup (Escalas
& Bettman, 2005), a s they seek self -congruity (Sirgy, 1982, 2018) . The brand -consumer
connection can go further when individuals feel an identity fusion with brands (Swann et al.,
2012), being immune to transgressions and negative feedback (Lin & Sung, 2014).
Although brand relationship scholars focused on positive and negative emotions and
behaviours towards brands, explored the functioning of brand communities, and investigated
brand-self interactions, few studies explored intense and idiosyncratic relationships between
consumers and brands, focusing more on particular types of relationships such as brand love,
hate, and friendships (Alvarez et al., 2023). Moreover, brand hate and avoidance remain nascent

17
topics in the literature, as scholars have paid more attention to positive relationships such as
brand loyalty , love, and attachment (Mushtaq et al., 2024; Roy et al., 2022; Yadav &
Chakrabarti, 2022) . Regarding brand polarisation, which comprises positive and negative
emotions towards brands, the topic is still scarcely studied (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019) and
underdeveloped (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2024).
1.2 Research objectives
First, we explore consumers’ idiosyncratic connections with their most loved and
admired brands in light of the consumer-brand relationship theory and consumer culture theory
(CCT). The CCT examines how consumers perceive meanings embedded in brands and
consumer products to make sense of themse lves and incorporate them into their lifestyles
(Arnould & Thompson, 2005). Second, our work investigates some brands that elicit polarised
consumer feelings, as they have lovers and haters. Brand polarisation comprises four
dimensions: brand passion, self -brand benchmarking, intra -group identification, and inter -
group dissociation (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2024). Third, this thesis explores the negative or dark
side of the relationship with brands, focusing on negative feelings and behaviours . Brand hate
is a multidimensional construct (Yadav & Chakrabarti, 2022) that includes negative emotions
(anger, contempt, fear, disappointment , etc.), which lead to reactions such as attack (negative
word of mouth) , avoidance (reduction or cessation) or approach (complaining and protest)
(Zarantonello et al., 2016).
In summary, our doctoral thesis explores consumers’ peculiar relationships with brands,
which can be positive or negative, and brands that provoke both polarising feelings, answering
a call to investigate new brand-consumer relationship types (Alvarez et al., 2023) . To clarify
what we understand by idiosyncratic relationships, we provide the following definition: brand
relationship idiosyncrasy concerns the peculiar and characteristic bonds, mannerisms, habits,
and mental conditions that consumers have towards brands, which are susceptible to particular
stimuli. We intend to answer the following research question: How do consumers have intense,
idiosyncratic relationships with brands they love and hate?
We adopted qualitative methods to better understand the idiosyncratic relationships
consumers have with brands, a research stream that remains underdeveloped and less theorised.
While positivist ontology and quantitative studies focus on measuring reality and proposing
general laws, interpretative approaches hold that reality is socially constructed and emphasise
understanding behaviour rather than predicting it (Hudson & Ozanne, 1988) . Choosing a

18
qualitative approach for the current thesis is adequate since few qualitative studies researched
the different types of brand relationships (love, passion, hate, friendships, addiction, and others)
in the past years, and the most prominent methodological approaches were Structural Equation
Modeling (SEM) and experiments (Alvarez et al., 2023; Gilal et al., 2023; Mushtaq et al., 2024;
Yadav & Chakrabarti, 2022).
1.3 Contributions
This research examines why consumers have peculiar bonds with the brands they love
and hate, unearthing new types of idiosyncratic relationships and how they are enacted. More
specifically, we contribute to theories of the self in consumer behaviour and branding, exploring
their interconnections with brand identity, personality, and core values. The intensity of the
relationship can be beneficial, nurturing passion and love (Gilal et al., 2023), helping structure
the self and provide meaning (Fetscherin & Heinrich, 2015), or might be associated with hate
(Mushtaq et al., 2024; Roy et al., 2022; Zarantonello et al., 2016; Zhang & Laroche, 2020) ,
addiction (Cui et al., 2018; Mrad et al., 2020; Mrad & Cui, 2017) , and aversion (Park et al.,
2013b).
More specifically, t his thesis contributes to consumer -brand relationship theory as
follows: (1) by theorising and defining the idiosyncratic relationships; (2) by understanding
how the relationships affect the consumer self and are a reflection of culture; (3) by proposing
a flawed consumer-brand relationship framework to explain the connections among dark brand
personalities, relationships, emotions, and coping mechanisms . The practical implications of
our study are to show marketers how consumers interact passionately with their brands and how
businesses can respond, nurture, foster, or manage these unique relationships.
1.4 Thesis structure
To accomplish our goals, we divided our doctoral thesis into three articles. The first
article focused on the positive pole of the idiosyncratic brand-consumer relationship, explaining
why consumers have tattooed brands. The second article discussed brands that elicit polarised
consumer reactions, examining the different motivations that lead consumers to either love or
hate them. The third and last paper explored flawed consumer-brand relationships, proposing a
framework to explain the interactions with negative brand personalities, elicited emotions, and
coping mechanisms.

19
Figure 1.1 shows the overall structure of the doctoral thesis. The first article on brand
tattoos represents the positive pole of brand relationship idiosyncrasy: consumers’ most alluring
feelings toward a brand. The second article concerns the negative and positive emotions and
behaviours that polarising brands elicit in consumers . The third and final article is at the
negative pole, discussing brands consumers dislike. The three articles examine consumers’
idiosyncratic behaviours when engaging with brands.

CHAPTER 2 – POSITIVE POLE: BRAND LOVE VIA BRAND TATTOOS1

2.1 Introduction
Consumers have relationships with brands as they would with people (Fournier, 1998;
Fournier & Alvarez, 2012). They develop deep emotional bonds with brands, sharing affinities
and enthusiasm with other like -minded individuals in communities (Fetscherin et al., 2021;
Fetscherin & Veloutsou, 2024). Scholars have studied the deep consumer-brand bonds, such as
brand love (Batra et al., 2012; Carroll & Ahuvia, 2006; Rahman et al., 2021) , brand passion
(Gilal et al., 2023; Swimberghe et al., 2014), brand attachment (Park et al., 2010; Shimul, 2022;
Thomson et al., 2005), brand engagement (Fernandes & Moreira, 2019), and brand pride (Kaur
& Verma, 2024) . Strong connections with brands have also been theorised under negative
relationships of brand hate (Mushtaq et al., 2024; Zarantonello et al., 2016; Zhang & Laroche,
2020) and, more recently, polarised brands, which attract passionate feelings of love and hate
(Monahan et al., 2023; Osuna Ramírez et al., 2024).
Although studies have advanced in understanding consumer-brand connections, there is
a gap regarding new brand relationship types to capture the diversity of connections, their
valence and strength (Alvarez et al., 2023; Fournier & Alvarez, 2013) , and how they interact
with the consumers’ identity projects. The literature is also silent about multiple and dynamic
relationships consumers have with the same brand, as scholars have theorised only about single
steady relationship types (e.g., brand lo ve, pride, addiction, friendship, and hate) (Alvarez et
al., 2023) or changes from one to another (e.g., love turning to hate or vice versa) (Grégoire &
Fisher, 2008; Langner et al., 2016; Zarantonello et al., 2018).
Consumer Culture Theory (CCT) scholars complement the brand relationship literature
describing consumers’ profound feelings for their beloved brands and discuss consumers’
identity projects under a fragmented sense of self (Arnould & Thompson, 2005) . The
understanding that people use objects and brands as part of their extended self (Belk, 1988) is
an evolving set of ideas which is transitioning to digitalised (Belk, 2013) and transhuman (Lima
& Belk, 2024) versions of personhood. Consumer researchers are shifting their view from
considering people to have stable core selves to understanding them as a network of assembled
experiences, practices, and narratives (C. J. Thompson, 2024) . This view has also been

21
discussed under the dialectical division of the consumer’s self and body as agentic and stable
versus unbounded and dynamic (Appau et al., 2020; Preece et al., 2024).
This paper discusses particular and multiple interrelations between brands and
consumers, epitomised by brand tattoos. There are few studies focused on extremely sturdy
connections between consumers and brands, including brand sacredness (Fuschillo et al., 2024;
Wang et al., 2019) and brand addiction (Cui et al., 2018; Ghorbanzadeh, 2024; Mrad & Cui,
2017). From this perspective, brand tattoos represent a deep bond between consumers and
brands but are only tangentially mentioned in the literature. For instance, studies show Harley-
Davidson aficionados tattooing brand symbols to represent their devotion (Rahman et al., 2021;
Schouten & McAlexander, 1995).
The interrelatedness between loyal consumers and tattooed brands seems
straightforward due to the identification of the self with the brand lifestyle (Orend & Gagné,
2009). However, a small number of studies have discussed the meaning of tattooed brands and
have not explored it from the consumer perspective, focusing on sponsorship tattooing
(Weidner et al., 2016) , tattooist perceptions related to brand tattoos (Bengtsson et al., 2005) ,
the body commodification by tattooed corporate logos (Orend & Gagné, 2009) or the extension
of brands to the body via advertising (Bjerrisgaard et al., 2013).
Scholars have explored the relationship between tattoos and post-modern consumption,
which considers the individual fragmented, seeking freedom of movement and not subjecting
to a single reality or way of being (Firat & Venkatesh, 1995). Tattoos are in the middle of the
fragmented tension between the post -modern self and the search for a coherent identity
(Patterson & Schroeder, 2010) . Tattooing brings out contemporary cultural contradictions,
showing a dynamic tension between durable versus transient consumption (Steadman, Banister,
et al., 2023; Steadman et al., 2019). It exposes the body’s and identity’s malleability, although
permanently marking them (Patterson, 2018), and fits the self -narrative as points of reference
that allow individuals to control their lives and express their idiosyncrasies (Oksanen &
Turtiainen, 2005).
This study aims to analyse the intense bond between consumers and their tattooed
brands by understanding why they tattoo them and theorising implications for the brand
relationship literature. Since there is scarce theorisation about branding and tattoos, this work
aims to fill this lacuna by contributing to the literature regarding consumer-brand relationships,
self, body, and tattoos and presenting the results from consumer interviews. Interpretative

22
Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) was adopted to explore the following research question:
what types of relationships do consumers have with the brands they tattoo?
This research has two main contributions to the literature. First, it extends the brand
relationship literature by discussing new types of consumer -brand connections uncovered
through brand tattoos that are new or scarcely theorised (Alvarez et al., 2023; Fournier &
Alvarez, 2013) : best friends forever (BFF), family ties, childhood buddies, teammates,
dealers/addicts, therapists/patients, gurus/disciples, soulmates, partisans, and vintage mates.
Second, this study reveals that consumers can have multiple and dynamic relationships with the
same brand, impacting their identity projects. Brand tattoos are polysemic and incomplete
symbols representing a desire for a stable sense of self.
2.2 Literature Review
2.2.1 Consumer-Brand Relationships
The relationship between consumers and brands has been extensively researched over
the past decades since the first seminal papers in the 1990s (Fetscherin & Heinrich, 2015;
Fetscherin & Veloutsou, 2024) . This research stream assumes that individuals see brands as
relationship partners (Fournier, 1998), while the level of passion determines the strength of the
connection (Fetscherin et al., 2019). Consumers develop feelings and want to be close to brands
(Veloutsou, 2007) , cultivating several interconnections (Bagozzi et al., 2021) and
psychologically benefiting from engaging with them (Razmus, 2025).
A variety of relationships have been proposed and analysed, such as arranged marriages,
best friendships, and enmities (Bagozzi et al., 2021; Fournier, 1998) . Even after years of
development from the original brand relationship typology (Fournier, 1998), only brand love
came up as a core construct in the last decades (Alvarez et al., 2023). There is a need for more
studies concerning new brand relationship types to capture a broader aspect of the phenomenon
(Alvarez et al., 2023).
Moreover, scholars have not focused on consumers’ multiple and dynamic relationships
with the same brand, studying single positive and negative consumer -brand bonds (Fetscherin
et al., 2019, 2021; Fetscherin & Heinrich, 2015; Fetscherin & Veloutsou, 2024) . Existing
research has focused on changes in the relationship (Alvarez et al., 2021), such as love turning
to hate (Grégoire et al., 2009) , ruptures that lead to divorce (Ferraz & Dallabrida, 2024) ,
functional, symbolic, and moral transgressions triggering consumer animosity (Tolunay &

23
Veloutsou, 2025), in paths that evolve from neutral or disliking to brand love (Langner et al.,
2016) or trajectories culminating in brand hate (Zarantonello et al., 2018) . Another recent
research stream has discussed polarised brands, which simultaneously have haters and lovers
(X. Luo, Raithel, et al., 2013; X. Luo, Wiles, et al., 2013; Osuna Ramírez et al., 2024) but not
examined multiple or mixed relationship types with the same brand (e.g., love-hate).
The literature has also focused more on positive relationships than negative ones
(Bagozzi et al., 2021; Brandão & Popoli, 2022) , which led some researchers to propose that
brand relationship should be defined as a bond based on positive experiences (Schreuder et al.,
2024). Scholars have explored the strength and intensity of relationships, proposing constructs
such as brand attachment (Park et al., 2010; Shimul, 2022; Thomson et al., 2005) , brand love
(Batra et al., 2012; Carroll & Ahuvia, 2006; Rahman et al., 2021; Robertson et al., 2022), brand
passion (Gilal et al., 2023; Swimberghe et al., 2014), brand engagement (Fernandes & Moreira,
2019), brand spirituality/sacredness (Fuschillo et al., 2024; S. Luo & Hamlin, 2022; Wang et
al., 2019), and brand pride (Helm et al., 2016; Kaur & Verma, 2024).
Although consumers seem to benefit from positive interactions with brands, they might
as well develop addictions to fulfil self -expression needs and status (Mrad et al., 2020) , have
compulsive and obsessive uncontrollable urges (Cui et al., 2018; Le, 2021) , be influenced by
their dark personality traits intensifying competitive behaviours (Shimul et al., 2025) or develop
brand addiction as a consequence from love and jealousy (Ghorbanzadeh, 2024). Addiction is
just one negative side of consumer-brand relationships since consumers can be subversive and
incorporate harmful behaviours, leading them to engage proactively or reactively against firms
(Wilson et al., 2022). They might take extreme measures like brand sabotage (Kähr et al., 2016)
and anti-brand activism (Dessart et al., 2020; Rodrigues et al., 2021; Romani et al., 2015) , or
less strong reactions such as brand avoidance (Lee et al., 2009; Odoom et al., 2019) .
Nevertheless, most studies explored hate towards brands as a more general phenomenon,
characterised as an attitude, motivation, or emotion (Mushtaq et al., 2024) . There is
multidimensionality in brand hate, which comprises a constellation of emotions such as dislike,
fear, and hatred (Yadav & Chakrabarti, 2022; Zhang & Laroche, 2020) , with consumers
showing passive or active brand hate (Zarantonello et al., 2016).
In sum, the literature review shows a need for further studies concerning new types of
brand relationships and a lack of investigation of multiple and dynamic relationships with the
same brand. There was a concentration on positive relationships and less on negative ones, with
few discussions related to mixed feelings.

24
2.2.2 Self & Body
The way that consumer research scholars discuss the mind -self-body interrelations is
first related to a contraposition between the inner self (personal) and the outer self (social)
(Featherstone, 1982, 2010; Kuuru, 2022), which is a dynamic socio-cultural process that varies
in a continuum (Turner et al., 1994) . The social structures are embodied by constituting
practices external to the person (Murphy et al., 2018), reflecting preferred social meanings and
ideologies of self-control (Thompson & Hirschman, 1995). For instance, there are tensions and
anxieties related to the mothering body against the exercising body (Spotswood & Gurrieri,
2024), advertising depicting women’s bodies (Balog, 2024; Joy & Venkatesh, 1994) , normal
versus deviant personal appearances (Holbrook et al., 1998), or changes during pregnancy and
immigrants’ acculturation (Min & Peñaloza, 2019).
The second focus is related to the fragmentation of the post-modern self (Belk, 2017) as
the extended self (Belk, 1988) transitions from a coherent and stable state to an assemblage of
life narratives structured under consumer distributed networks (Thompson, 2024). Consumers
are agentic and self-determined individuals with a core stable self and clear internal and external
boundaries. At the same time, they are also unfinished and dynamic dividuals with many porous
composites in which social structures are embedded (Appau et al., 2020) . Multiple
embodiments separate the person from the self-identity via disembodiment and re-embodiment
(Min & Peñaloza, 2019; Preece et al., 2024) , which can be a permanent or transient process
(Appau et al., 2020) . The fragmentation can eventually lead to merging with technology or
creating new versions of transhumans or even post -humans that transcend bodies and selves
(Lima & Belk, 2024).
The third dialectical discussion in consumption related to mind -body-self regards
perceptions and practices. Several forms of embodiment happen when consumers are involved
in bodily sensorial engagements that affect their behaviours and thoughts (Merleau-Ponty,
1962; Zanette et al., 2024) . For example, body techniques like swimming and motorcycling
help people embed shared knowledge and social practices (Murphy et al., 2018) . Consumer
subcultures mingle mind, body, and senses via embodiment (Kuuru, 2022), which can help
people feel inside and outside themselves, culminating in a cathartic moment (Preece et al.,
2024).
Consumer research also deliberates on imaginative and subjective relationships between
consumers, brands, and bodies. Even though it is impossible to escape one’s body when using

25
masks, tattooing the skin, and putting on makeup, people are projected into an imaginary
utopian body when doing so (Foucault, 2006; Roux & Belk, 2019) . In this sense, brands and
consumption objects are imbued with aesthetic meanings, passing through a process of
aestheticisation that transforms them into sublime, beautiful, and moving things (Dagalp &
Hartmann, 2022). The brands’ aestheticisation is incorporated and embedded by consumers via
their bodies and tattoos.
To summarise, scholars have contraposed inner (personal) versus outer (social) selves,
exploring the fragmentation of the consumer identity. There is a change from a coherent state
to an assemblage of narratives and distributed networks, as consumers are d ivided between
individuals with single, finished, and stable selves to dividuals with multiple, unfinished, and
porous characteristics. The meanings, subcultures, and knowledge are incorporated and
embedded by consumers via aesthetics, perceptions and social practices.
2.2.3 Tattoos, Culture, and Consumers
It would be possible to consider tattoos as symbols without meaning, fashion accessories
or temporary body modifications (Sweetman, 1999) since they are increasingly consumed and
widespread (Roux & Belk, 2019; Sierra et al., 2013) . However, tattoos are different from
consumption objects because they are permanent, cannot be divorced from their production,
and are a combination of body modification and cultural artefacts (Sweetman, 1999). Tattoos
are time markers as they inscribe memories on the body, bring continuity and stability
(Steadman et al., 2019) , delineate the body’s limitations (Fisher, 2002) , and are used as a
medium to cope with life transitions (Krtalić et al., 2025) . However, neither identity nor
meanings attributed to tattoos are necessarily fixed in time (Owens et al., 2023; Steadman,
Banister, et al., 2023).
As the self acquires meaning when expressed through an assemblage of narratives
(Thompson, 2024), the same process occurs with tattoos. People tattoo themselves to control
their lives and to serve as reference marks for their stories and personal myths (Oksanen &
Turtiainen, 2005; Velliquette et al., 2006). Since the body is intimate and controllable, it offers
a safe, close, and unique place for tattoos that remind deceased loved ones (Steadman, Medway,
et al., 2023) . Tattoo consumption reproduces a coherent and personalised narrative that
connects the past, present, and future (Patterson, 2018).
Some authors examined how people tattoo themselves and their motivations, from
aesthetics to personal narratives, affiliations, resistance, and spirituality (Wohlrab et al., 2007).

26
Body art is part of the extended self and brings satisfaction, but it might also lead to addiction
and regret (Velliquette et al., 1998) . Once considered a form of transgression, stigmatisation
and marginalisation, tattoos are increasingly accepted by society, although there are still
negative attitudes associated with tattooed individuals (Zestcott et al., 2018) . The decision to
tattoo oneself is influenced by trust in the tattooer and a desire for self-expression (Sierra et al.,
2013).
Tattoos are employed in advertising, digital media, and brands as a marketing strategy.
When tattoos are used in advertising, they reproduce subcultures and express the fashion
industry mindset (Bjerrisgaard et al., 2013). For instance, for younger people, digital tattooed
influencers are seen as unique and authentic, as their non -conventional appearance can help
build trust and effectiveness (Fernandes et al., 2022) . On the other hand, when athletes are
sponsored to tattoo corporate logos, the connection between the consumer and the brand will
be higher when there is congruence between the sport and the tattooed athlete (Weidner et al.,
2016).
The literature also explored consumer identity by scrutinising tattoos through CCT.
Consumers’ tattoos are polysemic emblems of identity construction, agency, and deviancy, part
of a body with permeable borders between self and the world (Patterson & Schroeder, 2010).
Tattoos personify consumers’ tensions, contraposing the body’s plasticity and self -expression
against the act of permanently marking it (Patterson, 2018). Tattooed individuals seek personal
projects to fit themselves in better places, considering body modifications enlightening and
transforming the body into an enacted mythical utopia (Roux & Belk, 2019).
Apart from discussing motivations, cultural meanings or personal narratives, some
academic studies have adopted a more critical approach. The body is commodified when
individuals tattoo corporate logos since it expresses loyalty to the cultural industry, particularly
brands and their lifestyles (Orend & Gagné, 2009). Corporate logo tattoos reproduce symbols
of capitalism, transforming people into human billboards (Orend & Gagné, 2009) and helping
construct post-modern consumer identities. They can also imprison consumers as companies
control the brand meanings, which might be changed according to the marketing strategy
(Bengtsson et al., 2005) . Nevertheless, tattooing is a way to reappropriate the physical body
against the social and diseased one, resisting the cultural forces that commodified it (Fisher,
2002).

27
In sum, studies contrapose the permanent and transient tattoo characteristics, as
memories and meanings are not unavoidably fixed. Tattoos are a collection of personal stories
and myths that connect past, present, and future. They are polysemic emblems of consumers’
identity projects and fragmented selves, wishing to propagate their self -expression and
reappropriate their bodies. The brand tattoos are in the middle of a contrast between being
creative and personalised with the dangers of becoming commodifie d symbols controlled by
marketing strategy.
2.3 Method
This exploratory research intends to understand why individuals tattoo brands and how
they make sense of them. The Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) was adopted to
answer these questions. The IPA examines the personal experience, combining
phenomenological and hermeneutical approaches, and recognises the need to interpret a
person’s involvement with the phenomenon (Smith et al., 2009) . The interpretative
phenomenology method opens the expectation that previous findings will be challenged and
new assumptions will be uncovered, respecting the participants’ voices, actions, and texts
(Benner, 2008) . IPA is adequate when the researcher wants to understand the person’s
interaction with the phenomenon, interpreting and attempting to make meaning from it (Smith
et al., 2009).
The phenomenological interview format was used to explore the participants’
experience in a first -person view, allowing them to describe the phenomenon in detail
(Thompson et al., 1989) . The interviews followed an interview guide, opening with a non -
directive question to be as unobtrusive as possible, called “grand tour” questions (McCracken,
1988): “Can you tell me about the relationship between your brand tattoos and yourself?”.
Additional questions covered how the person experienced brands and the decision to tattoo
them, the possible regret of tattooing a brand, and how the participant would fee l if the brand
owner were to change the brand meanings.
Participants were recruited by snowball sampling and mainly via Instagram using
hashtags such as “Coca-Cola tattoo”. After that, the posted images and videos were analysed to
ensure they had brand logo tattoos. The users were directly messaged and invited to participate
in the research. Table 2.1 shows the list of participants and the interview duration, which lasted
an average of 49 minutes. The interviews were conducted online, recorded, and transcribed
verbatim. Before beginning, the interviewer explaine d the study’s objective, that the

28
participation was voluntary and confidential, and that pseudonyms would be used, asking if the
interviewee agreed to participate. The participants were also asked if they would consent to
share a photo of their brand tattoos. The ones that agreed (12 out o f 18) decided to grant the
rights to use their tattoo images for academic purposes.
The inductive reasoning and axial coding were used to analyse the results, following the
premises of grounded theory (Corbin & Strauss, 2015) and IPA’s hermeneutical approach
(Smith et al., 2009) . The analysis was conducted with the support of Atlas.ti to code and
categorise data. The transcripts were understood and interpreted as a whole. After that, each
interview was related to each other to see commonalities, using axial coding to reduce and
reassemble initial coding (Saldaña, 2013) with a mix of emic and etic perspectives.
Four global themes emerged from a higher level of abstraction (Corbin & Strauss, 2015;
Smith et al., 2009; Thompson et al., 1989): close friendship and intimacy, acute bonds, catharsis
and sublimation, and ideology and subculture belonging. Each theme was analysed using a
hermeneutical circle approach, where the meaning of the whole text is determined by the
individual parts and vice versa (Arnold & Fischer, 1994).

2.4 Findings
The four identified themes represent the dimensions that organise consumers’
relationships with the brands they tattooed. The first two are realistic relationships, and the latter
are idealistic. Close friendships are realistic and outward -directed, compri sing relationships
related to family ties, childhood memories, best friendship bonds, and teammates. Acute bonds
are also realistic but inward-directed, surfacing sturdy connections related to therapists/patients
and dealers/addicts. On the other hand, cat harsis and sublimation are idealised and inward -
directed relationships between gurus/disciples and soulmates. Ideological and subculture
belonging are idealised and outward -directed, consisting of partisanships and nostalgic
memories.
2.4.1 Close Friendship and Intimacy
The interviewees considered their tattooed brands similar to close friends. They built
relationships and anthropomorphised their loved brands (Fournier, 1998), applying human-like
characteristics to them (Sharma & Rahman, 2022) and reciprocating the brand’s social and
economic investment in customer-brand relationships (Krishna & Kim, 2021).
Best friendships concern high trust, intimacy, and attachment (Fritz et al., 2014). They
also involve constant interactions, self -disclosure, self -congruity (Su et al., 2015) , loyalty,
dependence, mutual obligations, and social support (Price & Arnould, 1999). The participants
considered their relationship with the tattooed brand as best friends forever (BFF), trustful and
a partner when needed. Peter tattooed Skol and Instagram brands ( Figure 2.1) because they
helped him cope with loneliness: “Usually, on weekdays, I’m always there with a can, and it’s
a can of Skol, right? ... But that’s because my company is Skol, you know?” Similarly, the
reciprocity and mutual obligations (Price & Arnould, 1999) needed to be perpetually
materialised for Mark, who tattooed Skol to represent his connection with his best friends
(Figure 2.1).
The close bond between consumers and their tattoo brands can be associated with family
ties and be seen as childhood buddies. The participants showed loyalty to brands that reminded
them of their familial roots and positive associations with the past (Shields & Johnson, 2016).
One example is Melody’s M&M’s tattoo (Figure 2.1), which makes her feel close to her family
since the three M&M’s letters represent each family member’s favourite colour and their
interpersonal relationship: “But the meaning of the tattoo, in fact, it isn’t the brand, it’s not that
I like M&M’s (although I like them a lot) … I don’t know, it’s my family”.

The participants explained how they viewed the bonds with their favourite brands, not
