the camera is a connection with her mother, a professional photographer, and her childhood.
2.4.2 Acute Bonds
Acute bonds are concerned with the extreme personal relationships consumers have with
brands. These bonds can be positive, as in a therapist and patient relationship where the brand
helps the consumers cope with their problems, and, in turn, they reciprocate with higher loyalty
and commitment. However, the acute relationship can also be harmful, as in an addictive bond,
where the consumer feels threatened and anxious if prevented from consuming the brand.
The first acute bond regards the dealers/addicts relationship. Brand addiction refers to
a constant urge to buy brand products and services comprising dependence, obsession, lack of
self-control, hoarding, and other compulsive feelings and behaviours (Mrad & Cui, 2017) . It

33
also involves positive affectivity, gratification, irritability, bonding, and mental and behavioural
preoccupation (Cui et al., 2018).
Some participants described their relationship with the tattooed brand as beyond loyalty,
with a feeling of dependency and an irresistible desire to be together with it. One example is
Jessica’s addictive relationship with Coca -Cola Zero Sugar. She experie nces an abstinence
crisis when not drinking it (bad mood), and even family members and store clerks hide some
bottles in case the brand is out of stock (they know she cannot live without it). The brand tattoo
(Figure 2 .2) expresses Jessica’s strong relatio nship with her favourite brand, which is
anthropomorphised and compared to an animal companion who is always there with her. The
brand addiction is so strong that Jessica thinks it would be a tragedy if the flavour ever changes
or the brand stops being sold.
Apart from the beneficial feelings of loyalty and dedication, the negative emotions felt
by the participants in their dealers -addicts relationship with the brand contrast with previous
research that focused more on positive emotions and behaviours (Cui et al., 2018; Mrad & Cui,
2017). Besides the abstinence crisis that Jessica felt, Linda expressed her synchrony with the
Opala brand (Figure 2.3) and her obsession with it. When her husband crashed her car, and it
was a total loss, she was devasted: “It felt like a piece of me was being taken away”. Tattooing
the brand and the car was her creative way of compensating for her loss (Belk, 1988).

She faces dichotomies related to living more relaxed and joyfully (represented by the food

Some participants expressed deep feelings about their tattooed brands and how they are related

helping them cope with troubles. Carol explained that she was not happy with her profession
and job, which led to depression and a feeling that she was not listening to herself. Her life

I’m always seeing it [Harley tattoo]. If I’m driving, I’m seeing it. If I’m going to say

2.4.3 Catharsis and Sublimation
Catharsis is the process of releasing intense emotions to cleanse and purge them
(Aristotle, 1992). The result is a desired renewal brought to people, detaching them from the
work of art and author and resulting in exhilaration (Frye, 1957). Brand tattoos serve as a form
of revelation to the interviewees, as a cathartic moment (Oksanen & Turtiainen, 2005) to mark
a turning point in their lives and a symbol of healing and salvation from a personal crisis
(Velliquette et al., 2006). The brand is seen as a magical entity capable of saving the participants
and restoring their lives, for which they can be grateful and devote themselves (Fuschillo et al.,
2024).
Catharsis and sublimation are experienced in the gurus/disciples relationship. This
relationship has a veneration and enchantment component (Wang et al., 2019), as participants
are mesmerised by what the brand represents. It is also a totemic relationship between
consumers and brands expressed by their brand tattoos. The tattoo totems signal the individual
feelings of attachment ritualised in collective conduct, fixed or materialised into emblems or
arbitrary signs (brand tattoos) representing the group (Lévi-Strauss, 1963).
The brand is the guru that guides disciples and enlightens their path to the greater good.
The tattooed participants considered their loved brands as moral models to inspire their conduct,
devoting themselves to learning from their masters and being gratef ul for achieving higher
development. Daniel tattooed his university logo (Figure 2.5) after receiving his master’s degree
and starting his PhD studies. The university embraced the participant and was a tutor that

36
allowed him to achieve his dreams. The brand tattoo is a trophy he can display and a way to
thank his guru, incorporating it into the self.
Figure 2.5 - Brand tattoos: Daniel (Univali), Clara (Mercedes), and Andrew (Linux).

The relationships between gurus/disciples are consecrated with the brand tattoo,
condensing the spiritual connection and the symbolic meanings. For instance, Clara tattooed
the Mercedes logo on her right arm ( Figure 2.5 ), which she considers her spiritual side, to
symbolise what she wants to accomplish as a symbol of prosperity, success, and status.
Similarly, Steven believes that the most essential things in his life must be marked. His tattoos
are visible on his right arm, stressing that they are indeed his “right arm”, supporting him: “For
example, whenever we are going to take some kind of oath … we always raise our right arm,
you know? It’s always something that is used to symbolise”.
The consumer-brand relationship of soulmates triggers another cathartic and sublime
experience. The soulmate theory states that there is only one right and idealised person to be
loved passionately and discovered, contrasting to work-it-out theorists who believe that partners
can change and be moulded (Franiuk et al., 2002). For soulmates, assuming that the partner is
ideal is crucial for the satisfaction of the relationship. It can make them positively distort the
perception of the idealised partner, downplaying the faults, or negatively distort them if they
think they are not with the right person (Franiuk et al., 2004).
Andrew’s connection with Linux is strong and is related to collaborating with other
enthusiasts: “Linux, for me, represents a philosophy, a philosophy of life: the philosophy of
collaboration, that we all collaborate for the greater good”. The Linux brand is an idealised
soulmate that can teach about rebellion and creativity, free from the perils of commodification
and commercialisation. The Linux penguin mascot (Tux) symbolises a totem filled with the

37
brand’s values, which Andrew tattooed to reinforce his attachment to the brand (Figure 2.5) and
his communal relationship. The participant’s personal myth (Oksanen & Turtiainen, 2005;
Velliquette et al., 2006) is to think about the brand as a linchpin that allows his career change
from music teacher to IT programmer, which interlaces with the guru and disciple relationship.
2.4.4 Ideology and Subculture Belonging
This study understands ideology and subculture belonging as a wish to be part of a
cultural group of like-minded people. The participants expressed their values and related them
to what they understood to be the brand’s cultural codes, myths, and ideology (Holt & Cameron,
2010). They are affected by marketplace mythologies, which construct an ideal consumer
lifestyle towards an ideological direction, although not free from competing interests (C. J.
Thompson, 2004).
The socio-cultural and ideological relationships with the brand tattoos are expressed via
partisanship and nostalgic proneness. Both are idealised views of society concerning the present
and the future (partisanship) or the past (nostalgia). The brand purp ose impacts them, which
involves contributions to the betterment of society and transcends the company’s profits (France
et al., 2024). Brand activism also influences these brand-consumer relationships, as it involves
the discussion and challenge of existing moral judgements via persuasion or controversies
(Sibai et al., 2021) and is a result of a process that formulates, articulates, and implements the
activism as a marketing strategy (Pimentel et al., 2024).
The first type of ideology and subcultural belonging is related to partisans. Participants
expressed their ideological preferences and connected them with their brand tattoos. For
example, Keith tattooed the Nike Jordan tennis to show his affinity with the brand’s cultural
codes and activism, which are linked to the black movement, rap and ghetto, and the biding of
fashion (streetwear) and aesthetics:
So, today, Nike is a brand that sponsors many black people, taking many activities
and things to suburban areas to somehow help and collaborate with this culture,
which itself created around it … mainly in sports. So, I think there’s a lot of that too,
you know? … This victory issue, the suburban issue. It’s a combination of many
things that led me to be part of this club, to be a fanboy, up to the point of marking
my skin somehow (Keith).
Another strong subculture affiliation is outlined by Steven, who tattooed the Vans brand
and its slogan (“Off the wall”). He praises the brand for sticking with skating since the

38
beginning, rebuffing Louis Vuitton’s sponsorship of a Brazilian professional skater as
illegitimate and opportunistic (Sibai et al., 2021) since it is not part of the underground spirit of
skating. Steven summarises the “off the wall” subculture ideology as this:
When you skate, I think your view of the city changes. Because if you don’t skate,
you’ll see a sidewalk. You’ll say: “A sidewalk”. And, if you skate, you’ll look at that
sidewalk and say: “Wow, that trick would be perfect here!”… So, I think this
different vision would be “off the wall” (Steven).
Partisanship can also be expressed via participation in brand communities (Muñiz &
O’Guinn, 2001; Schouten & McAlexander, 1995) , which was the case of interviewees who
tattooed the Harley-Davidson logo. However, the brand meanings and cultural influences were
not the same for them. Paul engaged with aficionados of the Harley Owners Group (HOG),
considering himself a brand fan stereotype and associating the brand with conservative values:
“So, the Harley-Davidson owner, the Harley-Davidson guy, is a right-wing guy. That is because
Harley is an American brand, right?”. He cannot conceive that any Harley fan would not be
close to the idealised brand consumer (e.g., Caucasian, man, tall, and strong).
Carol shares another point of view about the brand. She praises the brand’s heritage, the
status it brings her, and family and friendship values. On the other hand, she is empowered as
a woman to strive despite struggles and win in a men’s world, deciding not to be part of the
HOG and ride with a women -only Harley group or with bikers who own other brands. She
understands the brand from a feminist perspective, rejecting male superiority and subverting
males-dominated culture (Joy & Venkatesh, 1994) . The contraposition between Paul’s and
Carol’s visions shows the competing views of Harley’s marketplace mythology.
The same feeling of feminine empowerment is shared with Linda. She is part of the first
women’s Opala brand community (Chevrolet’s car brand launched in the 1970s in Brazil).
Linda explains how the members gather at events and share their experiences and p assions,
stating that the Opala community is 90% masculine. However, she stresses her feminist point
of view that she can strive in a male-dominated environment, tattooing the Opala and Chevrolet
brands (Figure 2.3) and expressing her affiliation with drag racing.
The second idealised relationship is associated with nostalgic proneness: a favourable
longing for the past and days of yore (Holbrook, 1993). Nostalgia proneness is a broad concept
that can be narrowed to bonded nostalgia when focussed on a particular object or childhood
brand nostalgia, a positive attachment to a brand due to fond memories of one’s youth (Shields

39
& Johnson, 2016) . Brands might explore nostalgia via symbolic stories, utopian past worlds,
the contrast between old and new, and authenticity (Brown et al., 2003).
Some participants thought about their tattooed brands as vintage mates. James has a
special connection with the Kombi brand, which reminds him of the good old times and how
everything was better assembled. The brand epitomises a utopian past when life was simpler
and easier, as everyone could travel freely without worrying a bout troubles. Similarly, Linda
thinks that the Opala brand is an iconic brand that reminded her of the car's history, how it was
presented to the public in the 1960s and 1970s, the chan ges it has gone through and even that
former presidents used it. The brand is her connection with this idealised past, which is
consecrated via an old car brand community.
2.5 Discussion and Conclusion
2.5.1 Theoretical Contributions
This paper’s objective was to understand why consumers tattoo brands and how this
phenomenon contributes to their identity projects. This research’s first major contribution
concerns identifying new or under -theorised brand-consumer relationships, which an swers a
call to expand and diversify the coverage of relationships (Alvarez et al., 2023) . The second
significant contribution adds to the literature that consumers can have multiple and dynamic
relationships with the same brand since they transit between a core stable self and a multiple
porous one (Appau et al., 2020).
First, this research extends the brand relationship literature by presenting new types of
brand-consumer relationships (Table 2.2). Previous studies have pinpointed and commented on
some of these relationships, such as best friendships (Alvarez et al., 2023; Fournier, 1998; Fritz
et al., 2014), childhood friendships (Fournier, 1998; Shields & Johnson, 2016), dealers/addicts,
therapists/patients, teammates, and soulmates (Fournier & Alvarez, 2013). However, they have
neither defined nor explained how consumers could express them. The brand -consumer
relationships are organised under four quadrants, depicted in Figure 2.6. The first axis concerns
consumers’ inner and outer connections, and the second refers to the realistic and idealised
bonds with brands.
Recent research has conceptualised the relationships between consumers and brands
(Schreuder et al., 2024) , stating that consumers experience them as more functional and less
emotionally intense. Nevertheless, the inner consumer -brand relationships show that the

40
interviewees undergo deep feelings in a relationship exchange, benefiting from the interaction
(Veloutsou, 2007) and creating a bond and a sense of oneness with the brand (Yoshida et al.,
2021). These relationships can be mixed -valenced as some participants expressed their
addiction to brands (Cui et al., 2018; Ghorbanzadeh, 2024; Mrad & Cui, 2017) while others
sought therapeutical and soulful characteristics in them (Franiuk et al., 2002, 2004; Fuschillo
et al., 2024). Brand tattoos end up acting as mnemonic signs of crucial events (Steadman et al.,
2019), giving meaning to life (S. Luo & Hamlin, 2022).

On the other hand, the outer consumer-brand relationships show that consumers are not
simply human billboards (Baudrillard, 1998; Orend & Gagné, 2009) , contained in predefined
stereotypes (Bjerrisgaard et al., 2013) , commodified bodies (Bengtsson et al., 2005; Orend &
Gagné, 2009) or reflecting the cultural industry message (Horkheimer & Adorno, 2002) . The
practices, knowledge, and brands’ cultural discourses are incorporated (Kuuru, 2022; Murphy
et al., 2018; Spotswood & Gurrieri, 2024) as a person’s sense of self is constructed by
interconnections of the body with society (Merleau-Ponty, 1962).
On the realistic and idealistic axis, consumers seek down -to-earth relationships based
on close familial and friendship ties or as comfort for their troubles and problems. At the same
time, they develop idealised bonds with brands, using their brand tattoo s as totems (Lévi-
Strauss, 1963), reinscribing and reinforcing group affiliation (Razmus, 2025) and subculture
belonging (Fisher, 2002), and being affected by media culture imagery (Velliquette et al., 1998).

41
Interviewees are proud to be part of marketplace cultures (Patterson, 2018; Patterson &
Schroeder, 2010) while simultaneously expressing themselves as cultural producers.
Contrapositions and contradictions exist in the brand -consumer relationships, which
place one foot in reality and another in idealisation. For example, brand tattoos can empower
participants, particularly women, to resignify brand values, incorporate them to fit their life
stories, and not be subject to dominance, submissiveness, and weakness (Balog, 2024; Foucault,
1995). However, they might as well reinforce prejudice and be incorporated by consumers as a
type of polarised partisanship (Schoenmueller et al., 2022) , which could lead to buycotts,
boycotts (Flecha-Ortiz et al., 2024) and culture wars (Hashmi et al., 2025) . The idealised
relationships are also ambiguous since they positively and negatively distort brand
characteristics, potentially triggering passionate consumer behaviours and emotions that can
impact brand equity.
Finally, this research shows how consumers build their sense of self through brands
(Holt, 2002; Razmus, 2025), cultivating multiple relationships with them and broadcasting their
brand commitment through dynamic bonds. Brand tattoos symbolise polysemic and incomplete
meanings, representing a search for a desired and stable self (Appau et al., 2020) that stands out
and reclaims the body. They also reinforce individuality by representing personal life stories,
homages, and myths (McAdams, 1993; Oksanen & Turtiainen, 2005; Steadman, Medway, et
al., 2023; Velliquette et al., 2006).

2.5.2 Managerial Implications
Marketers aim to build strong customer relationships and create and sustain iconic
brands. The first practical implication of this study is that adopting a cultural strategy for a
brand pays off. Highly attached consumers have deep emotional connections wi th brands,
expressing their authenticity and values by tattooing them. Brand -tattooed consumers can be
considered cultural brand codes, reinforcing the brand’s identity and personality.
Understanding their behaviour and bonds with loved brands can guide marketers in developing
their cultural strategies and avoiding culture wars (Hashmi et al., 2025).
Companies should be aware of consumers’ multiple relationships with their brands.
They need to understand the different types of bonds and how they are formed. Through brand
tattoos, consumers signal a solid relationship and manifest their sturdy bonds. Ho wever, they
can also broadcast their relationship strength via different expressions, such as cosplay or cult-
like interactions. Marketers need to identify the cues that tie consumers and brands and
understand what types of relationships they fit in. For e xample, a guru/disciple relationship
could require more counselling, while subcultural belonging should be enhanced for
partisanship connections.
The findings also show that consumers might present mixed feelings, either negative or
positive, and ambiguous relationships with brands. They can resist brand identity changes or
twist it to fit their cultural values, reinforcing prejudices or stereotypes . The implication for
practitioners is strategically managing the relationship types and fostering initiatives to
influence positive behaviours and affection while minimising negative ones.
2.5.3 Limitations and Future Research
This paper presents some limitations that need to be pointed out. Only participants in
Brazil were interviewed, although with a balanced sample regarding age, gender, and number
of tattoos. Since the brand tattoo phenomenon is global, the perspectives of other cultures might
differ from what has been concluded in this paper. Interviews were conducted with consumers
who have tattooed mainly consumer goods brands but not B2B, sports teams, or music bands.
Future studies could compare the types of brand tattoo s and understand if their meanings are
different.
Future research could study other dynamic and multiple relationships between brands
and consumers. Understanding how these diverse relationships affect brand identity,

45
personality, equity, and other brand constructs is necessary. Scholars should also investigate
harmful relationship types, how they are formed and stimulated, and the consequences for brand
management. It would be interesting to compare single with dynamic relationships and negative
with positive ones, adding to the attachment -aversion theoretical proposal (Park et al., 2013a,
2013b) and the recent polarisation research stream (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019, 2024).
Further research should also look into how archetypes and storytelling interact with
brand tattoos and the psychological implications for brands. Are tattoos enacting personal
archetypes or reflecting brand ones? How can both co -exist? Researchers could st udy the
relationship between brand tattoos and other tattoos on consumer bodies. Since they also tattoo
unbranded products and symbols, what are their connections?

CHAPTER 3 – POSITIVE-NEGATIVE POLES: POLARISED BRANDS2

3.1 Introduction
Polarising brands attract both lovers and haters, aiming to boost positive outcomes while
avoiding harmful consequences (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019) . The more polarised a brand is,
the greater the heterogeneity in evaluations, which has a direct impact on stock returns but with
lower risk due to less price sensitivity or brand switching (Luo et al., 2013) . Relying on
polarised brands can be advantageous because they offer stronger self -expression,
distinctiveness, and a sense of belonging (Berendt et al., 2018; Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019). On
the other hand, intense rivalry can lead to avoidance, trash-talking, schadenfreude, and harmful
actions (Liao et al., 2023; Marticotte et al., 2016) , impacting brand equity (Luo et al., 2013;
Phillips-Melancon and Dalakas, 2014).
Brand polarisation differs from brand rivalry since it involves the simultaneous presence
of love and hate, not necessarily requiring a feud or a strong opponent (Osuna Ramírez et al.,
2024). Brand rivalry is a particular type of polarisation in which, instead of considering strong
feelings towards one brand, two rivals are considered (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019) . While
polarised brands have been scarcely theorised and studied (Monahan et al., 2023; Osuna
Ramírez et al., 2019, 2024) , brand rivalry has received more attention in the literature. It has
been conceptualised as oppositional brand loyalty since consumers define themselves by what
they consume and do not (Muñiz and Hamer, 2001). The rivalry is considered an ongoing battle
between competing brands (Alvarado-Karste and Kidwell, 2022; Berendt et al., 2018, 2024), is
driven by consumer-brand identification (Liao et al., 2021) , and enhanced by participation in
brand communities (Cheng et al., 2024; Thompson and Sinha, 2008).
Although brand polarisation studies addressed its conceptualisation (Osuna Ramírez et
al., 2019), proposed a scale to measure it (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2024) , analysed the effect of
hate-acknowledging ads (Monahan et al., 2023), and the impact on stock returns and risk (Luo
et al., 2013) , there is a gap in the literature on understanding the conditions that foster brand
polarisation (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019), how consumers behave toward it, and the similarities

and differences between negative and positive feelings concerning polarised brands (Osuna

This paper aims to address this lacuna by posing the following research questions. RQ1:
Why do polarised brands elicit antagonistic consumers’ feelings and behaviours? RQ2: How
does this polarisation process unfold? Previous research investigated polarised feelings of love
and hate toward brands (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019, 2024) but did not seek to understand why
particular brands evoke those feelings. Drawing from studies that identified polarised brands
and brand rivalries (Berendt et al., 2018; Cheng et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2013; Monahan et al.,
2023; Muñiz and Hamer, 2001; Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019; Phillips -Melancon and Dalakas,
2014), five brands were chosen since they trigger intense polarisation: Apple, Coca -Cola,
McDonald’s, Nestlé, and Starbucks.
This exploratory study interviewed consumers to understand their relationships with
polarised brands, adopting the Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis method (Smith et al.,
2009) to investigate the significance of the phenomenon and how consumers experience it, as
most research in brand polarisation and oppositional brand loyalty relied on quantitative
methods. The main contribution of this paper concerns understanding the brand p olarisation
phenomenon more broadly as a lightning rod effect. This effect occurs because polarised brands
elicit strong responses from consumers, who consider them as either iconic (loved) or anti -
iconic (hated), precipitating four distinct emotional stat es: brand salvation, brand damnation,
brand ambiguity, and brand agnosticism. They are driven by underlying, basic individual values
(Schwartz et al., 2012) and the expectations associated with the brand promise (Bhargava &
Bedi, 2022).
3.2 Literature Review
3.2.1 Brand Relationship Extremes: Love and Hate
The brand relationship literature has been growing over the last decades, investigating
consumer-brand deep bonds, polarity, and strength (Fetscherin and Veloutsou, 2024) . It has
developed under diverse streams of brand loyalty, love, community, self -connection, and
storytelling (Fetscherin and Heinrich, 2015) . Drawing from the seminal initial works that
identified different types of relationships (Fournier, 1998) , scholars have discussed intense
affectionate connections such as brand love (Batra et al., 2012; Carroll and Ahuvia, 2006;
Robertson et al., 2022) , hate (Kucuk, 2019; Mushtaq et al., 2024; Zarantonello et al., 2016;
Zhang and Laroche, 2020), and passion (Gilal et al., 2023).

48
Depending on the degree of intensity, the brand -consumer relationship can vary from
brand satisfaction or indifference to love and hate (Fetscherin et al., 2021). The brand love and
hate constructs are related to brand attachment, which is associated with self -brand
interrelations and prominence (Park et al., 2010). To measure the strength of emotional
attachment, scholars identified three first-order dimensions: affection, passion, and connection
(Thomson et al., 2005).
Another perspective analysed both brand attachment and aversion, including
consumers’ negative relationships with brands (Park et al., 2013) . However, this model was
criticised for not adequately capturing these negative relationships, as they are not necessarily
the opposite of positive ones (Fournier and Alvarez, 2013) . For example, some relationships
(e.g., secret affairs and masters-slaves) are mixed-valenced and imbalanced. In contrast, others
are neutral, lying midway on the attachment-aversion continuum (Fournier and Alvarez, 2013).
Although studies have explored the extremes of brand love and hate, less attention has
been given to other brand -consumer relationships, and most research has focused on broader
marketplace phenomena instead of scrutinising one type of relationship (Alvarez et al., 2023).
Additionally, recent research has explored the phenomenon of love turning to hate (Tolunay
and Veloutsou, 2025), but few studies have investigated ambivalent, contradictory, and mixed-
emotion relationships.
3.2.2 Oppositional Brand Loyalty
Scholars have studied rivalries between brands, such as Coke versus Pepsi, coining the
term oppositional brand loyalty to describe antagonistic choices that help consumers define
themselves (Muñiz & Hamer, 2001). Previous research has identified the ambivalent effect of
rivalries (Berendt et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2013), focusing on their negative consequences. The
intense competition leads to schadenfreude, which is the pleasure felt from others’ misfortune
(Cheng et al., 2024; Marticotte et al., 2016; Phillips-Melancon and Dalakas, 2014), and to trash-
talking against contestants (Ewing et al., 2013; Liao et al., 2023; Marticotte et al., 2016;
Phillips-Melancon and Dalakas, 2014). Stronger feelings may also be elicited by brand rivalry,
such as anti -brand actions (Cheng et al., 2024), rumination, resentment, and feelings of
unfairness (Alvarado-Karste and Kidwell, 2022), as well as a desire to harm the opposing brand
(Marticotte et al., 2016).
The rivalry between brands influences not only the consumers’ behaviour, but also
represents a risk to brand equity (Phillips-Melancon and Dalakas, 2014) , lower stock

49
performance (Luo et al., 2013), a threat to consumer identity (Liao et al., 2021), and, if used in
communication pieces, it might backfire (Berendt et al., 2024). On the other hand, studies have
identified positive aspects of oppositional brand loyalty, such as defending the brand that is
under attack (Muñiz and Hamer, 2001) , reinforcing the brand’s distinction and uniqueness
(Berendt et al., 2018) , ingroup identification (Ewing et al., 2013; Phillips -Melancon and
Dalakas, 2014), engagement, and willingness to pay a premium price (Cheng et al., 2024).
Studies have also debated the antecedents of brand rivalry regarding three main aspects:
brand, self -identification, and engagement with rivals. The brand aspects that influence
oppositional brand loyalty include brand prestige, uniqueness (Liao et al., 2021) , and loyalty
(Marticotte et al., 2016). Consumer self-brand connection (Liao et al., 2021; Marticotte et al.,
2016), moral identification (Cheng et al., 2024), identification with the preferred brand (Liao et
al., 2023; Phillips-Melancon and Dalakas, 2014), and disidentification with the opponent brand
(Liao et al., 2023) concern the psychological motivations that enhance rivalries. Regarding the
engagement with rivals, the literature identified as crucial aspects of oppositional brand loyalty
the brand community participation (Ewing et al., 2013; Marticotte et al., 2016; Muñiz and
Hamer, 2001; Thompson and Sinha, 2008) and long-running rivalry history (Alvarado-Karste
and Kidwell, 2022; Berendt et al., 2024; Ewing et al., 2013; Muñiz and Hamer, 2001).
3.2.3 Brand Polarisation
Brand polarisation is defined as “an affective phenomenon where beliefs and emotions
of a significant number of people induce a simultaneous move to the extremes involving
passionate positive and negative feelings and convictions towards the brand, like -minded
consumers and opposite-minded consumers” (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019, p. 620) . However,
few studies have investigated brand polarisation (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019) , as it remains
underdeveloped in the literature (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2024) and has received limited attention
(Monahan et al., 2023).
The brand polarisation construct was conceptualised based on characteristics from
political science, social psychology, polarised products, and oppositional brand loyalty (Osuna
Ramírez et al., 2019) . Polarisation in political science refers to partisanship, the tendency to
identify with one party, viewing co-partisans positively and adversaries negatively (Iyengar &
Westwood, 2015). Polarisation can be affective and lead to animosity, but it is not necessarily
ideological (Iyengar et al., 2019). Polarised feelings shape consumption patterns, as consumers
acquire products as a defence mechanism against events that threaten their identity or group

50
affiliation, such as the election of an opposing party or when a brand takes a political or
ideological stand (Schoenmueller et al., 2022).
Brands face a double-edged approach to polarisation. Their communication might lead
to boycotts and buycotts (Flecha-Ortiz et al., 2024), and their marketing communication might
be seen as a moral failure (Biedenbach, 2025). Brand activism could be considered inconsistent
(Malik et al., 2025), trigger advocacy or backfire (Kim & He, 2025). Nevertheless, remaining
politically silent can be seen as a betrayal and a lack of care (Zaman Malik et al., 2025).
In social psychology, scholars have studied group polarisation. When exposed to group
discussions, individuals adjust their position to maintain social desirability (Myers & Lamm,
1976), not deviating significantly from their ideal position and remaining close to the group’s
central one (Isenberg, 1986). Polarisation happens when there is a shift toward the preferred
pole, while extremisation is the movement away from neutrality (Myers & Lamm, 1976). This
change depends on the number and strength of pro and con arguments, but they will be
considered invalid and unpersuasive if there is intense animosity toward an outgroup (Isenberg,
1986).
Past research has applied social psychology and political science definitions and
concepts to brand polarisation, revisiting the oppositional brand loyalty construct (Osuna
Ramírez et al., 2019, 2024) . In this sense, brand rivalries were considered a special type of
polarisation involving intense hatred and love among supporters and detractors toward two
opposing brands rather than one (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019).
Although the literature has discussed consumers’ perceptions about the advertising of
polarised brands (Monahan et al., 2023) , the performance of polarised brands in the stock
market (X. Luo, Raithel, et al., 2013) , and identified the dimensions of brand polarisation
(Osuna Ramírez et al., 2024) , there is a gap on understanding why and how particular brands
evoke polarisation, which the present research aims to fill. More exploratory research is also
needed since most papers employed a quantitative research strategy (Table 3.1), primarily using
structural equation modelling and conducting experiments.

It is essential to understand the similarities and differences between positive and
negative emotions toward a polarised brand (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2024) and to examine further
the reasons for fostering brand polarisation (e.g., consumers becoming detrac tors and

only brand love and hate relationships or if they might have ambivalent and mixed -valenced
connections with consumers (Fournier & Alvarez, 2013).
3.3 Method
The Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis was employed in this research, as it is
suitable for understanding consumers’ relationships with the world, focusing on the attempt to
interpret and make sense of their behaviours and activities (Smith et al., 2009). The emphasis
is on analysing the informants’ experiences and points of view, grasping the phenomenon’s
essence and broad cultural perspective (Spiggle, 1994).
The interpretative phenomenology method enables researchers to uncover new
assumptions and challenge existing ones (Benner, 2008). It also stresses that reality is socially
constructed, multiple, holistic, and contextual, and that it involves an interactive and
interpretive research relationship (Hudson & Ozanne, 1988) . As the brand polarisation
phenomenon is scarcely researched and underdeveloped (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2024) ,
interpretative phenomenology can yield new understandings and propositions by combining
phenomenological and hermeneutical insights.
Since this work aims to investigate why particular polarised brands elicit negative and
positive feelings and behaviours, five brands were selected: Apple, Coca -Cola, McDonald’s,
Nestlé, and Starbucks. These brands were chosen based on past research on oppositional brand
loyalty and brand polarisation (Table 3.1). To recruit consumers to participate in the study, the
authors searched online communities on Reddit and Instagram posts using the brand’s name
and negative keywords such as “fuck”, “boycott”, or “sucks”. The same process was undertaken
using the brand’s name and positive keywords such as “love”, “enthusiast”, and “fan”. The
authors scrutinised the posts to ensure that the users were active members, directly messaging
and inviting them to participate in the research.
In-depth online interviews were conducted in English, Portuguese, and Spanish, with 26
consumers from the selected brands (13 lovers and 13 haters), as seen in Table 3.2. The
interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim, lasting an average of 61 minutes. Verbal
consent was obtained during the interview, with participants informed that it was confidential,

54
voluntary, and recorded, in accordance with procedures approved by the local ethics committee.
Data collection ceased when theoretical saturation was reached, as the sample was deemed
adequate for theory development, and further efforts would lead to redundancy or the discovery
of minor new elements (Saunders et al., 2018).
The software Atlas.ti was used to codify and analyse the data. The codification
considered the grounded theory premises (Corbin & Strauss, 2015), using structural coding as
the first cycle method and axial coding as the second (Saldaña, 2013). The data structure was
organised into first-order concepts, second-order themes, and aggregate dimensions, following
the Gioia methodology to explain the phenomenon of interest with increasing abstractness
(Gioia et al., 2012) . The hermeneutical circle was employed to complement the interpretative
phenomenology, allowing for the understanding of the meanings of the entire set of interviews
as determined by the individual elements, and vice versa (Arnold & Fischer, 1994).

3.4 Findings
Four aggregate dimensions emerged from the data collected from the interviews. The
first dimension is named brand salvation , as consumers viewed their favourite brands as
idealised and trustworthy partners, with whom they had a strong positive attachment and a self-
brand bond. These interviewees adhered to a teleological approach to ethics, morally evaluating
actions by their consequences (Macdonald & Beck -Dudley, 1994) . The second dimension
concerns the opposite pole, referred to as brand damnation, as participants had strong negative
feelings towards polarised brands because they felt betrayed, considered that brands violated
moral and ethical codes, and wanted to get back at them by boycotting or spreading negative
word of mouth. These participants followed a deontological approach to ethics, judging actions
by their characteristics rather than their consequences (Macdonald & Beck-Dudley, 1994). The
third dimension, brand agnosticism , considers how detached or indifferent participants felt
towards polarised brands, being more concerned with utilitarian benefits rather than showing
positive or negative affections. The final dimension, brand ambiguity, is related to a mix of
love and hate, as consumers had conflicted relationships and feelings towards polarised brands.
3.4.1 Brand Salvation
In brand salvation, brands are used as a symbolic system of positive precepts to cultivate
virtue and promote finer qualities (Douglas, 2001) . Salvation is a spiritual goal achieved
through efforts that contribute to that end, and it has implications for how individuals should
behave morally (McCleary, 2007). Past research has explored how brands act as a conduit for
revelation and healing (Fuschillo et al., 2024) and how consumers develop a spiritual
relationship with them (Ryu et al., 2025) . Ultimately, brands achieve sacredness when
consumers believe they are superior, enchanting (mesmerised by their powers), and evoke a
sense of social community (Wang et al., 2019).
The participants viewed their preferred brands as idealised partners, whom they
unquestioningly trusted to provide a good experience whenever they bought their products.
Theo explains that he always goes to McDonald’s because he loves the experience and
sometimes because it gives him a happy ending to his day. He started going out with one girl,
but had a hard time since she did not like the brand: “I can’t figure out where to go out with her
(...) It’s a little weird to go to the mall and not to McDonald’s afterwards. They’re sort of glued
together. And my fondness for her is definitely a little affected”. Theo is rethinking the
relationship because they cannot share the same passion for McDonald’s.

57
Trusting brands brings comfort, as interviewees feel taken care of and provided with
everything they need. When asked about the Apple ecosystem, Lucas thinks that it brings
security and protection from viruses and other problems, even helping him with a po tential
health issue, detected when wearing an Apple Watch: “But it also saved my life. It’s provided
me a health alert that indicated that I had a heart condition that I didn’t know I had, so I’m very
fond of that”. The same feeling is shared by Hudson, w ho sees his relationship with Apple as
akin to marriage, forgiving minor problems that happened along the way.
The love for the brand can be very intense and often stems from a strong connection
with family members. When asked to describe Nestlé as if it were a person, Mia answered that
it would be like her mother or her son, associating the brand with traditional values and family
bonding. Similarly, Iris connects Nestlé with birthday parties, family gatherings, and sweet
memories: “If I make a pudding with condensed milk from another brand, it won’t have that
‘mother’s taste’, that ‘grandmother’s taste’”. Ava has the same familial feelings, talking about
being connected with Starbucks since she first met her wife in a store, going there frequently
with her professor and mentor, and feeling welcomed as part of a community.
Another aspect of loving brands involves considering them as something special or
unique to be savoured. The interviewees saw their relationships with their loved brands as a
way to cheer them up, as explained by Aaron. As an autistic, he is loyal to relia ble brands,
searching for comfort and hedonism: “I like getting excited. And the joy that you get from it
and the feel, the escapism that you get from going and just escaping everyday life”. Eleanor
discussed her connection with Starbucks and how the brand was vital to maintaining her peace
of mind, interacting with the baristas, and refuelling her energy.
Apart from refuelling and escapism, Stanley also consumes polarised brands to display
his sense of achievement and power. He feels proud of what he has accomplished after a
difficult childhood in a family with a below-average income. Stanley later faced problems when
divorced from his wife, turning to Starbucks and Coke as his salvation: “So, I’m gonna have
what I want within what my financial means are. And I don’t really care what anybody else
says. And one of those things, a big thing, is food that I like and drinks that I like”. In the same
sense, Penelope explained how owning an Apple iPhone is a significant achievement that sets
her apart from others and makes her feel accepted.
Participants considered the loved brands as aesthetically appealing, perceiving them as
beautiful, sublime, and moving (Dagalp & Hartmann, 2022). Some interviewees were drawn to

58
the brand’s identity, such as Cooper, who is fond of Apple and Coke because he enjoys
advertising and the appeal both brands have. As a marketing person, Lucas also praises iconic
brands (Apple and Coke) and their branding. However, he explains that aesthe tics and utility
must work together, which is what he appreciates in the brands he loves.
3.4.2 Brand Damnation
Contrasting with brand salvation, brand damnation is used by consumers as a symbolic
system to suppress evil and combat vice, anomalous, polluted and aberrant events (Douglas,
2001). Unlike previous research that investigated the journey of salvation by a brand (Fuschillo
et al., 2024), brand evangelism and ritualism (Wang et al., 2019), and brand faith (Ryu et al.,
2025), this paper addresses the opposite religious meaning of damnation. Damnation happens
when the moral wrongdoings are not forgiven, and one is condemned to eternal fire (hell)
(McCleary, 2007) . Polarising brands trigger the contrast between salvation and damnation,
placing consumers on opposite poles.
Brand damnation is not just about anger, contempt, and fear (Zarantonello et al., 2016),
or protests, boycotts, avoidance, and complaints (Zhang & Laroche, 2020) . There is not only
an effect of ideological interest and political knowledge (Flecha-Ortiz et al., 2024), since brand
damnation also has a strong moral component that directs consumers’ hatred. Consumers feel
deceived and retaliate, wanting to protect the universal values they cherish, but not due to a
“love becomes hate” effect (Tolunay & Veloutsou, 2025) . The participants’ values fuel their
outrage toward the hated brands without the need for a rival, which complements past research
related to moral identity (Cheng et al., 2024; Rosendo-Rios et al., 2025).
Participants who condemn brands to eternal damnation are concerned with universal
values, such as human rights, a commitment to equality and justice for everyone, and the
preservation of the natural environment (Schwartz et al., 2012) . The criticism is concentrated
on universal access to natural resources (such as water and harvesting raw materials), deceptive
and overpromising advertising (hiding true intentions, being hypocritical, and displaying
arrogance), mistreatment of workers ( e.g., slave labour or anti -union), political motivations
(e.g., not properly supporting Ukraine or Palestine), or ideological views (as a symbol of
capitalism, globalisation, commodification or consumerism).
Talking about Nestlé, many interviewees expressed their outrage at the fact that the
company was exploiting natural resources, as Dylan explains: “I think a former CEO of Nestlé

59
(…) has said that it’s not a human right to have clean drinking water. And then, that is something
that I truly don’t have in my own values”. They feel deceived and upset because the brands are
not only making a profit but also harming the environment. This feeling is even stronger when
related to Nestlé’s baby formula, as the company has been accused of promoting its product
over breastfeeding. For most haters, the polarised brands have crossed a red line and will never
be forgiven for their sins, as Peter explains why he would never trust Nestlé.
I personally don’t see how they could make things right. And there are more than
enough other products out there that I could never buy Nestlé my entire life and
suffer zero repercussions. There are plenty of alternatives. So, even if Nestlé
somehow reversed time, resurrected all the kids, gave all the water back, paid it.
Like, if they somehow managed to do something as ludicrous as that. (Peter)
The participants felt deceived when they discovered that polarised brands were the
parent company of other brands they had purchased. It seemed like a game of hide -and-seek,
where the big corporations were disguising themselves and their dark secrets. Amel ia is a
vegetarian and started buying a meat substitute from a Swedish brand called Hälsans Kök when
she suddenly discovered something else: “I turned the package over and it says Nestlé on the
back. And I was like, ‘What the fuck!’ I’m trying to do something good for the planet and I’m
still supporting this shitty company”. Another situation happened with Violet, who felt betrayed
by Fairlife, a brand that supposedly sells cruelty -free dairy products. When a whistleblower
uncovered the brand’s wrongdoings, she became angry and later discovered that the brand was
part of the Coca-Cola Company.
The way the polarised brands were narcissistically advertised, portraying an idealised
consumer, was seen as problematic and manipulative. The participants complained that Apple’s
marketing created the perception that its consumers were superior and exceptional, while stating
that the brand was overpromising and underdelivering. Evelyn felt particularly annoyed by
Apple, arguing that consumers were falling under the brand’s spell: “I’ve never really liked
brands trying to manipulate me, saying that if I buy that product, it will make me feel special
because I’m the best”. Brand haters perceived Apple as arrogant and snobbish because it
presented itself as a status symbol or badge of honour. They did not consider the brand superior,
enchanting, or communal (Wang et al., 2019). Albert commented about being bullied for using
Android, even though he believed his phone was better: “People assume you’re poor, people
assume you’re stupid. It’s like if you had half a brain”.

60
Geopolitical and political inclinations influenced how participants evaluated the
polarised brands, which were held accountable for their actions and were under greater scrutiny.
Henry boycotted McDonald’s for not leaving Russia and prioritising its economic interests over
human rights, which also prompted Evelyn to stop buying Coca -Cola. After the Israeli -
Palestinian conflict started, Edward ceased going to McDonald’s because the brand was
accused of feeding Israeli soldiers. The participants understand th at they can pressure big
corporations harming their bottom lines, which is something Karen did with a targeted focus
following the Boycott, Divest, and Sanctions (BDS) Palestinian -led movement. Interviewees
also see the polarised brands as exploiters and against workers trying to unionise, which made
Edward, Henry, and Karen angry with Starbucks.
Another aspect highlighted by the interviewees is the consumerism and
commodification that the polarised brands represent, with harmful consequences for
consumers. Finley believes that McDonald’s sells standardised unhealthy meals, while
consumers should look for local small businesses that use more nutritious ingredients. He also
thinks that it is paradoxical that the brand once sponsored the Olympics. As a dentist, Oliver
follows the same reasoning to explain his hatred for Coca-Cola: “And then, I dislike Coca-Cola
even more than fast food brands, because it’s kind of ubiquitous, right? When someone is
actually, quote, addicted. And then, the health concerns, because it’s too much sugar, diabetes,
dental problems, cavities...”.
With a different approach, Roger uses his art to protest commodification and
consumerism, selling T -shirts that mock Coca -Cola and other brands by creating puns, as
writing “little water” (agüita in Spanish) with Coke’s typeface. He also creatively uses a term
he saw on Twitch, “jajan’t”, which combines “jaja” (a Spanish expression of laughter) with the
English negative to express that one might be laughing but is actually hurting oneself. Thus,
Roger aims to draw people’s attention by exposing the contradi ctions and hypocrisy of
consumers, who continue to purchase items that are unhealthy, violate moral codes, or are
unnecessary.
Besides consumerism and commodification, participants dislike how big corporations,
epitomised by polarised brands, symbolise savage capitalism and do not care about society’s
well-being. Peter reflects on how brands should be behaving, “So, it would be ni ce if
everyone.... if everything produced, everything done was done with a meaning, and the profit
is a means to continue that, as opposed to the profit is the purpose”. When asked if brands

61
should have values and purpose, Evelyn stresses that there needs to be a balanced relationship,
as brands cannot only have a utilitarian purpose: “(…) the brand has to give something to
humanity too, to have a moral-ethical balance, right? It’s not just profit, profit, profit”.
The interviewees reacted against polarised brands, considering them a collective effort
to cause harm to society and universal values. The fact that several people made controversial
decisions in a board room is unexcused and worsens the brand’s guilt, as Henry outlines it:
“(…) it’s like multiple people had to sign off on that. Multiple people had to say ‘we’re OK
with this’, that I’m a lot less forgiving of companies for letting bad decisions happen”. Some
participants felt disappointment, anxiety, and de spair, as if they were fighting with a higher
dark force surrounding them, such as Violet, claiming that it was similar to a deadly disease.
To display their dissatisfaction, participants believed in their collective strength against
the polarised brands. Karen rebuffs the idea that brands can be socially or politically neutral
(Zaman Malik et al., 2025), saying, “I think anything we do with our money is a moral choice.
(…) I think silence is still a message”. Most interviewees stressed that they can vote with their
wallets and make a difference, as Dylan and others noted. Thus, interviewees are not only
participating in boycotts and protests, or trying to evangelise friends and family, but also silently
protesting. Even though some recognise that it is a small gesture, it is a significant one, as when
Peter realises that it is like “throwing a tiny stone at a giant monolith”.
3.4.3 Brand Agnosticism
Agnosticism differs from damnation or salvation, as it refers to individuals who neither
affirm nor deny religious claims and are less verbally opposed to religion compared to atheists
(Baker & Smith, 2009). Brand agnostics neither strongly support nor oppose any brands. Most
participants who loved polarised brands had a hard time thinking about brands they hated, and
the same was true for the haters, who showed no positive affection for any brands. Haters a nd
lovers believe that their opponents would change their minds if they were adequately informed,
agreeing with their beliefs.
Apart from that and in line with past research demonstrating that neutrality concerning
social issues does not necessarily lead to negative reactions (Zaman Malik et al., 2025), the
interviewees liked brands that remained silent and from which they were pu rchasing for
utilitarian purposes. Participants were willing to give these brands the benefit of the doubt,
believing that a whistleblower would uncover the wrongdoing.

62
When talking about activism, Albert does not like the way brands try to push their
agendas instead of selling their products: “If you’re a company that sells Coca -Cola, then sell
Coca-Cola. If you want to be an activist in your own time, I think that’s great. (…) I just don’t
love when a company is trying to push a message on me”. Peter shares the same opinion, saying
that he wants to buy products, not for brands to engage in activism. He comments about
McDonald’s and how their burgers are not gay and do no t vote: “ You know, if McDonald’s
says, ‘We support gay rights’. Cool. I’d have a problem if you say: ‘We don’t like gay rights’”.
Theo comments that some friends were arguing with him because he did not stop buying from
McDonald’s, even with the accusations that the brand was supplying food to the Israeli army
against Palestine: “Look, leave me alone! (...) I didn’t do anything. I me an, I didn’t buy this
burger out of hate, but they treat you like you’re sending a bomb yourself”.
One interesting story illustrates another facet of brand agnosticism and is told by Jack,
who has painful memories concerning Apple. He used to be a brand lover and worshipped
everything Apple launched, “I was very much a fan, a loyalist, right? In a way that no rational
person would do”. After a whole night finishing a school project, his Mac computer crashed in
the middle of the presentation, an embarrassment that made other students mock him . He
suddenly started hating Apple and vocalising his anger thro ugh social media. As he puts it, he
went from a rabid supporter to a rabid hater, and then to apathy. Jack explained how he was
affected by “magical thinking”, expecting things to be perfect and now having to be brand
agnostic. He compares Apple to a relationship with his ex-girlfriend, who cheated on him, but
he did not want to leave her.
It’s a weird thing to say, but I do think it’s the same thought process. (…) In my
mind, this person was very irreplaceable. She had certain properties that I
appreciated and I thought were important for my life. Like, yeah, those things are
still rare, but I’m living very happily without them. (Jack)
3.4.4 Brand Ambiguity
Some participants shared experiences they had with polarised brands that fell
somewhere between love and hate. Apart from brand addiction (Cui et al., 2018), these mixed
and conflicted feelings have been less explored in the literature (Fournier & Alvarez, 2013),
highlighting a need to uncover new relationship types (Alvarez et al., 2023) and understand a
middle ground in the attachment -aversion relationships model (Park et al., 2013a) . The
interviewees are caught in a zone of indeterminacy, where good and evil coexist, and ambiguity

63
and uncertainty prevail (Appau et al., 2020). Three sets of stories illustrate this brand ambiguity:
(1) Ava’s and Hudson’s abusive relationships with Starbucks and Apple; (2) Penelope’s and
Iris’ guilty pleasures with McDonald’s; and (3) Theo’s nostalgic and ambiguous relationship
with Nestlé.
The relationship between Ava and Starbucks is intense. She regularly visits two different
stores to grab her coffee, chat with friends, and socialise. Her life moments intertwine with the
brand, as she uses Starbucks to study, work, spend time, and feel pa rt of a community,
interacting with the baristas. Ava loves the brand atmosphere since it stands out from
competitors: “And that mermaid, I don’t even know who she is, but it’s just alluring. (…) It’s
just very magnetic, charismatic, consistent”. Her love for Starbucks was first described as a
midsummer affair. However, when provoked by the interviewer to explain how it would be
considered an affair if she had a long history with the brand, Ava offered a different perspective,
realising that she has mixed feelings towards Starbucks.
I think it’s so long because I know how bad it is. I’m a Type 2 diabetic. My sugars
are super high because of Starbucks. (...) I’ve drunk it since Middle School from
Starbucks. So, I’m 30 now. So, that’s a pretty long affair, I guess. But, you know, I
know I shouldn’t be having it, but I still go to it every day. (…) I love it! It’s just the
sugar that I feel bad for every time. You know, it’s like going back to a domestic
abuse situation and like, you know: “Why do you go back?”, they ask you. And I’m
like, you know, you can’t answer it really. (Ava)
Talking about Apple, Hudson explained how he tries to evangelise family members and
friends to buy it, recognising that the brand is using him and benefiting from his free advertising.
The interviewee also talked about how the brand only started to use the USB-C connector when
it was forced, as well as the lack of innovation, showing that Apple is tricking consumers: “So,
it’s kind of in that sense of ‘fool me that I like it’. At the same time, you’re not fooling anyone,
not even yourself”. Thus, Hudson und erstands that Apple abused its fans by launching high -
priced new phones every year with minor updates.
My cousin jokes that I’m a masochist, that I like to be beaten. (…) Then we see that
there are times when she [Apple] abuses consumers, and there are many consumers
who look and say, “Yes, in fact, here I was whipped and I liked it”. (Hudson)
The second set of stories concerns the guilty pleasures interviewees have. Penelope
loves McDonald’s and associates the brand with affectionate memories from her childhood.

64
Nevertheless, she believes her relationship with the brand is toxic because of the unhealthy
food. Penelope consumes McDonald’s by impulse and hides it from her fiancé, who only eats
healthy food. She ends up feeling guilty: “But I’m a little embarrassed, maybe, to eat it because
it’s not so good for my health, because maybe it’s like, ‘Wow, geez, you’re eating that food
made out of cardboard’, you know? [laughs]”.
Iris has a special connection with McDonald’s, having worked there during her
adolescence, which has instilled in her a deep respect for the brand. The interviewee recounts
that she tried for seven years to get pregnant, eating healthily at the beginning t o increase her
chances. When Iris finally got pregnant, she was regularly eating at McDonald’s. At a routine
check-up, the doctor said he had to deliver the baby immediately, but she had just eaten at

3.5 Discussion and Conclusion
3.5.1 Theoretical Contributions
To answer why polarised brands elicit antagonistic feelings and behaviours in
consumers (RQ1), the present research describes and explains the phenomenon as the lightning
rod effect , complementing the brand polarisation literature (Monahan et al., 2023; Osuna
Ramírez et al., 2019, 2024). This effect occurs because strong brands elicit a strong, polarised

65
emotional response from consumers (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019), who discharge their positive
and negative reactions on them, as seen in Figure 3.1. In this sense, polarised brands are beacons
that guide attention and attract consumer response. Nevertheless, the polarisation is not
necessarily sparked by oppositional brand loyalty, confirming past research that identified
rivalry as a specific type of brand polarisation (Osuna Ramírez et al., 2019).
The five brands chosen (Apple, Coca -Cola, McDonald’s, Nestlé, and Starbucks) are
iconic or hold high international status (Holt, 2004) . Past research focused on the positive
aspects of iconic brands (Holt, 2004) or the de -iconisation of a brand (Testa et al., 2017) .
However, their iconic status has a double -edged sword effect, epitomised by the lightning rod
effect. Thus, this paper also contributes to cultural branding theory by demonstrating that
iconicity is not only positive, evoking a sense of belonging, but also negative, as iconic brands
can face hatred and despise. Polarised brands can be iconic to lovers but anti-iconic to haters.
To understand how the polarisation process unfolds (RQ2), this paper analyses and
organises how the polarised brands release four emotional states, using the semiotic square
(Greimas & Rastier, 1968) , as depicted in Figure 3.2. The polarised brands also unearth new
types of brand -consumer relationships, which answer a call to capture more diversified ones
(Alvarez et al., 2023). The first side of the square is the complex axis, contrasting the emotions
of love and hate. In this axis, there is brand ambiguity, as love and hate intermingle, indicating
relationships that fall midway in the attachment -aversion model (Park et al., 2013a) :
dealers/addicts, guilty pleasures, and abused victims. The first relationship was identified by
previous researchers (Alves & Strehlau, 2025; Fournier & Alvarez, 2013) , but this paper
proposes the latter two.

The opposite side is the neutral axis, which contains the terms non -love and non-hate.
This axis concerns brand agnosticism, in which consumers view brands as neutral and do not
display strong emotions towards them. Brand agnostics remain sufficiently distant from brands
to properly evaluate them while still appreciating aspects, such as product features or
advertising. Consumers tend to shift towards a strong pole (either love or hate) regarding
particular polarised brands, while simultaneously having deta ched, agnostic, and utilitarian
relationships with other brands (polarised or not). The present research extends the attachment-
aversion model of customer-brand relationships (Fournier & Alvarez, 2013; Park et al., 2013a)
by demonstrating that both lovers and haters can be brand-agnostic towards neutral or utilitarian
brands if no tipping point triggers a reaction.
The two remaining sides of the semiotic square illustrate complementary relationships
between love and non-hate, and between hate and non-love, showing that love and hate are not
exact opposites (Fournier & Alvarez, 2013). The first regards brand salvation, where consumers
consider some brands preferred and loved, without harbouring any negative feelings towards
other brands. Apart from relationships identified in previous research and also present in this
research’s findi ngs – such as family ties, childhood buddies, teammates, therapists/patients,
soulmates, and vintage mates (Alves & Strehlau, 2025) – new ones are proposed: admirers,
aesthetes, blind lovers, escapists, and marriage. The last side of the semiotic square concerns
brand damnation, in which consumers express hatred rather than affection towards brands.
Although brand divorce has already been discussed in the literature (Ferraz & Dallabrida,
2024), new relationships involving activists, anti -narcissists/snobs, and deceivers/deceived
have been uncovered. Activism has not only an ideological and political drive, but also a strong
moral-ethical one, which differs from the partisan relationship of past research (Alves &
Strehlau, 2025).
To further explain why and how consumers feel and behave regarding polarised brands,
the theory of basic individual values was employed (Schwartz et al., 2012). There is a personal
focus on how individuals express their inner characteristics, contrasting with a social one on
how they interact with the world. Figure 3.3 illustrates the four groups of values adapted from
theory (Schwartz et al., 2012) , which were combined with the semiotic square depicting the
four emotional states associated with polarised brands. Consumers exposed to these brands tend
to behave and make decisions based on the underlying values they believe are more critical.
Brand haters are concerned about the preservation and appreciation of people’s and nature’s
welfare, which are components of self-transcendence. At the same time, lovers value personal

68
success, social status, and prestige, which are part of self-enhancement. Brand ambiguity shows
that consumers are driven by their independent thought to seek challenge, excitement, and
novelty. Finally, brand agnostics are conservative, restraining their actions and looking for
safety and stability.

Not only can the theory of basic individual values explain what lies beneath consumers’
motivations toward polarised brands, but consumers also expect brands to comply with
normatively binding promises that are sometimes not explicitly stated (Bhargava & Bedi,

and should not profit from savagely exploiting resources, the environment, or the workforce.
Their self-direction and self-transcendence drive them. On the other hand, lovers are tied to the
brand promise of self-enhancement and conservation, unwilling to delve into the brands’ secrets
or realise that all companies can have some degree of wrongdoing. As seen in Figure 3.4, a
brand that keeps its promise, regarding individual values, leads to brand salvation.

3.5.2 Managerial Implications
Consumers have distinct relationships with polarised brands, ranging from strongly
positive to negative poles. On the one hand, they can be loyal and view brands as idealised
partners without displaying strong negative emotions. This type of consumer is mo re worried
about their personal values and how the brand can fulfil them. On the other hand, brand haters
strongly oppose polarised brands because of their broken promises towards universal values
and society’s well-being. Brand managers need to identify t he different types to enhance their
relationship with lovers while mitigating the negative impact of haters.
Practitioners should be aware of the impact iconic brands have on consumers, as they
can both positively and negatively affect brand equity. This understanding can help managers
create brand strategies to identify and track movements that can lead to hatre d or love. For
instance, a move from lovers to ambiguity can weaken the brand strength if it leads to addiction.
At the same time, a change of haters to agnostics can diminish a bad reputation. However, once
the consumers are drawn to one of the poles, it is unlikely and difficult to move them from
there, which is a problem with brand haters.
There is a tipping point that sparks consumer hatred, usually a moral deviation.
Companies should be aware that this situation can trigger a chain reaction, leading individuals
to distrust their actions and have a ripple effect on the entire market. The wr ongdoings of one
brand can spill over to the others, turning consumers into activists. There is a Pandora’s box
risk for brands when they unleash their sinister secrets, which can affect the market.
For brands that are activists and purposely position themselves on one side of the
spectrum, they should adopt strategies to cope with haters who will never buy their products
and boycott them. However, polarised brands are subject to the lightning rod eff ect, pushing
their consumers to opposite poles, whether they want it or not. Brand strategists need to develop
plans that simultaneously address both brand fans, who see it as iconic, and detractors, who see
it as anti-iconic.
3.5.3 Limitations and Agenda for Future Research
This study has some limitations that need to be considered. The participants were
recruited solely from social media and may already be opinionated or influenced by a polarised
environment. A more diverse sample of consumers is needed to understand brand p olarisation
better. Another limitation concerns the narrow list of brands chosen for the study, which are

76
global and well-known. Future studies could investigate smaller and local brands to determine
whether the results would be the same.
More investigation is needed to understand the relationship between polarised brands
and their promises. There may be other underlying consumer motivations that trigger
polarisation beyond those suggested in this paper, including individual values and bran d
promise. The connections between brand salvation, damnation, agnosticism, and ambiguity
require further articulation and exploration through studies that focus on brands’ symbolic
meanings and religiosity. Other types of brand relationships may emerge, p articularly those
with polarised feelings, whether negative, positive, or ambiguous.
Finally, future research should investigate the relationship between polarised and iconic
brands. There is a need to understand further brands’ anti -iconicity, their interactions with
identity myths, emotional bonds, and storytelling. The clashes between i conic and anti-iconic
characteristics should be examined to understand their impact on branding strategies.

Although studies have identified negative consumer -brand relationships and
personalities, discussed behaviours and coping mechanisms to deal with them, and identified

2026), focused on emotions rather than relationships (Aziz & Rahman, 2022; Yadav &
Chakrabarti, 2022), and lacks an integrated organising structure of antecedents, interactions,
relationship types, and outcomes (Alvarez et al., 2023). Moreover, the negative consumer-brand
relationships were less discussed in the literature, with some studies defining types such as
dealers/addicts (Alves & Strehlau, 2025, 2026; Fournier & Alvarez, 2013) , enmities,
enslavements (Fournier, 1998), domestic abuse (Alves & Strehlau, 2026), masters/slaves, and

Another research stream studied consumer coping strategies and mechanisms. Coping

preventing, or controlling emotional distress (Pearlin & Schooler, 1978; Skinner et al., 2003) .
Consumer researchers studied coping when dealing with technology adoption (Mick &
Fournier, 1998) , facing stressful consumption events (Duhachek, 2005; Yi & Baumgartner,

(Bayarassou et al., 2020), engaging in brand communities (Weijo et al., 2019), and considering

those studies have not made a connection between negative brand personalities, dysfunctional
consumer-brand relationships, and coping mechanisms.
To address these knowledge gaps, our research asks h ow flawed consumer -brand
relationships are fostered, cultivated, structured, and handled. Drawing on this central question,
we further ask what types of negative relationships exist between brands and consumers,
triggered by negative brand personalities, and what coping strategies and behaviours are used
to address them. We conducted phenomenological interviews with consumers, analysed
secondary data, and followed an online forum as part of a netnography to understand how
consumers deal with broken relatio nships with brands. Throughout the investigation, we
uncovered untheorised n egative consumer-brand relationships and coping strategies, relating
them to negative consumption experiences.
Our main contribution is the proposal of a novel theoretical framework that shows how
flawed consumer-brand relationships are triggered by dark brand personality traits (Malär &
Giuffredi-Kähr, 2024), appraised, cultivated, and coped with through diverse mechanisms and
behaviours. Since the seminal work of Fournier (1998), who proposed a brand relationship
quality model, no similar attempt has been made to develop a framework for flawed
relationships. The closest initiatives were from Dietrich and Russell (2021) , who proposed a
framework for brand contestation; from Kähr et al. (2016), who developed a contestation model
for aggressive consumer behaviour; and from Wilson et al. 2022, who identified four forms of
