consumer subversion. Nevertheless, these studies are more closely related to anti-consumption,
activism, hostility, and crisis management than to investigating negative consumer -brand
relationships, coping mechanisms, or understanding the role of brands’ negative personalities.
Second, we advance knowledge of negative consumer -brand relationship types by
suggesting novel ones, such as dictator/subjects, absent/orphans, crooks/suckers, and
spies/targets. Third, we define four coping mechanisms of accommodating, distancing,
confronting, and reframing, adding to the consumer coping literature by explaining how they
are connected to negative brand relationships, elicited emotions, and negative brand
personalities. Our findings have implications for theory on dysfunctional brand relati onships
and negative brand personality.
4.2 Theoretical Foundation
4.2.1 Negative Consumer-Brand Relationships
The literature on negative consumer -brand relationships is fragmented and
underdeveloped (Yadav & Chakrabarti, 2022) , leading to theoretical confusion and diverse
conceptualisations (Aziz & Rahman, 2022; Ladeira et al., 2026) . The efforts to define brand
relationship types are limited, and years after the initial typology (Fournier, 1998), only brand
love emerged as a key construct (Alvarez et al., 2023) . The fact that brand hate has been
conceptualised as a combination of negative emotions (Aziz and Rahman 2022) does not help
clarify the distinct emotions and behaviours involved.
The first research stream on negative consumer -brand relationships is centred on the
definition of brand hate, its antecedents, consequences, and intensity. Most researchers have
conceptualised brand hate through a negative -valenced emotional lens (Aziz an d Rahman
2022), primarily drawing on the duplex theory of hate (Sternberg, 2003), which considers the
negation of intimacy (disgust), passion (anger/fear), and commitment (devaluation/diminution)
as components of hate. Studies have explored the active and passive aspects of brand hate
(Zarantonello et al., 2016), which some authors consider as a continuum, ranging from mild to
extreme hate (Bryson & Atwal, 2019; Fetscherin, 2019; Kucuk, 2019). The idea that consumers
do not have ecstatic emotional responses led to the exploration of trajectories from love to hate
and vice versa (Grégoire et al., 2009; Johnson et al., 2011; Tolunay & Veloutsou, 2025;
Zarantonello et al., 2018).

80
The fragmentation of studies on brand hate shows that authors consider a myriad of
emotions related to it, such as sadness (Zhang & Laroche, 2020) , anger (Fetscherin, 2019;
Kucuk, 2019; Zarantonello et al., 2016) , fear (Zarantonello et al., 2016; Zhang & Laroche,
2020), and worry (Romani et al., 2012). Scholars also studied other emotional states related to
branding constructs, such as brand shame (Weitzl & Hutzinger, 2025) , repulsion (Dessart &
Cova, 2021), and negativity (Dessart et al., 2020). One problem with the dispersed theorisation
is that brand hate could end up encompassing every non -positive aspect of consumer -brand
relationships, behaviours, and emotional states, rather than having a more accurate definition.
Indeed, in the field of psychology, emotions such as fear, anger, love, and sadness are
considered fuzzy sets without clear boundaries, represented by prototypes or most
representative examples (Shaver et al., 1987). They can be combined into primary and
secondary emotions to form other emotional states, like love and sadness, which can give rise
to nostalgia or yearning (Kemper, 1987). However, the negative consumer -brand relationship
literature has given disproportionate attention to hate rather than exploring other combinations
of negative emotions and has treated brand hate as an umbrella construct.
A second research stream has prioritised a behavioural perspective of the negative
relationship between consumers and brands. Consumers can adopt a contestation nature to
disrupt, negotiate meanings, and resist brands (Dietrich & Russell, 2021) . They participate as
activists in anti-brand communities to get control over brand meanings (Hollenbeck & Zinkhan,
2010), deconstructing them using humorous and subversive messages (Krishnamurthy &
Kucuk, 2009; Kucuk, 2015). Some might engage in opposition to brand hegemonic culture (C.
J. Thompson & Arsel, 2004; Thota, 2021), boycotting and culture-jamming (Cova & D’Antone,
2016), while others, imbued with an ideological mindset, consider hated brands anti -iconic
(Alves & Strehlau, 2026; Dessart & Cova, 2021).
Dislike for brands can be triggered by moral transgressions (Mahmud & Guzmán, 2025;
Romani et al., 2015; Rosendo -Rios et al., 2025) , political or ideological incompatibility
(Sandıkcı & Ekici, 2009) , and the protection of self -esteem and rejection of an undesired self
(Hogg et al., 2009). It can also be part of a brand-bullying process, where those who experience
it show negative feelings towards brands used for bullying (Kucuk & Aledin, 2022) . On the
other hand, some scholars have consolidated motivations into a brand avoidance construct, in
which consumers choose to avoid or reject a brand due to identity incongruity, ideological
incompatibility, or unmet expectations (Lee et al., 2009; Odoom et al., 2019).

81
The third research stream has studied types of negative consumer -brand relationships.
Contrary to other research that analysed nostalgia in a positive light (Alves & Strehlau, 2025;
Brown et al., 2003; Davari et al., 2017) , one study has found that consumers may be attached
to brands due to nostalgic feelings, even when they dislike them (Demirbag-Kaplan et al.,
2015). Other articles explored diverse negative relationships related to activism, narcissism,
and deception (Alves & Strehlau, 2026); masters/slaves and stalker/prey (Fournier & Alvarez,
2013); and enmities and dependencies (Fournier, 1998).
Another aspect of negative relationships is their dissolution. Few studies have explored
how consumers and brands part ways, which can be associated with a change in perception and
spiritual transformation (Sussan et al., 2012), be the result of wrongdoing or misconduct (Alves
& Strehlau, 2026) , or follow trajectories that can lead to brand hate, neutrality, or aversion
(Ferraz & Dallabrida, 2024). Opposed to dissolution are relationships where the consumer feels
forced to consume, as in abusive (Alves & Strehlau, 2026; Fournier & Alvarez, 2013) or
addictive ones (Alves & Strehlau, 2025; Cui et al., 2018; Mrad & Cui, 2017) . Even with the
identification of some negative consumer-brand relationship types, the literature remains scarce
and is more centred on positive bonds, such as brand love, communal relationships, and
friendship (Alvarez et al., 2023).
The three research streams – the first focused on emotional aspects, the second on
behavioural actions, and the third on negative relationships – lack further integration. Scholars
have presented proposals and theoretical discussions, but have been restricted to particular
negative consumer reactions , antecedents, or typologies . A preliminary discussion of
integrating negative relationships was presented by Fournier (1998), who distinguishes their
dissolution into stress and entropic models. The first is caused by environmental, partner -
oriented, and dyadic stresses, while the second is due to a failure to maintain the relationship.
Nevertheless, the proposed dissolution mo del focuses on antecedent types rather than
elaborating on coping mechanisms, adverse events, or specific negative consumer -brand
relationships. Another framework was discussed by Dietrich and Russell (2021), who proposed
a contestation wheel with processes of negotiation, disruption, and expression. However, this
framework concerns changes in brand meanings unintended by the legal owners (such as those
arising from cultural appropriation, cooptation, opposition, and condemnation), not necessarily
restricted to negative consumer -brand relationships. Similarly, Wilson et al. (2022)
conceptualised and discussed four forms of consumer subversion, but their work is restricted to
behavioural actions. It does not elaborate on antecedents, relationship types, emotions, or

82
coping strategies. Finally, Kähr et al. (2016) presented a conceptual framework to organise
consumers’ aggressive reactions towards brands, including stimuli, appraisals, and reappraisals.
However, the authors analysed only extreme forms of behavioural reactions (e.g., consumer
brand sabotage) and did not specify how the negative relationships would unfold.
4.2.2 Negative Brand Personality
Studies on brand personality have predominantly focused on positive aspects (Aaker,
1997), assuming that brands have only favourable attributes. Brand personality is based on the
Big Five Model of human personality, although it is not a perfect match, as some factors may
or may not apply (Aaker, 1997; Caprara et al., 2001). Since brand personality relies on human-
like traits, although not perfectly, other authors have suggested that it should comprise both
positive and negative aspects that differentiate the brand (Saeed et al., 2022).
Previous research has acknowledged that brand personality can affect how consumers
react when brands misbehave (Aaker et al., 2004) , but limited research has examined its less
favourable aspects. Negative feelings, such as anxiety, tension, and frustration, were considered
part of a negative conceptualisation of brand personality, which, according to an early study,
comprises egotistical, illogical, boring, irresponsible, and critical dimensions (Haji et al., 2012).
More recent research developed a scale based on the dark triad of human personality
(narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy) to include traits related to manipulation,
exploitation, and lack of empathy (Malär & Giuffredi-Kähr, 2024), reassessing the fragmented
and scant literature on this matter. Given the very few studies on negative brand personality
(Malär & Giuffredi-Kähr, 2024; Saeed et al., 2022), its impact on consumer behaviour, emotion
appraisal, and coping strategies remains unknown.
4.2.3 Consumer Coping
Coping mechanisms are strategies people use to manage life strains, such as stressful
situations, frustrations, conflicts, and threats (Pearlin & Schooler, 1978). Negative events elicit
primary and secondary emotions that are appraised in terms of their quality and intensity,
triggering coping responses associated with problem -solving, positive reappraisal,
confrontation, and distancing, grouped into problem -focused versus emotion -focused
categories (Folkman & Lazarus, 1988) . However, authors criticised the definition of core
categories, as coping is a multidimensional construct comprising several individual behaviours,

83
cognitions, and perceptions that can form families of coping, such as information seeking, self-
reliance, or submission (Skinner et al., 2003).
In the consumer behaviour field, the same criticism was directed to conceptualising
coping as either problem-focused or emotion-focused, prompting the proposal of a theoretical
model with eight coping strategies, ranging from active coping to avoidance (Duhachek, 2005).
Other authors proposed similar coping typologies appropriate for consumer behaviour settings,
criticising the abstractness, difficulty in classification, and problems in measuring coping when
only problem -focused and emotion -focused categories are consid ered (Yi & Baumgartner,
2004).
When facing brand transgressions, consumers can adopt active coping strategies that
confront the company to seek revenge, or passive ones, such as avoiding and ignoring the
problem (Zourrig et al., 2009). Not all coping strategies are detrimental and can be constructive
or neutral, even after negative incidents (Klütz & Albrecht, 2025). However, transgressions are
not easily forgotten and can become ingrained in a brand community’s collective memory,
permanently damaging the brand’s reputation, as consumers vent, ruminate, avoid, and act
against it (Weijo et al., 2019) . Other stressful situations demand confrontative and avoidance
strategies to manage paradoxes in society, as in the case of technology (Mick & Fournier, 1998),
to deal with social and temporal comparisons, catalysing coping mechanisms to pursue self -
esteem and self-compassion (Karanika & Hogg, 2016), to mitigate decision-generated negative
emotions (Luce, 1998) , or to adopt different types of compensatory behaviours, such as
escapism, addiction, or compulsive buying (Rauber et al., 2024).
Although the coping literature in consumer behaviour has addressed brand
transgressions, negative incidents, compensatory behaviours, and coping strategies and
mechanisms, it is unclear how these are connected to negative brand relationships and
personalities. The literature on consumer behaviour and branding lacks a more comprehensive
understanding of how brand stimuli trigger emotions and broken relationships, which are
ultimately handled through coping mechanisms and behaviours.
4.3 Research Methods
4.3.1 Data Collection
We drew on diverse data sources to explore our phenomenon with theoretical depth and
achieve a thick description (Geertz 1973), as shown in Table 4.1. The first source was

84
phenomenological interviews conducted by the first author in English and Portuguese with 30
consumers from 10 countries, scheduling them to accommodate different time zones. To recruit
participants for the study, a combination of techniques was applied. Multiple keywords were
used in Reddit to find posts related to negative consumption experiences, such as emotions
(e.g., hate, sadness, frustration), swearing (e.g., fuck, what the fuck, shit), negative words (e.g.,
horrible, stupid, insane), behaviours (e.g ., boycott, protest, avoid), and brand names (e.g.,
Apple, Nestlé, Southwest). Potential candidates were direct messaged and invited to participate
in the study. Snowball sampling was used to complement the total number of respondents. The
interviews lasted an average of 63 minutes and were transcribed verbatim. We followed the
ethical procedures approved by the faculty’s ethics committee, including a free and informed
consent form shared orally with the participants, who verbally agreed to participate.
Our sample comprised 14 female and 16 male respondents, aged 22 to 60, as shown in
Table 4.2, and covered a wide range of brands across sectors. The interview started with a non-
directive grand tour question (McCracken 1988), asking the respondents to talk about the brands
they disliked. Usually, the conversation began with a specific negative consumption experience
identified by the researchers during the recruiting phase, and then evolved to explore any other
dysfunctional ones. The interviewer followed a phenomenological dialogue as a non -directive
listener, avoiding intrusion and allowing participants to provide lengthy and thick descriptions
(Thompson, Locander, and Pollio 1989) . An interview guide was used as a reference for the
conversation, but not as a set of semi -structured, pre -defined questions, prioritising how
consumers experience and live through the phenomenon (Adams and van Manen 2008) and
focusing on their reflections on the significance of the negative events (Smith, Flowers, and
Larkin 2009).
Apart from the interviews, the second source was a netnography conducted from
September 2025 to March 2026 on one online Reddit forum : mildlyinfuriating, launched in
2012, with 9.6 million weekly visitors (Reddit 2026). We selected this forum since it is focused
on venting a wide range of negative experiences, not restricted to a particular brand or sector.
The first author engaged as a netnographer and non -participant observer, reading posts and
comments to select the ones related to negative consumer-brand experiences. The collected data
were organised into field notes, including the posts and relevant comments, following the
netnography procedures (Kozinets 2020). To protect users’ identities and their content, quotes
used in this article were altered to ensure anonymisation, and a new digital pseudonym was
assigned (Kozinets 2020).

4.3.2 Analytical Procedures
We applied the premises of Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis to explore how
consumers experience and make sense of significant events, interpreting them through
hermeneutics (Smith et al., 2009) . Grounded theory was also applied to build and derive
theoretical contributions inductively from data (Corbin & Strauss, 2015). The first author coded
the interview transcripts, field notes, and secondary data using initial and axial coding (Saldaña,
2013), using MAXQDA 24 qualitative data analysis software. The pieces of data were
compared with one another and with the whole, following a hermeneutic circle (Arnold &
Fischer, 1994). After that, the three authors engaged in discussions, iterations, and comparisons
with theory to fine -tune the interpretation of the data and reach theoretical saturation , as the
complete range of constructs comprising the theoretical contribution was represented in the data
(Saunders et al., 2018). Ultimately, our research relied first on inductive reasoning and second
on abductive theory construction to propose an innovative framework (Janiszewski & van
Osselaer, 2022).
4.4 Findings
Our findings show that flawed consumer -brand relationships are organised into three
structural blocks. The first concerns stimuli that consumers receive and appraise, specifically
negative brand personality, which leads to dysfunctional experiences stemming from how
brands act and present themselves. The second is the development of problematic relationships
caused by stimuli that elicit a diverse range of emotions. The third and final structural block
concerns how consumers cope with negative incidents thr ough four mechanisms: confronting,
distancing, reframing, and accommodating.
4.4.1 Dark Brand Personality
Respondents faced dysfunctional experiences with brands, initiated by negative brand
personalities. They considered them to have human -like dark personality traits, such as

89
manipulativeness, deception, coldness, lack of empathy, exploitation, and snobbery. When
confronted with a negative incident or impressions stemming from negative brand traits,
consumers appraised the situation according to several factors: the situational state, their
motivation, the probability of the outcomes, and their agency and power (Roseman et al., 1990).
Brands falling in love with their own image . Narcissistic brands are full of themselves,
arrogant, egocentric, controlling, overinflated, annoying, and snobby. Jane felt dominated by
Instagram and its algorithm, considering that she was unable to control her feed. She was
annoyed by the number of unnecessary things she bought and by not being able to turn off ads.
When asked to describe the brand, she thought about a controlling figure:
I think it would be a man. A Trump -like man. Like, “Everything is mine [opening
her arms], because I liked this thing, I’m going to buy it. I liked this thing, I’m going
to have people killed, fuck what they think! And if you fight with me, I’ll triple the
tariffs!” you know? [laughs]. I think it would be a dictator in that sense, like,
“Everyone look at me and like what I’m doing. And if you don’t like it, you’re trash!”
That’s it. (Jane)
Informants felt frustrated by their dependence on services they cannot get rid of or are
obliged to use. Wilson described Microsoft similarly to how Jane thinks about Instagram: “ So,
this is Microsoft currently: big, fat, with a lot of money, and can do whatever, absolutely
whatever they want.” Tim also commented on how Microsoft dictates how consumers must use
their products: “So, when they want to force an architectural change, a structural change at the
machine level, they don ’t care about you at all. Y ou’ll have to buy it and figure it out. ” For
them, the brand’s egotistical, arrogant nature is only thinking about itself. Most participants
also mentioned how technology brands, such as Google, Microsoft, and Meta, are pushing AI
features that nobody wants, as Raymond stressed out: “It is one of the most annoying pushes I
have ever seen, both Copilot and Gemini, with how hard they’re trying to shove it down your
throat! I don’t want to use it.”
Not only do brands demonstrate their power, but they also suppress local competitors
by buying them and wiping out the country’s culture. That is how Scarlett feels about Nestlé
since the company bought a Czech chocolate brand. She feels powerless against the brand’s
autocratic force, comparing the small Czech brand to barnacles that would not hurt a giant
whale: “I can’t imagine someone who would love these big firms that are literally eating all

90
those small ones, right? What is there to like about it? (...) How can a small company from the
Czech Republic hurt such a whale?”
When it comes to arrogance, Aaron, Bruce, Tim, and Xavier dislike how Apple presents
itself as overpriced, elitist, and cult-driven. Tim explains his point of view: “I never wanted to
participate in the Apple cult either. (...) I find it kind of crazy this whole issue of exorbitant
prices and having to constantly upgrade to the latest thing, which doesn’t change much.” With
the same reasoning, Ruth criticises luxury brands, such as Prada, Gucci, and Yves Saint
Laurent, for showing off and selling only a name: “So, I feel like they upsell and they use brand
names to do it. (...) You’re taught that this has value because it’s called Prada. Because it’s
called Gucci, because it’s Yves Saint Laurent.”
In this sense, narcissistic brands exercise power by being snobs and superior, but they
can also combine several dark traits inherited by their CEOs, which are intrinsically connected
to them (Bendisch et al., 2013). One comment on Reddit, in a thread discussing how Elon Musk
is covering the Earth with SpaceX satellites, exemplifies it: “Each day, that person increasingly
resembles a stereotypical comic book supervillain” ( anythingbeatsmuch – mildlyinfuriating).
Many participants commented on the CEO’s personality and how it affected the brands they
consumed. Alexander explains how CEOs are only thinking about themselves and not about
the consumers:
But with Meta, with, you know, Tesla, anything by Musk, with Amazon, you have
sociopaths, avowed sociopaths, clearly sociopathic people, charismatic sociopaths
who are running the show. And their values and their goals are typically opposed to
the values a nd goals of the consumers using those services or purchasing those
products. (Alexander)
Lacking empathy for the consumer . Brands that have psychopathic traits act
unscrupulously, lacking moral values and empathy. They are insensitive to consumer demands
and feelings, inflicting harm, discriminating, being neglectful and irresponsible. In a Daily Mail
news article, chief rep orter Sam Greenhill explained his quest against TalkTalk, a British
telecommunications provider. He had problems with his phone and tried for months to get it
fixed by the company without success, ultimately taking them to court and winning the case:
My efforts to alert TalkTalk to this telephone fault descended into farce. It was like
Groundhog Day. I spoke to a different person in its Far Eastern call centre each time,
none of whom knew anything about my previous calls. Few seemed remotely

91
bothered about our problem. (...) TalkTalk’s call centre offered me a desultory £5
discount to make up for the problems. We said they should come and fix the damage.
(...) I was nearly ready to throw in the towel. I suggested to TalkTalk that I would
settle for £300 and an apology — so we could all move on. But TalkTalk stuck to its
guns, saying the £60 discount was its ‘full and final’ offer. And then it added insult
to injury. It sent a letter accusing us of ‘only noticing’ after two months that our
phones were not working. The reality was we had ‘noticed’ when we desperately
needed the emergency services, but TalkTalk only took notice of our complaint after
two months of phoning its call centre. That was the moment I resolved not to let it
drop. It had become a matter of principle. (Greenhill, 2017)
Informants and users reported several incidents involving brands that mistreated them
by denying refunds, failing to deliver purchased items, incorrectly charging, cancelling paid
services, or selling malfunctioning products. They felt frustrated and angry because the
companies did nothing to repair the damage, failed to solve the issue, and showed no concern
for them. One Reddit user complained about Air Canada, as the company delayed the flight,
made him miss two connections and left the family with a dog for hours without assistance:
“Air Canada didn’t get us anything: no meals, no hotel, absolutely nothing. We ended up paying
$250 for lounge access so we could sit with our dog. Another family got upgraded, and we were
stuck with cramped seats.” (3 20_BootySorcerer – mildlyinfuriating). On YouTube, users
posted videos to vent their anger, document the lack of quality, and warn other consumers not
to buy the brand, as Emira Tolban did. She recorded a video to “warn the American public”
that a Ford Focus was garbage due to several issues, stating that Ford knew about the problems,
continued selling the vehicles, and that the dealers lied about it.
Repeated problems with no solution led informants to dystopian realities, as Martin
narrates his odyssey against Xfinity, a Comcast subsidiary. It started when the company
installed internet in his house, inadvertently cutting off the neighbours’ connectio n the day
before the Super Bowl. The relationship with the company went downhill since then, with
modem connection problems and not being able to solve them: “ And every time I have to
interact with their customer service, whether it be on the website, in a chat or on the phone,
each time it’s just more of a pain in the butt than it was the last time .” When technicians went
to fix the problems, they blamed the previous ones, leaving him empty-handed. Martin also had
his service turned off because the company failed to debit his bank account. In a nutshell,

92
Xfinity was neglectful, irresponsible, and lacked empathy. He summarises the relationship as
painful and burdensome: “So, it’s just been 30 years of frustration with them!”
The lack of care for consumers can reach alarming levels in healthcare. Justin explains
that his health insurance, from Intermédica, took a long time to approve his request: “ And it’s
an emergency surgery, right? So, after appendicitis was detected, I waited almost 48 hours for
them to operate on me.” After being asked how he felt and reacted to being left waiting, Justin
answered: “Oh, I felt scared, you know? Because if it ruptured, it’s a risk. (...) But at the time,
I even had the impression that they w anted it to rupture so the surgery would be more
expensive.” Thus, the brand is seen as egoistic and irresponsible, putting consumers in danger.
The same feeling is shared by Daisy, who considers healthcare insurance companies terrible
and unwilling to help consumers, particularly United Healthcare:
Awful, evil, evil company! I know so many people in the healthcare industry. I have
a friend who’s a doctor, and I’ve listened to him talk about the things he has to do to
advocate for his patients when insurance doesn’t want to pay for their care. And
somebody who’s not even a doctor will make the call that somebody doesn’t deserve
to have their care paid for, and it’s fucking absurd! These companies are really evil.
(Daisy)
Manipulating the consumer. Machiavellianistic brands exploit their relationships with
consumers for their own interest, deceiving and lying to them, spying, stalking, and making
them addicted to their products. Bruce has a hard time with banks, saying they should not exist,
though he loves the stock market and uses it for his personal and business activities. He pictures
the banking system as a necessary evil that can be managed. However, Bruce dislikes banks for
being manipulative and serving their own needs, rigging the stock market. He explains how he
won a case against Wells Fargo: “They’re the biggest criminal entity in the world as far as for
banking. (...) I’ve been a victim to their fraudulent practices, seriously, to the point that I’ve
even gotten checks, you know?”
Informants often commented on exploitation and manipulation, stating that they were
being scammed and tricked or that the system is fraudulent. After going to McDonald’s and
wanting to try a Monopoly raffle, one Reddit user was flabbergasted and realised that the odds
of winning did not seem right: “What the fuck? Odds of 1 in 60 billion??? And it doesn’t stop
there: there are others like 1 in 12 billion and 1 in 30 billion. This is completely ridiculous! Is
this even legal?” (Kittora2005 – mildlyinfuriating). Answering his question, others jumped in

93
to comment that it was easier to win the lottery or that McDonald’s purposely launched a
sweepstakes that is statistically impossible to win.
Several situations prompted consumers to complain online about how brands are
shrinking packaging and the amount of products while keeping prices, with some feeling that
they are buying empty containers and are being deceived by the brands, as one Reddit u ser
posted about Pampers: “Why is so much stuff for babies a rip -off? People always go on about
how expensive it is, but paying the same price for LESS diapers is ridiculous!! ”
(Relentless_Tension642 – mildlyinfuriating). Other users complained about service providers,
saying it was difficult to rely on them and that they seemed like parasites: “Instead of cancelling
my membership, they wanted to charge me monthly to freeze it. Fuck You LA Fitness! ”
(_midnightglow_ – mildlyinfuriating). The parasitic nature of some brands is often seen in
technology, as another user commented about Motorola pushing Glance, their AI feature: “This
motherfucker parasite! (...) I tried hunting down the app so I could delete it. I CAN’T DELETE
IT. So I disabled it. It’s still fucking running.” (Frozen-Sketch1743 – mildlyinfuriating).
Brands can also stalk and spy on consumers, storing information about them and using
it for their own interest. Participants were concerned about their privacy, as brands and
governments hide their true intentions when collecting data. When asked if tech brands are not
being transparent, Damian agrees and adds: “T hey’re collecting it (...), but it’s not being
disclosed to the consumers and the people about exactly how that data is being used and where
it’s going, and what it’s being used for. ” As a sales re presentative of a technology company,
Carter understands how companies can be invasive, gathering data to offer products and
services, sometimes even embarrassingly, which could cause serious troubles:
And many years ago, Target observed their customers, you know? And the story
goes. There was a young lady who bought very specific items when she went there.
And those very specific items were very indicative of the behaviours of somebody
who is about to be a new mother. (...) Target sends a leaflet, a piece of mail, to that
house. And the father sees it and puts two and two together and goes, “Oh my God,
my daughter’s pregnant!” And how does Target know about it? (Carter)
Participants reported that brands create addictive features to hook consumers to their
products and services, manipulating how they feel, behave, and have relationships with other
people. Scarlett stresses her distrust of pharmaceutical companies, of how t hey do not care for
patients, and are not interested in finding the cure for diseases to keep consumers buying their

94
drugs: “They are basically trying to make you ill a bit, just so you would be dependent on their
medications over and over and create this loop of dependency.”
Other informants talked about social media and technology brands as problematic and
a source of addiction, but most felt they were unescapable, a necessary evil. Carter believes that
modern technology is a necessity and that consumers do not have a choice, as if people were
selling their souls: “I think there was a Reddit thread that said, ‘Internet and a phone are basic
human needs,’ you know? So, people are equating it to , like, shelter.” Even when participants
did not think that brands were addictive, they admitted that they were indispensable, as Amazon
is to Daisy: “I wouldn’t say it’s an addiction, but I would still say they’re probably like a drug
dealer. Like, yeah, I don’t want to deal with them, but I really need this thing right now
[laughs].”
4.4.2 Negative Consumer-Brand Relationships
We identified 13 negative consumer-brand relationships associated with the three dark
personality traits, as seen in Table 4.3. To provide thicker, deeper descriptions, we selected
exemplary stories for each, grouping them according to their respective dark brand personality
traits. The relationships are not mutually exclusive, as informants may have multiple
relationships with the same brands, consistent with previous research (Alves & Strehlau, 2025).
Narcissistic consumer -brand relationships . Narcissistic brands break promises by
leaving their consumers orphans and sad, or betray their trust by going against the beliefs and
values they once defended. We start by discussing two stories from Southwest that exemplify
the absent/orphans relationship.
Zachary used to be a loyal Southwest customer. He tried to use a flight credit, but the
company would not allow it, even after he booked a full-fare ticket. Southwest was convenient
for Zachary because one of their airports is 15 minutes from his home. He was upset with the
recent changes at the company, which made it more anti-consumer, introduced reserved seating,
and dropped its free bag -check policy. When asked how he would describe the brand as a
person, Zachary thought about how the changes are affect ing the brand’s culture and
personality: “It’s like they were an idealistic young person, and as they’ve gotten older, they’ve
become more cynical and driven by their needs versus their customer needs (...) they’re making
a decision based on just money versus who they are. ” Zoe also felt abandoned and orphaned
when Southwest changed its policies: “So, I always felt like they were reliable. I felt like I was

95
taken care of. I never had any issues.” However, Zoe felt that the company was selling its soul
by becoming more of the same, similar to other airlines: “ So, it’s extremely disappointing,
particularly in today’s world , to see them chase after normalcy [laughs] (...) take away all the
things that make them unique. It’s just really sad!”
Another way that brands break the consumer’s trust is by going against what they once
believed or broadcast as their values. The traitors/betrayed relationship is exemplified by
Nathan’s story, who was a fan of BrewDog and its founders because it was an in dependent
company, compassionate towards its employees, and different from other British beer brands.
However, internal changes began to surface, damaging the brand’s reputation. BrewDog
promised to be an independent beer company, but sold part of the comp any to expand to the
US. Nathan even invested in the firm, but later realised that BrewDog was not issuing real
shares, which cost him money. The brand also stood for values such as protecting the
environment and having a good workplace. “ Then, yeah, sadly, all those things that they said
they stood for have faded away. They’ve changed drastically. ” Nathan felt betrayed by the
changes and, particularly, by the toxic character of James Watt, one of the founders, who was
accused of abusing employees: “I think he’s a classic example of someone who just got too rich
and too powerful. And it’s probably just been very mean and nasty , and it’s just too full of
himself.”
The second aspect of narcissistic brands is how they exert their superior might against
consumers. Cecil explains how he is obliged to buy from some companies in a forced marriage
relationship. When asked about how he dealt with energy, gas, and water comp anies, Cecil is
not happy to be stuck with limited options and complained about the privatisation of services
in the UK, saying that energy prices became the most expensive in Europe. Commenting on
British Gas, he believes the company provides poor service for a public concession: “They went
private and aren’t very good. I mean, the prices that they offer are about average for most
houses, but what they don’t offer is anything beneficial. ” Even when there is a choice, like in
car insurance, it is mandatory, Cecil points out that all alternatives are equally bad: “ You have
to have it. But it’s a racket, you know? There’s no real way of competing, finding a good deal
on it because everything is extremely expensive.”

Apart from forced marriages, brands can act like dictators, subjugating consumers to
obey their orders. Carter talks about several big corporations and how ubiquitous they are,
making them indispensable and unavoidable: “ But I think it is bothersome because the big
companies, the biggest companies are Apple, Meta, Amazon, and so on. And they sort of control
the narrative, don’t they? They sort of decide .” Talking about Fonterra, a New Zealand dairy
corporation, Carter is blunt: “ You couldn’t avoid Fonterra because all our milk comes from
Fonterra. It would be near ly impossible, unless you stop drinking milk. ” He is pragmatic and
thinks that people often are cynical and hypocritical when criticising these companies, as he
comments about the movie The Gods Must be Crazy: “Because, at some point, the bushman is
going to drink a Coke, you know? He’s going to submit himself to modernity, as awful as we
think it is.”
The last narcissistic relationship regards sadists/masochists. Even though there is
asymmetrical power and the brand controls the relationship, the consumer benefits. It might be
contradictory, but there is a positive outcome for the person. Bruce complain s about Verizon
and how the company has got worse over the years: “ I remember back in the day, when you
had Verizon, there was a difference in quality (...) Right now, hell no! Verizon is like cricket.
Damn near like the same shit! [laughs].” However, when he was provoked by the interviewer,
saying he kept using it, Bruce confessed that he has been with Verizon for 20 years and was
sincere: “But every time that I try to leave, they’d be giving me some nice deals, and I just keep,
you know? [laughs] (...) But the thing is what I’m paying, what I’m getting... It’s gonna be hard
to match it.”
Psychopathic consumer-brand relationships. Psychopathic brands lack empathy for the
consumer, being insensitive and causing harm. The first relationship concerns domestic abuse,
which is different from a forced marriage since it involves mistreatment and stronger negative
emotions. However, the consumer benefits from the interaction with the brand, or does not have
better options, even though they suffer abuse.
Sophia told two consumption stories that illustrate this relationship. She flies Ryanair
from Portugal to other countries because it is a low -cost airline that suits her needs. Sophia
described a bad experience at the airport when travelling with her girlf riends. A Ryanair
employee checked her bags to see if they fit with the stipulated measures: “ And the lady was
really mean to us, like, I ended up having to put my backpack there [into the bag sizer] four

100
times, even though mine fit right away .” The employee told another that the girls were a
problem, and started complaining that Sophia had brought a second item:
So, I went to swipe my ticket, and the lady who called the supervisor saw that I had
my wallet. And she turned to me, looked me in the eyes, and shouted, “I already told
you that you can’t bring the second item!” And I just looked at them, “Look, your
colleague said I could,” “But I’m the one in charge here!” (Sophia)
Sophia also had a hard time with Ticketmaster. As a Harry Styles fan, she was anxious
to buy a good seat for the show and slept two nights in a mall to be one of the first in line. When
her way finally came, the Ticketmaster website crashed because of high demand, forcing her to
try several times without any luck: “And I think they do it on purpose, because years and years
go by and nobody likes buying concert tickets, because it’s always awful!” She felt devastated
by not being able to buy the tickets she wanted: “I cried a lot, and it was very dramatic because
I spent two nights at the mall, which was horrible!”
Different from domestic abuse, a criminals/victims relationship regards stronger brand
wrongdoings, causing severe damages to the consumers, either psychologically, emotionally,
or financially. Oliver had a serious problem with a Brazilian phone carrier, C laro, which sold
two cell phone lines without his consent. He was not a client, but Claro used his name, ID, and
a fake address to sell the lines. Eventually, the unpaid bills were sent to a debt collection agency,
as he was trying to fix the problem cause d by the brand: “ Trying to solve it with them was
awful, terrible! In fact, it’s not fixed. I'm taking them to court because of this.”
Another psychopathic relationship concerns moral enmity. Consumers have strong
negative feelings towards brands that deviate from moral standards or act against the person’s
values. Maya dislikes Hobby Lobby for denying employees access to birth control in their
insurance, finding it unethical: “ And I don’t think that you , as my employer, except in very
specific roles, get to determine what religion I follow, what my ethics or morals are, as long as
I’m not doing something illegal.” Zachary also hates Hobby Lobby for being immoral: “I would
never, ever shop with them! I consider them just immoral and decrepit in six ways to Sunday.”
He explains that the company is anti -LGBT and was convicted of stealing historical artefacts
from Iraq: “I teach history, and it’s just the fact that they would be ripping off (...) relics from
people’s home countries (...) and lying about it, is just as terrible corporate behaviour as you
could possibly imagine!”

101
The last psychopathic relationship is related to bullies/bullied. In this type of
relationship, the brand bullies consumers, is neglective, or creates an environment that lets
inappropriate behaviour happen, as in the case of sexism, racism, ageism, or any derogatory
conduct. Jane used to play League of Legends, but she no longer does. She dislikes how the
game is toxic for women, as a lot of men play it, harassing them: “People will make fun of you,
saying things like, ‘Oh, it had to be a woman, go wash the dishes!’, you know? So, sometimes
there are these really annoying extremes.” Similarly, Barbara suffered prejudice and sexism for
being a woman playing games, sometimes using a male username or muting gamers to deal
with the stress: “[Fortnite] i s not very accessible for girls to play with . There are a lot of
perverted men there.” She also stressed that if a player did not perform well in a match, some
users would bully them, without any reaction from the game developer: “ That doesn't provide
a good experience; it becomes really toxic, you know? It makes playing Fortnite, or any other
online game, a really bad experience.”
Machiavellian consumer-brand relationships. Machiavellian brands deceive consumers
by manipulation and exploitation, promising something and not delivering. Brands are seen as
crooks who build trust, but ultimately trick them and make them feel like suckers. Hugo bought
a cleaning robot from a brand called Neato, which worked fine. At some point, Vorwerk bought
the brand and promised to maintain the infrastructure to keep the robot working, since it
depended on cloud servers. However, Hugo was one day warned by the company that it would
no longer support the product. He felt frustrated and deceived by the lack of care:
I was livid! I mean, I had a working robot vacuum that I used at least five times a
week, and now I can’t use it anymore. It’s basically useless! (...) So, from one
moment to another, they turned a functioning robot vacuum into a pile of garbage.
And I can’t do anything about it, and they’re not compensating me. So, yeah, I’m
furious! [laughs] (Hugo)
Sometimes brands are not directly or necessarily deceiving consumers, but exploiting
them in host/parasite relationships. Alexander was a loyal user of Adobe products for years,
since he depended on them for graphic design. He is particularly annoyed by th e subscription
model, which he sees as a money grab, and has led him to stop buying Adobe’s products.
Alexander goes on to say that the company’s mindset is not beneficial for the consumers since
the prices are too high, and users depend on their products: “It’s geared towards professional
users who need it. And it’s almost like the mafia. These professional users have to use Adobe.
(...) So, it’s kind of, you know, like highway robbery in a sense.”

102
On the other hand, another parasitic relationship concerns Airbnb, as Claire explains
how the brand exploits the city where she lives, driving up rents and house prices, and gradually
replacing local shops and culture with an infrastructure to serve tourists. Airbnb behaves like a
parasite, taking advantage of its host and changing the city for the worse, which might even kill
it:
I do think it is parasitic. (...) So, whenever those people, the culture bearers of the
area, the reason why people come here, can’t afford to live here, then the city’s going
to die. Then, I think at a certain point, people won’t want to come here if it’s just a
bunch of half -empty houses being rented as Airbnbs. It won’t be interesting
anymore. So, I could see it even killing the culture of a place. (Claire)
Machiavellian brands also resort to asymmetrical power, such as in relationships
between dealers and addicts. Three distinct negative aspects of Instagram illustrate this type of
relationship. Barbara reports the first one, calling attention to how people are not themselves
on the platform, only praising their qualities, especially influencers: “ It's very bad when
someone uses the platform to do evil, to show off a life they don't have. ” She used to spend
eight hours per day on Instagram and felt an abstinence crisis after deciding to stop using it.
A second harmful aspect concerns social comparisons and a sense of group. Ann felt
bad using Instagram because she compared herself with slimmer girls who went to the gym and
had beautiful bodies. After leaving the platform, she was surprised that her friends did not look
for her, as if they had a fake bond: “ So, the impression I get is ... after I left social media, I'm
dead. I'm dead! I don't feel like I have any real friends, like, that I can count on, you know?”
The third negative aspect concerns consumerism. Jane was addicted to Instagram,
spending a lot of money on things she did not need. She tried to avoid ads, but the app continued
to bombard her with them, as a dealer filling her with drugs: “I kept saying I didn’t want to see
it anymore, but then another one would come along. (...) No matter how many ads you don ’t
wanna see, they’ll put one back in its place.” Reflecting on how social media works, Zoe sums
up the relationship with them: “Not feel like I’m forced, like I have to keep looking. And I can
turn it off when I want to. It’s like somebody stopped giving me cocaine. It’s really nice
[laughs].”
The last Machiavellian relationship regards how consumers feel spied on by brands, as
if they were targets. Wilson works with IT and, because of that, he knows how technology
companies have been making their products worse over the years, calling it enshittification, a

103
recurring theme among most informants and Reddit users. He is worried about brands spying
on what he does, as he comments about Microsoft: “This is my computer, I want to use it, and
I don’t want you and your over 3000 partners to know what I’m doing on my computer.” Wilson
complains that Google is forcing users to provide their real names and IDs to develop
applications. He also affirms that Apple listens to conversations even when told not to: “ They
also sell your data. They also collect a lot of your data. I could pull up my pie hole statistics
right now and see that every 15 minutes , my wife’s MacBook is sending a ping to Apple’s
servers.”
Tim also dislikes how brands gather data that they were not supposed to store,
explaining that Google had information that he lived in a rented apartment based on his search
history: “That’s when things start to get scary when you don’t explicitly provide them, because
it gives them a lot of power over how they present the information or (...) how they want you
to act online and as a consumer. ” Cecil shares the same level of worry about technology
companies spying on consumers and getting annoyed by ads tha t stalk him across the internet.
However, he sees it more as spying rather than stalking: “ It’s espionage, definitely, because
they are taking data about you without your consent and without your knowledge.”

Confronting brands. Some informants dealt with the stress of flawed consumer -brand
relationships by planning actions to address the problem or by expressing their emotions. Layla
is disappointed with Tim Hortons for lowering their service quality over the years and losing
their Canadian tradition, eventually being sold to an international group. She coped with the
situation by boycotting the brand, which is also true for other brands sold to American
corporations: “I’ve always, in my whole life of being , boycotting America [ laughs]. (...) So,
yeah, of course it bothers me to see that slowly but surely other companies , basically, be
swallowed up by American ones.”
Another confrontational strategy is when consumers vent their rage against brands to
make it even with them. Even after 10 years of a bad experience with Eir, a telecommunications
provider in Ireland, Aaron does not get tired of complaining and spreading n egative word-of-
mouth, which was his main motivation to participate in the interview: “Any opportunity I have
to talk about Eir, I’ll convince people to stay away from them. They’re just brutal! They’re
really, really bad. ” When participants expressed hatr ed, it reverberated in their behaviour, as
Xavier avoids being near Fiat cars and warns everyone about them: “ I don’t like seeing them,
and I avoid stopping near them. (...) I even have a friend who (...) wants to buy a Fiat Doblò.
So I tell him not to, because it will ruin his life.”
In some situations, participants had to file formal complaints to solve their problems or
even go to court. That happened to Damian, who had his flight cancelled by American Airlines

105
and was left without accommodation or meals, leading him to file a complaint against the
company. Another type of reaction regards how consumers creatively resort to subversive
actions to cope with a bad experience. Martin does not approve of how Disney is using AI in
their productions and decided to boycott its newer movies, but still consumed the old content.
However, Martin decided to be subversive: “I would gladly pirate their content to avoid giving
them money because I don’t like what they’re doing now.” Similarly, Oliver cancelled Netflix
after realising that the third Twin Peaks season was not available and decided not to trust the
streaming services anymore, resorting to piracy as well.
Distancing from brands . Another way that consumers cope with flawed relationships
with brands is by avoiding, quitting, or fleeing them. Cecil avoids Trago Mills, a British retailer,
since the company does not care about the environment. Also, the CEO was involved in
controversies and discriminatory behaviours: “(...) he’s an extremely homophobic man who
advocated for gay men to be chemically castrated immediately, which isn’t really a good look
for a large company [laughs]. ” With the same rationale, Alexan der explains that he avoids
companies for their lack of moral values, such as Nestlé and, particularly, Japan Tobacco:
They know they’re harming society, and they do it anyway. I was going to work with
Japan Tobacco at one point. They wanted me to be an account manager for their
consumer research projects. And they wanted me to figure out a way to get smokers
not to quit. (...) “They’re already smoking. Why quit? And let’s find out what we can
say to them, so they don’t quit”. And I quit that job. I quit that company, the company
I was working for. “No, I’m not going to do that”, and I just left. (Alexander)
The way companies operate and their philosophy also prompt participants to avoid them,
as Raymond and Louise noted that Hewlett -Packard forces consumers to subscribe to its
services while delivering a poor experience. Louise once trusted the brand but chan ged her
mind: “(...) your printer doesn’t function right if you don’t sign up for their subscription has
completely changed the way I feel about them . (...) I will avoid that brand because of that. ”
Raymond has a similar understanding, which stopped him fr om using his HP printer: “ They
were trying to get me to buy a subscription for printer ink. The moment it was plugged in! (...)
That feels rather predatory in ways.”
Reframing the brand relationship. Not only do consumers confront brands and distance
themselves from them, but they also re -evaluate their appraisal of the relationship. Some
participants rationalised their choices, understanding that they were the best available option.

106
Although disliking American brands, Layla still shops at Walmart: “They’re cheaper. I hate the
fact that they’re Walmart and they’re American. But what can you do? ” In the same sense,
Sophia explains she grew up with fast-fashion retailers like Zara and is familiarised with them,
but avoids Shein: “They’re both bad, but Shein is like ten times worse.”
Another strategy to reframe how the brand is perceived is to cultivate a positive mindset.
Zachary commented on the way Chick -fil-A, an American restaurant chain, supported causes
he disagreed with. However, he reformulates his thinking to justify going there: “(...) they offer
amazing customer service. And they’re locally managed , and locally they’re franchises. (...)
And, you know, they get back to the community and all that. ” Maya also minimises the fact
that Chick-fil-A corporation was accused of being anti-LGBT: “(...) we finally, you know, have
a Chick-fil-A where I live here, and I go , I would say about half the employees are clearly
LGBT. So, it’s like what their corporate says and what they do seems quite different.”
Accommodating to the brand experience . The last coping strategy concerns how
consumers resign themselves and accept the flawed relationship with the brand. Even though
having negative feelings towards Google, Louise keeps using it because the research results are
good, conforming to the situa tion: “And I think that that’s part of the conversation , that how
difficult will it be to make a switch or find an equal alternative over just accepting something
that’s an annoyance .” Sometimes, the product can be irre sistible, despite the bad brand
reputation. Zoe thinks Nestlé is an evil company, but makes an exception: “ But do I still buy?
Did I buy a chocolate chip cookie, Nestlé cookies , literally this morning? Yes, they’re in my
fridge. (...) But I really want a cookie, though [laughs].”
There are also situations in which the consumer feels helpless, unable to confront the
situation. Several informants reported that they could not do anything other than accept having
a relationship with a particular brand. This situation is common for public concessions, such as
water, energy, and gas. Xavier commented that the water company in his area is not trustworthy,
as it fails to keep a steady water supply, but conforms to the situation: “ It’s like you’ve been
forced only to have this option your whole life, you know? You never expected another
alternative. So, I think it’s a conditioning to accept it.” It is an unescapable harsh reality to be
forced to buy from some companies, as Aaron points out: “ It’s just the price of electricity and
gas has gone very expensive. But everyone has to pay. So, what can you really do?”
Although consumers tolerate a bad brand relationship, that does not mean they are happy
with it. In some cases, they yearn for what the brands used to be. Louise dislikes how Chips

107
Ahoy tastes today to the point of giving up on it: “I used to love Chips Ahoy, and now we buy
them, and we don’t even finish the package because they’re just like, ‘Nah!’”. However, she
still got excited about a new co-branded packaging with Stranger Things, reminding her of her
childhood in the 80s. Ellie also feels nostalgic about Fiat, which reminds her of her young years
living in Italy. Nevertheless, she is mad about the corporate fusion with Chrysler, but it did not
prevent her from buying a Fiat car: “I felt sad. (...) But I will tell you, I did buy a used Fiat
Cinquecento. Used. It was five years old, stick shift. I missed Italy! [laughs].”
4.5 Discussion
This research reveals how flawed consumer-brand relationships are triggered, appraised,
developed, and coped with. We extend knowledge of a growing body of studies on negative
aspects towards brands, including brand hate, betrayal, avoidance, sabotage, and divorce
(Ferraz & Dallabrida, 2024; Kähr et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2009; Weitzl & Hutzinger, 2025;
Zarantonello et al., 2016) . Our research answers a call to investigate new brand relationship
types, define triggers, and explore the interactions and outcomes of these relationships (Alvarez
et al., 2023).
Since the initial work by Fournier (1998), whose primary focus was on positive
consumer-brand relationships, few studies have proposed frameworks to organise and explain
negative consumer-brand relationships. We expand on prior literature that proposed typologies
and theoretical models directed to brand contestation (Dietrich & Russell, 2021) , consumer
subversion (Wilson et al., 2022), and brand sabotage (Kähr et al., 2016). Our research also has
implications for negative brand personality (Malär & Giuffredi -Kähr, 2024), showing how it
interacts with emotions, behaviours, and coping mechanisms.
We make three interconnected contributions to literature. First, a framework is
introduced to explain the flawed consumer -brand relationships and their connection to stimuli
and coping mechanisms. Second, we discuss that dark brand personalities, appraisals of events,
relationships, emotions, coping strategies, and behaviours are interrelated and
multidimensional. Third, we build on the fragmented literature on brand hate to examine how
negative brand-related constructs relate to emotions and coping mechani sms. We detail these
contributions next.

108
4.5.1 Development of flawed consumer-brand relationships
Flawed consumer-brand relationships are developed through a series of processes and
interactions, as shown in Figure 4.1. Consumers face negative experiences triggered by the dark
brand personality traits (Malär & Giuffredi-Kähr, 2024). Their emotions will be influenced by
appraising the events along five dimensions (Roseman et al., 1990) . Motivation refers to
seeking awards or avoiding punishments, while the situation determines whether they are
present. Probability concerns whether the event is certain or uncertain, and legitimacy regards
whether a positive or negative outcome is deserved. Finally, the agency determines if the event
was caused by the self, the other, or the circumstances.
Figure 4.1 - Flawed consumer-brand relationships.

Source: author’s own work.
After appraising the negative events, consumers interact with the brands, eliciting
emotions and developing flawed relationships (Table 4.3). The emotions are combined with
coping mechanisms and behaviours (Table 4.5), leading to confrontation, accommodati on,
distancing, or reframing. The proposed framework organises and explains how diverse, flawed
consumer-brand relationships are structured, developed, nurtured, and handled. Different from
other models that focused on contestation, which refers to a chang e in brand meaning by
consumers (Dietrich & Russell, 2021), or on sabotage and how consumers aggressively attack
brands (Kähr et al., 2016), our framework is more comprehensive to encompass a diverse range
of negative reactions, relationships, and coping strategies. The identified negative consumer -

109
brand relationships surface more complex and nuanced experiences, not limited to anger or
meaning hijacking.
We also contribute to the scarce research on negative brand personality (Saeed et al.,
2022) by expanding the dark personality traits identified by previous research (Malär &
Giuffredi-Kähr, 2024). Our research illustrates how the dark traits, relationships, emotions, and
coping mechanisms interrelate, as consumers struggle to handle psychopathic, Machiavellian,
and narcissistic brands. Dark personality traits influence how consumers interact with brands,
with implications for consumer -brand relationship theory and customer relationship
management.
4.5.2 Multidimensional flawed relationships
Although we present a framework that could be seen as a linear movement from stimuli
to reactions, our research revealed that consumers are affected by dysfunctional relationships
not necessarily in a linear order. They might be coping with negative experi ences for years,
unable to get rid of the brand, or they could gradually divorce from a brand relationship. Rather
than defining a monolithic phenomenon, we draw on rock music, specifically Pink Floyd’s The
Dark Side of the Moon, for a metaphor. Figure 4.2 shows that when negative events pass
through a prism (The Dark Side of Brand Use), like white light, their composition can be seen.
Figure 4.3 draws on another metaphor to illustrate how the brand’s negative event can
be broken down. In a Rubik’s Cube, there are multiple combinations of colours, as the player
can rotate it upwards, downwards, and sideways. In the same vein, negative ex periences with
brands are multidimensional, comprising dark brand personality traits, appraisal of events,
emotions, relationships, coping mechanisms, and behaviours. These dimensions can take on an
infinite number of combinations depending on the consumer ’s experience, forming a flawed
relationship cube.

Figure 4.4 illustrates how one possible combination could be formed. Ticketmaster’s

that only Ticketmaster sold, as in a domestic abuse relationship. The company’s website and
system crashed, preventing her from buying what she wanted, leading her to view the event as
certain and caused by the brand. S ophia cried a lot, feeling sad, and was very angry at

she went to the show because she could only accommodate the situation and conform to it. As

4.5.3 Going Beyond Brand Hate
Our research shows that life exists beyond brand hate. The fragmentation of the
literature (Yadav & Chakrabarti, 2022), multiple conceptualisations, a focus on psychological
rather than behavioural aspects (Aziz & Rahman, 2022), and the lack of a cohesive framework
(Ladeira et al., 2026) have turned brand hate into a fuzzy umbrella construct. Also, there are a
multitude of negative related constructs, such as brand shame (Weitzl & Hutzinger, 2025) ,
brand repulsion (Dessart & Cova, 2021), brand sabotage (Kähr et al., 2016) , brand avoidance
(Lee et al., 2009; Odoom et al., 2019), brand divorce (Ferraz & Dallabrida, 2024; Sussan et al.,
2012), and brand negativity (Dessart et al., 2020).
The proposed flawed consumer -brand relationship framework ( Figure 4. 1) helps
organise and integrate the different negative brand -related constructs. They can also be
combined with emotions and coping mechanisms ( Table 4.5). These combinations show that
negative experiences go beyond anger and fear, encompassing sadness and happiness as well
(Figure 4. 5). When sabotaging or expressing schadenfreude, for example, the consumer is
simultaneously angry and happy. On the other hand, it is possible to feel happy a nd sad if one
is addicted to a brand or yearns for an idealised past. In this sense, brand hate cannot account
for all negative consumer-brand emotions, relationships, and coping strategies and behaviours.
The multidimensionality of dysfunctional consumer-brand relationships shows that consumers
navigate a complex phenomenon far beyond mere hate.

112

4.5.4 Limitations and Future Research Directions
This research does not fully capture the complexity of negative consumer -brand
relationships. The limited interview sample and data from netnography and secondary sources
provide a partial understanding of how flawed relationships are triggered and developed. Future
research should further investigate how dysfunctional relationships can be theorised and
integrated with brand constructs, such as brand hate, shame, and sabotage. Our framework is
an initial step towards a theory of negative consumer-brand relationships, which should also be
compared and contrasted with the brand relationship quality framework from past research
(Fournier, 1998) . Future studies could empirically test our model to determine whether the
proposed appraisals, emotions, coping strategies, and behaviours align with theoretical
expectations.
We encourage future investigations to increase our understanding of negative consumer-
brand relationships. The identified types in this research are not exhaustive, as more nuanced
and distinct ones might emerge from other research. There is a need to deve lop the brand
relationship spectrum further and clarify its boundaries (Alvarez et al., 2023) , as well as to
compare negative and positive relationships. The development and the trajectories of flawed
consumer-brand relationships also deserve more attention. Future studies could investigate how
they start, grow, develop, and end over time, compari ng the trajectories of different
dysfunctional brand-consumer relationships.

113
CHAPTER 5 – CONCLUSION

The objective of this doctoral thesis was to investigate idiosyncratic consumer -brand
relationships, understanding and identifying the peculiar positive and negative bonds derived
from them. Although prior research examined a diverse range of relationships, they were
concentrated in a few, such as brand love and friendship (Alvarez et al., 2023) or brand hate
and avoidance (Mushtaq et al., 2024; Yadav & Chakrabarti, 2022) . Chapter 2 explored the
positive consumer -brand relationships, epitomised by brand tattoos, while Chapter 3
investigated polarised brands, explaining the different motivations regarding love and hate
feelings. Finally, Chapter 4 discussed the flawed relationships consumers have with brands ,
focusing on negative brand experiences.
5.1 Theoretical contributions
Our research has three key contributions to the consumer-brand relationship theory.
First, we have identified 34 new or less theorised idiosyncratic relationships, evaluated as
positive (13), negative (14), ambiguous (4), or neutral (3). The identification of these
relationships responds to a call to investigate other types that have not been previously studied
(Alvarez et al., 2023). Table 5.1 summarises all relationships identified in this work.

Vintage Mates.

Host/Parasite, Moral Enemies, Spies/Targets, and Traitors/Betrayed.

The identified relationships show that consumers have complex interactions with the
brands they love and hate , which can bring intense positive emotions and benefits, as in a
therapist-patient bond, but can also be dysfunctional and stressful, as in a criminal -victim
relationship. Other relationship types lie in the middle , such as in a guilty pleasure one,
revealing ambiguous bonds that can be simultaneously beneficial and detrimental.

114
Second, our work revealed that consumers have dynamic , polysemic, and multiple
relationships with the same brands. They use brands to develop identity projects (Arnould &
Thompson, 2005), seeking a desired, s table self in a fragmented world (Appau et al., 2020) .
The connection with brands is evaluated based on consumer values and the implicit brand
promise (Bhargava & Bedi, 2022), thereby unearthing strong feelings towards them .
Consumers build their individual and social selves through intricate, complex, and idiosyncratic
relationships with brands, tattooing them (Chapter 2), developing polarised feelings (Chapter
3), or coping with negative experiences (Chapter 4).
Third, this doctoral thesis extends consumer-brand relationship theory by investigating
the dark side of brand use. Our research shows that negative brand personalities (Malär &
Giuffredi-Kähr, 2024; Saeed et al., 2022) foster broken relationshi ps, which consumers cope
with through accommodation, distancing, confrontation, or reframing. While previous research
focused primarily on brand hate as an umbrella construct, this work pursu ed a broader
investigation of negative emotions and behaviours. The proposed framework helps explain how
dysfunctional relationships are nurtured, developed, understood, and confronted.
5.2 Managerial implications
The first key implication of our research for marketing and branding managers concerns
the identification of several consumer -brand relationships. Understanding them enables
addressing consumers as idiosyncratic individuals rather than a monolith. They develop strong,
deep relationships based on emotions and experiences. Managers need to identify these
relationships, quantify them, manage their implications, and propose marketing strategies to
enhance their positive aspects while minimising their negative ones. Promotional activities can
be tailored to each relationship, enhancing the bond with the company’s brands. For example,
a vintage-mates relationship can be nurtured through the launch of nostalgic products, while
teammate-based relationship s can reinforce the idea that the brand is a vehicle for the
consumer’s success.
Given that consumer-brand relationships are dynamic and multifaceted, this should be
considered a point of attention for brand managers. Practitioners cannot consider that their
brands foster only one type of relationship. If multiple relationships occur simultaneously, it is
crucial to investigate how they interact and impact the brand’s development. It is also important
to understand whether a particular product or service fosters one type of positive relationship,
while another might trigger a negative one. For instance, a soulmate relationship is beneficial

115
to the brand, but it can also lead to addiction, which would need to be addressed by a responsible
policy from the company. Thus, there is no “one size fits all” strategy regarding consumer -
brand relationships.
The dark side of brand use demands a reflection from managers and companies.
Practitioners need to revisit how their brands interact with consumers and investigate whether
they exhibit negative brand personality traits. A change in approach is needed to address the
negative aspects , minimising or su ppressing them. Bad experiences deeply affect how
consumers buy and express their feelings, shaping how the brand performs not only in the
present but also in the long run. Even minor mistakes can haunt the brand for many years ,
condemning it to damnation. Apart from that, brand managers need to understand that even
iconic brands are not unanimous, sparking strong reactions from detractors, who consider them
anti-iconic. The management of these brands thus has to consider palliative measures to address
anti-brand activists.
5.3 Research limitations and future research opportunities
This work has some limitations that need to be disclosed. The relationships identified,
either positive, negative, ambiguous, or neutral, are pieces of a greater puzzle. Our research
does not fully capture the interrelations between them and brands. There is a need for further
development of a general theory of consumer-brand relationships that accounts for the myriad
of beneficial and dysfunctional bonds. We encourage scholars to d elve into current research
and propose innovative approaches to understanding how consumers build relationships with
brands and to discover other relationship types . As we have argued that the relationships are
multiple, complex, and polysemic, future studies need to take that into account for proposing
new theoretical perspectives. Our proposal for a flawed consumer -brand relationship
framework is a preliminary , modest step towards this end, but it focuses sole ly on negative
experiences.
Although our research unearthed new consumer-brand relationships, it was focused on
idiosyncratic ones, which can be restricted to specific groups. Future studies need to investigate
further their frequency and deepen their understanding across other brands, sectors, and
companies. In this sense, this work relied only on qualitative methodology, prioritising a
phenomenological approach. Our narrow methodological choice needs to be complemented
with other qualitative and quantitative methods. Other epistemological views would diversify
how consumer-brand relationships are understood and theorised.

116
5.4 Social Implications
The research conducted in this PhD thesis has several social implications that could be
subject to future public policies. Findings from the three studies show that consumers nurture
intense relationships with brands, which are not always beneficial. They reported addictive
behaviours towards brands that have implications for mental and physical health. For example,
some ingested high doses of sugar while others spent hours consuming digital technology. Also,
there were alarming accounts about bullying and sexist behaviours while consuming brands .
Public policies and regulations should be proposed to control and lower the exposure of
individuals to addicti ve behaviours and to punish brands for allowing bullying and
discriminatory episodes while using their services.
Another social implication regards consumer rights protection. Our informants brought
innumerable examples of flawed consumer-brand relationships that were triggered by negative
brand personalities. There were reports of mistreatment, manipulation, misleading advertising,
monopolistic enforcement, deceptive promotions, and many others. Governments could
propose regulatory measures to strengthen consumer rights protection, thereby disincentivising
predatory company behaviour and the development of negative brand personalities.
Finally, our work also has implications for environmental and social policies.
Participants reported a strong aversion to brands that polluted, mistreated workers, disregarded
unions, took advantage of universal public goods (such as water), tested products on animals,
failed to protect minorities, or backed countries that started wars. Government bodies could
rethink public policies to increase companies’ responsibility towards the United Nations’
Sustainable Development Goals (e.g., responsible production and consumption and good health
and well-being), thereby diminishing the corporate impact reported by our informants.
